events.title: U.S. East Asian envoy says investors are overpricing Taiwan risk
events.summary: Investors are overestimating the risk of conflict across the Taiwan Strait, according to Michael DeSombre, U.S. assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs. Beijing has sought to increasingly solidify its military presence near the island, with reports revealing an unprecedented sighting of a military vessel off the coast. SINGAPORE – Investors are overestimating the risk of conflict across the Taiwan Strait, a top U.S. East Asian diplomat said, stressing that deterrence and "substantial consequences" would keep Beijing from taking the island by 2027. While the U.S. government has often indicated Beijing's directive for the People's Liberation Army to be ready for military action in Taiwan by 2027, Beijing has never publicly confirmed the timeline. "I actually think the most mispricing is with regard to Taiwan, where actually I think people are overpricing the risk of something happening across the Taiwan Strait," said Michael DeSombre, assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, told CNBC on Thursday. "Both China and the U.S. don't want conflict, and we're able to deter conflict," he told CNBC's Sri Jegarajah in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the Milken Institute Asia Summit. "Concerns of that perhaps are priced at too high a level." Beijing claims Taiwan as its territory and hasn't ruled out force to bring it under its control. The democratically governed island's government rejects Beijing's claims. China has also sought to push Washington for a change in its longstanding diplomatic stance on the island to formally "oppose" Taiwan independence. However, the summit last month between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping did not yield any public agreement on Taiwan. The U.S. President has held back approval of a new package of arms sales to Taipei worth $14 billion after an earlier package of $11 billion in arms sales to Taiwan had drawn a sharp response from Beijing in December. Days after the leaders' summit, Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung visited Arizona for the opening ​of a new de facto consulate in ‌Phoenix. Beijing has sought to increasingly solidify its military presence near the island in recent months. A Chinese military boat was spotted along with two vessels off Taiwan's Pacific coast for the first time in August, Reuters reported, citing a surveillance report. It has also been courting Taiwan's opposition party, the Kuomintang, since last year to pull the island into its orbit as it prepares for the presidential election in 2028. Asked whether plans to "reunify Taiwan" by 2027 were a cause for concern, DeSombre said that Xi is "a very rational actor ... To the extent that he realizes that it can't be done, or it can't be done without substantial consequences, it won't happen." DeSombre played up the importance of keeping deterrence credible. "That's why it's important … ensuring that we have the deterrence in place with our allies and partners to make sure it does not happen." Taiwan is the world's leading ​manufacturer of cutting-edge computer chips and TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, has invested tens of billions of dollars in facilities in Phoenix. The projects have received ​significant U.S. subsidies as Washington seeks to revive domestic semiconductor manufacturing.

events.title: Judge seems poised to reinforce block of Trump's White House media ban
events.summary: President Donald Trump speaks to the news media, including CNN news anchor Kaitlin Collins. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images A federal judge appeared inclined to extend his block on Trump's ban on three media outlets from the White House. The judge said on Thursday that one of the administration's arguments is contradicted by the president's own words. "That's an uphill climb," the judge said of the DOJ's effort to defend the ban on national security grounds. A federal judge appeared inclined to extend his block on President Donald Trump's ban on three media outlets from the White House. The administration's argument that the ban was based on national security concerns is contradicted by the president's own words, US District Judge Timothy Kelly said during a hearing Thursday. "That's an uphill climb," Kelly said of the Justice Department's effort to defend the ban on national security grounds, noting Trump's claim that his ban was based on his disapproval of the outlets' coverage. Kelly is weighing whether to grant a lengthier block of Trump's move to ban POLITICO, CNN, and MS NOW from the White House. The Trump-appointed judge already lifted the ban last month, issuing a two-week restraining order , which he extended through Tuesday, that enabled the three organizations to regain access to the West Wing. But he now appears to be leaning toward a more durable injunction that would maintain the outlets' access during what could be months of litigation. Kelly's original ruling found that the ban likely violated the news outlets' due process rights, since the White House restricted access without any notice and without setting out any identifiable standards for news organizations to follow to maintain their credentials. "That's probably the biggest hurdle you all have," Kelly told the government during a hearing that drew a swath of media executives, reporters and First Amendment attorneys to the federal courthouse in Washington, D.C., leading Kelly to remark on the vastly outnumbered Justice Department attorney assigned to the case. In what has been a recurring theme in court battles across the country, Kelly pointed out that Trump's own comments — declaring repeatedly in interviews and on social media that he banned the outlets for writing "negative" stories about him — conflicted with the Justice Department's later efforts to claim the ban was a response to the outlets' publication of sensitive national security information. A lawyer for the news organizations, Theodore Boutrous Jr., urged Kelly to reject Trump's ban for a second reason: a violation of news organizations' First Amendment rights and an effort to chill the free press. Boutrous argued that a recent interview Trump gave to Time magazine "amounts to a confession" from the president that he revoked the journalists' press passes because he considered their stories to be too negative. "That interview really is the coup de grace," Boutrous said. He also pointed to a recent comment from Attorney General Todd Blanche that Trump banned the outlets from the White House due to their "one-sided reporting." Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik argued that the Trump administration had, in fact, provided due process to the news outlets — after Trump's ban went into effect. He cited unsigned letters from the White House press office delivered in the days after the lawsuit was filed, identifying a handful of stories the administration viewed as "misinformation" or "national security" risks. Velchik argued that the outlets "defaulted" by failing to respond to those letters. He also repeatedly attributed the letters to Trump himself, even though they were unsigned and Trump never referred to them publicly. Boutrous, calling this after-the-fact effort a "sham process," underscored the absence of any indication Trump had signed off on — or even had any awareness of — the letters. Velchik also repeatedly argued that the courts should give the president more leeway than might apply in other contexts, where decisions about reporters' access are made by federal agencies. "The White House is a sacred place," Velchik said. Kelly asked whether the president could ban a news organization from the White House based on stories that were demonstrably false. Boutrous said no, while Velchik articulated a more malleable standard. "From our perspective, it's within the discretion of the president," Velchik said. Kelly emphasized that his assessment of the issue was constrained by longstanding precedents that forbid the White House from barring access to the West Wing press areas based on disagreements with content, along with requirements that revoking such access must be based on clear standards and potential consequences spelled out in advance. The Justice Department has said it disagrees with those decisions, but the judge made clear he is bound to follow them. events.title: Breaking: Hollard insurance fined $2m for handling of claim that destroyed home
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Insurance giant Hollard fined $2m after claim delays leave house uninhabitable The Federal Court has ordered Hollard insurance to pay $2 million. ( Supplied ) Insurance giant Hollard has been fined $2 million for taking so long to process a home insurance claim that a house in regional Victoria became uninhabitable. The corporate watchdog ASIC sued Hollard in April last year, alleging the insurer "breached its duty of utmost good faith" in its handling of a claim made by a couple in October 2021, two days after a storm damaged their roof. The Federal Court ordered Hollard to pay $2 million for failing to promptly assess the damage, delaying rectification work and for failing to properly protect the property from further damage. It was also found to have taken too long to find temporary accommodation for the couple, failed to consider expert reports, and not clearly communicate with the couple throughout the claims process. Hollard has also been ordered to pay ASIC's legal costs. ASIC says delays caused unnecessary and prolonged harm Hollard is a privately owned insurance company and one of the largest in Australia, underwriting insurance for motor, home, contents, bicycle, pet, and business products. It is the company behind brands including CBA's insurance product, Everyday Insurance, Real Insurance, Australian Seniors and Steadfast. In 2024, the company had an estimated annual revenue of about $2.3 billion. Hollard initially accepted the couples' claim, before repeatedly delaying inspections, reports and repair work, only to then reject the claim in April 2023. ASIC said the rejection was based on a non-expert opinion, despite prior expert reports outlining the damage. ASIC alleged the combination of delays in decision-making, poor communication and ignoring expert advice exposed the couple to unnecessary and prolonged harm. Sarah Court says Hollard's delays mean the home in regional Victoria needs to be demolished. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) This conduct, according to ASIC, breached Hollard’s duty of good faith in handling the claim, as implied by the Insurance Contracts Act. "In the end, because of the excessive delays by Hollard and the failure to undertake make-safe works, the home has become so riddled with moisture, mould and decay that it is uninhabitable and now needs to be demolished and rebuilt," ASIC chair Sarah Court said in a statement last year. ASIC says decision sends clear message Once Hollard denied the claim, the couple lodged a complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), which determined the storm caused structural damage to the roof. Hollard had an estimated annual revenue of about $2.3 billion in 2024. ( Supplied ) Hollard then agreed to pay the couple a cash settlement of more than $1.5 million for the total loss of the building, as well as temporary accommodation. ASIC sued Hollard after the cash settlement. The penalty Hollard has been ordered to pay goes to the Commonwealth of Australia, to be paid within 28 days. This is the first time the corporate watchdog has sued an insurance company over an individual claim. Ms Court said other insurance companies needed to take note. Hollard has been approached for comment.

events.title: Protests, debate follow death of Maricarmen, 87, Spain protest symbol
events.summary: Thousands of protestors honor Maricarmen Abascal’s life, while tributes within parliament spark debate. Thousands of Spaniards protested outside Spain’s parliament after the death of Maria del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction ignited nationwide protests and sparked a snap general election . Meanwhile, tributes to Abascal were debated within the legislature as lawmakers accused each other of exploiting the case ahead of the election. list 1 of 3 Photos: Protests erupt after 87-year-old evicted woman dies in Madrid list 2 of 3 Maricarmen dies at 87 after eviction sparked Spain housing protests list 3 of 3 Spain’s Sanchez announces snap election amid pressure over housing crisis Maricarmen Abascal died on Wednesday after being hospitalised for severe anxiety and exhaustion since her eviction on a stretcher from her Madrid home on September 23. While in the hospital, she reached a deal to return to her home but died before she could return. No cause of death has been announced. “They killed her through heartbreak,” Diana, a demonstrator, told Al Jazeera. “Taking an 87-year-old woman out of her home after she had lived in the same house for 70 years, that is killing someone.” Diana joined thousands of protesters outside Spain’s parliament. Outside Abascal’s building, mourners left flowers, candles, handwritten notes and children’s drawings. “They’re not deaths; they’re murders,” protesters chanted as they walked from a protest camp in the central Puerta del Sol square to Abascal’s former home on Thursday. Protests over home shortages and surging rents following her eviction prompted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap general election for November 29 after parliament failed to pass emergency housing measures. Tributes to Abascal in the Madrid region’s legislature caused arguments as lawmakers accused each other of exploiting the case ahead of the election. Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the conservative opposition People’s Party (PP), accused Sanchez and the Socialists of trying to exploit the housing crisis for political gain ahead of the election. “We will not allow this attempt to manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people; all of this has happened during their eight years in government. It won’t fly,” Feijoo said. The PP, which holds absolute majorities in the Madrid regional and local assemblies, refused to observe a minute of silence in her honour. Instead, hard-left deputies staged one outside City Hall and gave Abascal a 60-second standing ovation during a tense debate in the regional assembly, while PP lawmakers remained seated with folded arms. Left-leaning parties criticised conservatives for rejecting legislation in parliament aimed at curbing soaring rental prices. A survey carried out in June and published by state pollster CIS on Thursday found that 76.3 percent of Spaniards supported intervention in the market to guarantee access to housing, while 79 percent believed the right to housing should take precedence over treating homes as a market commodity. Ombudsman Angel Gabilondo said addressing the housing crisis would require greater commitment from all levels of government. He said his office was preparing a housing report and reiterated proposals to expand public housing, restrict tourist rentals, increase rent assistance and strengthen protections against evictions for vulnerable households.

events.title: Nvidia-backed Firmus shelves IPO, eyes private funding
events.summary: Firmus will withdraw its application to list on the Australian Securities Exchange, according to a statement on Oct 9. - Firmus Grid has withdrawn its Australian Securities Exchange IPO after market volatility made the offer unattractive, and it will now seek private funding. - The Nvidia-backed data centre firm had aimed to raise up to US$5.5 billion and a A$43.7 billion valuation, but investors worried about pricing and share overhang. - Firmus, founded in 2019, is expanding AI data centre projects in Australia, Singapore and Batam, with support from Nvidia, Blackstone and other investors. Australian data centre company Firmus Grid has shelved its initial public offering plan and will consider other funding options. Firmus will withdraw its application to list on the Australian Securities Exchange, according to a statement on Oct 9 . “Having considered recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions, the board determined that the terms on which the offer could proceed would not appropriately reflect the strength of the company’s business and long-term growth outlook,” it said. “Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options.” Bloomberg News earlier reported the company was set to postpone listing plans and was instead weighing a private funding round, according to people familiar with the matter. The Nvidia-backed company is in talks with existing investors and others for a private funding round, according to people familiar, asking not to be identified as the information is not public. Order-taking for the IPO closed as scheduled on the morning of Oct 8, yet there was no clear indication of the price or deal structure, Bloomberg News reported earlier. Firmus was looking to raise as much as US$5.5 billion (S$7 billion), including a greenshoe option, at a price that would have implied a valuation of A$43.7 billion (S$38.9 billion). Some potential investors turned more cautious as the deal progressed, voicing concern over existing shareholders potentially flooding the market soon after the company’s debut, people familiar with the matter have said. The overhang added to questions over what some investors see as an aggressive pricing strategy, they said. “I’ve never seen an IPO so polarising,” Jun Bei Liu, co-founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap Investment, said on Bloomberg TV. “There was a lot of international investor interest, however, when it comes to the crunch, the demand seems like it isn’t there when they were asked to put up the capital that’s required.” Firmus began as a Bitcoin mining operation in Australia in 2019 and has benefited from surging demand for AI infrastructure across Asia, with a pipeline of data centre projects in Australia and Singapore. Proceeds from the listing would have funded purchases of graphics processing units for its first data centre project in Batam, Indonesia, being developed with DayOne Data Centers, as part of an eight-year partnership with Nvidia. Singapore-headquartered DayOne has filed for a US IPO and is seeking to raise as much as US$5 billion, people familiar with the matter have said. Firmus has inked a number of large deals, securing US$2 billion in commitments from investors including Nvidia and Blackstone. Other existing shareholders include Jane Street, while Firmus also raised US$505 million in a Coatue Management-led funding round in April. Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase & Co, Morgan Stanley and Morgans Financial. are acting as joint lead managers on the listing. Bloomberg

events.title: Nvidia-backed Aussie AI firm Firmus withdraws historic IPO, citing market volatility
events.summary: The company said the proposed offering terms did not adequately reflect its business strength and long-term growth outlook, and it will instead pursue private funding options. Firmus had reportedly sought to raise $5 billion through the IPO, which would have valued the company at about $30.6 billion, nearly triple its valuation in August. Australian AI data center operator Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia , has withdrawn its planned mega initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, the company said in an emailed statement to CNBC. Firmus said its board determined that the terms of the proposed offering did not adequately reflect the strength of its business and long-term growth outlook. "The board therefore concluded that proceeding with the offer was not in the best interests of the company and its shareholders," Firmus said in a statement. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options," it added. Firmus had reportedly planned to raise $5 billion in its IPO, pricing shares at A$11 apiece, which woul have made it the second-largest new share sale in Australia's history. The IPO valued the company at around $30.6 billion. In August, the company announced a $2 billion funding round backed by Nvidia, Coatue Management, Blackstone and Jane Street, bringing its total equity raised over the preceding year to more than $3 billion and its valuation to over $10.5 billion. Firmus also announced agreements with Meta last month to provide GPU computing capacity at its AI data centers in Southeast Asia, built on Nvidia's DSX platform, to support Meta's AI research, model development and training.

events.title: UN extends Darfur arms embargo, blocks broader Sudan sanctions proposal
events.summary: Russia and China block US efforts to expand the Darfur arms embargo to cover all of Sudan amid ongoing conflict. The United Nations Security Council extended the arms embargo on Sudan’s Darfur region by two months but failed to agree on a US proposal to widen it to the whole country, after permanent members Russia and China opposed it. The 15-member council unanimously adopted Resolution 2830 on Thursday, extending the sanctions regime until December 11 to allow more time for negotiations. list 1 of 3 The battle for Kordofan: The corridor linking Sudan’s east and west list 2 of 3 Washington’s diplomacy in Sudan has backfired list 3 of 3 Sudan’s army says it captured RSF stronghold in North Kordofan It also extended the mandate of the panel of experts that monitors the measures until January 11, 2027. The UN described the text as a short-term “technical rollover”, after the regime was last renewed for one month on September 11. The sanctions were first imposed in 2005 under Resolution 1591. The council set up an arms embargo on armed actors in Darfur , a travel ban and an asset freeze on designated individuals and entities, and a five-member panel of experts to monitor them. Despite weeks of discussion, the United States failed to secure approval to expand the embargo. Russia and China have argued for keeping the existing regime. “The current sanctions regime is over 20 years outdated, and is insufficient to address the realities of the war today,” US Ambassador Jeff Bartos told the council last month, urging it to “expand the arms embargo across the entire territory of Sudan”. Russia’s deputy UN ambassador, Anna Evstigneeva, said at the time: “We will not allow even a hint of broadening the restrictions by the council on Sudan.” Sudan’s UN ambassador, Al-Harith Mohamed, argued that a total embargo goes against the UN Charter’s guarantee of the right to self-defence. The war between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in April 2023, has killed at least 59,000 people, though aid groups warn the toll could be far higher . It has also displaced about 13 million people and pushed parts of the country into famine. The army holds central and eastern Sudan, while the RSF controls Darfur in the west and parts of the south. Darfur, a region about the size of Spain, has seen some of the worst violence, with displacement camps attacked and repeated ethnic massacres killing thousands at a time.

events.title: USS Lincoln returns to US after long deployment supporting war on Iran
events.summary: Crew members express relief upon return from record-breaking deployment of 265 days that strained conditions on board. The United States aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has returned to its home port after a 322-day deployment, including a record 265 consecutive days at sea, during which it helped wage the US-Israel war on Iran. The vessel returned to Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, California, on Thursday, where members of its crew were greeted by family and friends. list 1 of 3 US Navy confirms ‘eight suicide attempts’ on USS Lincoln: What we know list 2 of 3 Pentagon polygraphs dozens of US military staff over media leaks list 3 of 3 New aircraft carrier, 10,000 US troops: Is the Iran war about to escalate? “It feels amazing,” 20-year-old Abel Ramirez told The Associated Press news agency, adding that his parents had driven from Texas to meet him. “There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off.” The record-setting deployment of the USS Lincoln became a symbol for larger criticisms of the US war effort, which has dragged on since February with no clear end in sight and has strained US military stockpiles. The prolonged deployment prompted a series of news reports calling attention to deteriorating conditions, food shortages and a series of reported suicide attempts by crew members. Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth praised the sailors on Wednesday in remarks that accused the media of trying to turn the ship into “a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”. President Donald Trump and members of his administration have frequently lashed out at the news media for critical reporting on the war on Iran. Trump himself has called the reporting about the USS Lincoln “fake news”. “The Lincoln has been out there for a period of time, a good period of time,” he said at an Oval Office meeting on August 17. “I know people on the Lincoln, and they say it’s beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of.” Earlier that month, when confronted with the amount of time the USS Lincoln had spent at sea without a port stop, Trump quipped that its deployment was “ not nearly long enough “. The reports of mental health strain on the USS Lincoln come as public opinion polls show low approval ratings among US voters for the war against Iran. On Thursday, the Pew Research Center released a poll that found 65 percent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s handling of the war, compared with 33 percent who approved. The war has also fuelled concerns about the cost of living ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. Since the war began, Iran has hindered commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the trade of fuel, fertiliser and other goods. Sailors returning home on the USS Lincoln said that they were looking forward to fresh meals and spending time with their families. Alma Solano Velez said that her husband, one of the US service members on board, shared a list of foods he had been craving over his 10-month deployment: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas, among others. She added that he had spoken about “the lack of food and showers” and was looking forward to seeing their four-year-old daughter.

events.title: Nvidia-backed Firmus IPO being pulled sends AI funding warning
events.summary: The planned US$5.5 billion listing foundered after the deal failed to attract enough support for the A$11 marketed share price. - Firmus withdrew its planned US$5.5 billion IPO after weak demand for its A$11 share price, despite earlier interest that pointed to a US$30 billion valuation. - Investors worried about high valuations, heavy data centre spending, limited built assets, and the need for more debt and equity to fund Firmus’ AI expansion. - The failed float adds to wider fears about AI funding, with rising rates, stricter financing, and warnings from figures like Ray Dalio and Michael Burry about a possible bubble. The dramatic cancellation of an Nvidia-backed data centre company’s initial public offering is revealing fresh cracks in the AI funding boom. The planned US$5.5 billion (S$7 billion) listing by Australia’s Firmus Grid foundered after the deal failed to attract enough support for the A$11 marketed share price. Some investors turned cautious just days after the company said it received indications of interest well above the offer size, putting it on track for a US$30 billion valuation. After closing order books on the morning of Oct 9 Sydney time, Firmus announced it was withdrawing the IPO and would pursue capital from private markets, confirming earlier reporting by Bloomberg News. The failed deal underscores growing concern over how much capital AI infrastructure companies are demanding from public markets at a time when borrowing costs are rising. Much of Firmus’ valuation was based on the company successfully building a pipeline of data centres across Asia serving customers such as Meta Platforms and OpenAI. Currently it operates two data centres. The IPO proceeds were needed to help fund construction of the broader network. “Investors still believe in AI,” said Maxence Visseau, Dubai-based chief investment officer at Arkevium Capital, a multi-strategy investment firm. “What they won’t do is pay any price for companies that spend huge amounts on data centres, depend on a few big customers, and promise profits years from now.” Concerns about Firmus ranged from its lack of a proven track record to high valuations and the risk that existing shareholders could flood the market soon after listing – with about 58% of shares free to trade from day one – according to discussions with at least 10 investors and advisers. Increasing regulatory scrutiny and tighter financing conditions of data centres were also cited as a deterrent. In its Oct 9 statement, Firmus said that due to “recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions” the board decided that the terms on which the IPO could proceed would not “appropriately reflect” its business and long-term growth outlook. UniSuper, one of Australia’s biggest pension funds, was among institutional investors that did not take part in the IPO process. “We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn’t have a compelling valuation,” chief investment officer John Pearce said in an investor update published on Oct 8 . “So much has to go right to justify the valuation.” The fund was also concerned that Firmus would have to continue to raise debt and equity to fund its expansion plans, he said. “Investors are increasingly on edge,” Phil Wool, head of portfolio management at Rayliant Global Advisors, said on Oct 8 . “Firmus was going to be one of the biggest Australian IPOs ever, so from that perspective, it registers as a historical fail.” Firmus was founded in 2019 as a bitcoin miner by Oliver Curtis – who served a prison sentence for insider trading – as well as Tim Rosenfield and Jonathan Levee. The company became the subject of tabloid fodder i n 2026 as the prospect of an IPO materialised, partly due to Curtis’ criminal background and his partner being PR executive Roxy Jacenko, a prominent socialite. Around the world, investors are beginning to question the ambitious targets and lofty price tags attached to AI endeavours. In September , data-centre company Accelevation Holdings priced its US debut below its marketed range. South Korea’s Kospi is down 27% from its June peak as a boom around memory chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix subsided. Warnings about inflated valuations are getting louder. Billionaire Ray Dalio said this week that AI is a “classic bubble” that is near bursting due to the huge amount of debt taken on to fund the technology and rising rates. Michael Burry, famous for betting against the US housing market before the financial crisis, said in an X post on Oct 6 that the stock market is “quite obviously in its first stage of grief, denial. Per 2000 and 2008, this stage lasts six to nine months”. Bain & Co projects the AI industry needs to earn US$6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to justify the capital being deployed to build data centers.

events.title: Judge issues arrest warrant for Eduardo Bolsonaro, brother of presidential candidate
events.summary: A Brazilian Supreme Court justice issued a warrant on Thursday for the arrest of Eduardo Bolsonaro SAO PAULO -- A Brazilian Supreme Court justice issued a warrant on Thursday for the arrest of Eduardo Bolsonaro, one of the brothers of presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Eduardo Bolsonaro was sentenced in June to four years in prison for lobbying the Trump administration. Bolsonaro, a 42-year-old former lawmaker who lives in Texas and is a green card holder, was sentenced for lobbying to impose sanctions against members of the Brazilian government and implement higher tariffs on the country’s exports during the trial of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, for a coup attempt. His lawyer didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press. Members of the Trump administration have never made comments about Eduardo Bolsonaro's conviction. Justice Alexandre de Moraes' decision came less than three weeks before a runoff for the country’s presidency between incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, who won the most votes in the first round on Sunday. Eduardo Bolsonaro has been a key link between his brother and the Trump administration. De Moraes, who the Bolsonaro family regards as a political enemy, also canceled Eduardo Bolsonaro's Brazilian passport. The judge chaired the investigation that led to Jair Bolsonaro being sentenced last year to 27 years in prison for a coup attempt, but has since been involved in corruption accusations. The justice said in his ruling that Eduardo Bolsonaro should start serving his sentence immediately and warned the country's federal police that he should be arrested if he returns to Brazil. “The defendant cannot benefit from his own wrongdoing by fleeing the national territory to an unknown location for the purpose of thwarting the application of criminal law,” the judge said. Eduardo Bolsonaro has lived in the U.S. since 2025, which has caused him to lose his seat in the Brazilian National Congress and his job as a federal police investigator because of his long absence. The U.S. and Brazil signed an extradition agreement in 1961, but the Trump administration would have to approve an extradition request for Bolsonaro, which is unlikely, said Raphael Vieira da Fonseca Rocha, a law professor at the Federal University of Juiz de Fora. Due to the unlikeliness of an extradition being granted, “requesting it through the existing diplomatic channels of international legal cooperation would weaken the Supreme Court,” Fonseca Rocha said. He said the Supreme Court probably won’t even try and instead appeared to be applying pressure by cancelling his passport. As a consequence, “the United States would have no legal basis to extradite Eduardo Bolsonaro,” he said, adding that there was also a territorial question since Eduardo Bolsonaro was in the U.S. when he committed the crimes which led to his conviction in Brazil. The former lawmaker gave his brother's presidential bid a boost on May 26 by taking him to the White House to meet Trump. At the time, Flávio Bolsonaro was under fire for his confessed links to a disgraced banker , which analysts believed could derail his candidacy. AP journalist Eléonore Hughes contributed to this report from Rio de Janeiro. Clouds and pundits alike advise using multiple geographically dispersed availability zones, and cloud suppliers, to improve resilience. events.title: Will Ethiopia’s neighbours intervene as Tigray war escalates?
events.summary: Tigray’s renewed war is testing Ethiopia’s already strained regional ties. Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – After nearly two weeks of fierce fighting, Ethiopian federal forces entered the Tigrayan capital of Mekelle as forces from an alliance of rebel groups, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), withdrew from the city. The fighting that erupted late last month has effectively ended the 2022 Pretoria ceasefire and the fragile peace that followed the devastating Tigray war. But Mekelle’s capture may mark the end of conventional warfare rather than the end of the conflict. Fighting has continued elsewhere in Tigray, while reports of Eritrean troops entering northern Tigrayan towns have added a potentially more dangerous regional dimension. Ethiopian federal forces used air power and ground forces to advance across Tigray. After suffering successive defeats around the towns of Alamata and Kobo, rebel forces withdrew into the surrounding countryside. They have pledged to continue fighting. “We will confront the enemy on our terms and where we choose,” TPLF leader Debretsion Gebremichael said. There are echoes of the war that began in 2020, when Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government declared victory after federal forces captured Mekelle. Tigrayan forces subsequently regrouped in the mountains, retook much of the region and recaptured the capital, prolonging the war for nearly a year and a half. The renewed conflict could follow a similar trajectory, particularly if the TPLF and other armed groups succeed in turning the mountainous terrain into a prolonged armed rebellion. Ethiopia is already fighting insurgencies in Amhara and Oromia, raising the prospect of its federal forces being stretched across multiple fronts. But the battlefield reversals suffered by the rebels could have implications well beyond Tigray. They have raised concern in Egypt and among other Ethiopian rivals, according to Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an African analyst at the Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute. “Egypt views the Renaissance Dam, and any Ethiopian [army] move towards the Red Sea, as a strategic threat, so it has allied with Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia against any Ethiopian unilateralism,” Ibrahim told Al Jazeera. “Ethiopia is seeking a sea outlet; Eritrea sees this as an existential threat.” Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea won its war of independence in 1991, leaving Addis Ababa heavily dependent on neighbouring countries for access to international trade. Abiy has increasingly made access to the Red Sea a strategic priority since 2023, raising concerns in Eritrea over Ethiopia’s ambitions, particularly over the port of Assab. Ethiopia currently relies heavily on Djibouti for maritime trade, while also pursuing alternative arrangements, including through Kenya and Somaliland. After being sworn in on Monday for another five-year term following his party’s victory in the June 1 election, Abiy again put the issue at the centre of his parliamentary address. “Based on the principle of give and take, we will work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea,” he told parliament. The issue has increasingly become part of a wider regional contest. In recent months, Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia have found themselves sharing concerns over Ethiopia’s regional ambitions. On October 4, the leaders of the four countries met for a quadrilateral consultative summit in New Alamein, Egypt, where they discussed regional issues and pledged to strengthen political, economic and trade cooperation as well as consultation and coordination. The meeting does not amount to a formal military alliance, and the four countries have different interests in their dealings with Addis Ababa. The summit’s joint declaration also called for respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, noninterference in internal affairs and the peaceful resolution of disputes. But their concerns increasingly overlap around Ethiopia’s ambitions in the Red Sea, the Nile and the wider Horn of Africa. Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have also deteriorated sharply since the Pretoria ceasefire. Ethiopia closed its embassy in Eritrea and expelled Eritrean diplomats on October 1, accusing Asmara of hostile acts and involvement in the renewed fighting. Eritrea responded by severing diplomatic ties, while denying that it supported the opposition alliance. Egypt and Sudan have also denied Ethiopian accusations that they are backing the alliance. The Ethiopian army’s advance into Tigray has added another layer to that rivalry. “The [Ethiopian army’s] advance in Tigray directly threatens [Eritrean President] Isaias [Afwerki] and the Eritrean state,” said Etana H Dinka, an assistant professor of African history at the University of Miami. Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopian troops during the 2020–22 Tigray war, but relations between Abiy and Isaias have since deteriorated.

Anthropic insists it wants to give defenders access to the tools attackers are already using. Under a program name that sounds like a forthcoming Tom Cruise film – "Anthropic Cyber Mission" – the Claudefather is directing its effort into two areas. The first is a Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, because no one wants AI models showing miscreants how to shut down public utilities with newly discovered zero-day SCADA vulnerabilities. The program combines the company's priciest models with on-site engineers – sometimes now referred to as forward deployed engineers – because despite the sophistication of AI coding agents, human security experts are still useful and many organizations lack in-house talent tutored in the ways of machine learning. Anthropic aims to tackle this challenge with the help of a stable of partners: Accenture, Booz Allen, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC, and Rockwell Automation. These organizations have ties to critical infrastructure organizations and are already working to safeguard the fragile technical framework being probed constantly by AI agents. The second area of focus for the Anthropic Cyber Mission involves a service called OSS Scanner , "which offers open-source projects regular security scans from our strongest models, for free." The offer does not extend to all open-source projects, nor is it entirely free. Anthropic has borrowed the eligibility criteria used by Google for its OS-FUZZ project and will therefore work on "established projects that have a critical impact on infrastructure and user security." So if you just have a public web app repo languishing on GitHub, you can instead turn to existing tools like Socket , Dependabot , OSV-Scanner , Trivy , Renovate , or something similar. And maybe you'll be able to get your AI coding agent of choice to audit your site without balking when faced with a security audit. But for those involved in influential and widely used open-source projects, reinforcements are at hand, so long as project maintainers don't mind having their "materials" – inputs and outputs – used for model training, per the consumer terms of service Anthropic applied to OSS Scanner . Really though, most established open-source projects have already been captured in training data sets. Projects allowed to enroll can expect periodic automated scans that provide details about how identified bugs may be exploitable. These reports go out without human review, but Anthropic has assembled a set of quotes from participating OSS maintainers who believe the robo-reporting is worthwhile. At the beginning of the year, according to Anthropic, automated AI bug reports were considered mostly slop but are now considered high-quality bug reports . LLMs, the company said, now find more than 85 percent of vulnerabilities, up from 20 percent at the start of 2025. The AI biz predicts that in two years, defenders will have the advantage because AI will catch bugs before they ship. But until then, attackers have the upper hand. "Defenders of critical infrastructure and the OSS community have decades of security experience but have faced severe resource shortages that are exacerbated by this moment," Anthropic said in a blog post.

events.title: Tokenization could unleash tens of billions of dollars in trapped capital, Nasdaq CEO says
events.summary: Tokenization could allow banks and financial institutions to move collateral more efficiently, freeing up tens of billions of dollars in capital, Friedman said at TOKEN2049 in Singapore. The shift toward 24/7 trading would require major changes to financial infrastructure, with AI expected to play a growing role in real-time risk management. Kraken co-CEO Arjun Sethi said companies outside the U.S. are exploring tokenization and seeking greater access to American capital markets. Tokenization could free up tens of billions of dollars in capital tied up in assets used as collateral across the global financial system, Nasdaq CEO Adena Friedman said. Tokenizing assets such as Treasurys, equities and money market funds, along with the flow of money, could make collateral more liquid, Friedman told CNBC's Joanna Ossinger , managing editor and head of APAC Digital News, at the TOKEN2049 conference in Singapore. "If you tokenize all those instruments along with the flow of money, then the collateral becomes very fluid," Friedman said. Tokenization involves representing financial assets, such as stocks and bonds, as digital tokens that can be transferred using blockchain technology. Friedman said institutional interest in tokenization has grown over the past year, pointing in part to the passage of the Genius Act in the U.S., which established a regulatory framework for stablecoins. "If we can tokenize money, then we can tokenize the flow of capital," she said. That growing institutional interest is converging with demand from retail investors, who have long sought the ability to trade around the clock, according to Friedman. The retail ecosystem "has been about 10 years ahead," she said. Moving to a fully 24/7 market would be a major undertaking for the financial industry, Friedman said. "The easiest part is the exchange infrastructure," she said. Friedman said that financial institutions have traditionally had periods when markets are closed to update systems and manage risk. But operating around the clock would require those processes, including risk and collateral management, to take place continuously. "Everything has to be real time all the time," she said. Artificial intelligence could help financial institutions manage that transition. Nasdaq has launched a series of digital agents within its risk management platform that initially provide recommendations, Friedman said. Over time, banks could use those agents to take more direct action, she added. "AI is critical for 24/7," Friedman said. Bridging crypto and traditional finance Companies outside the U.S. are showing interest in tokenization and access to American capital markets, Arjun Sethi, co-CEO of cryptocurrency exchange Kraken, told CNBC. Sethi pointed to a company generating roughly $25 million in revenue that was exploring ways to access capital markets, as well as larger international companies interested in tokenization and U.S. public listings. He said tokenization could help expand access to capital markets for companies around the world. However, round-the-clock trading may not be suitable for everything, according to Friedman. "Not every asset is liquid enough to support a 24/7 environment," she said. Still, greater connectivity across the global financial system could also open up access to asset classes that were previously out of reach for some investors, Friedman said.

events.title: Kenyan patient suspected of Ebola infection tests negative
events.summary: Preliminary lab results ease fears of a second case in Kenya, after the country reported its first-ever case this week. Preliminary laboratory results from a Kenyan patient who was suspected of contracting the Ebola virus have come back negative. Fears of a second case of Ebola in the East African country were allayed on Thursday after the governor of Wajir County, where the patient is being treated, revealed the test results. list 1 of 3 Kenya confirms first Ebola case as man dies in Nairobi after DRC return list 2 of 3 Kenya on high alert amid concern over screening after first Ebola death list 3 of 3 Why single Ebola death in Kenya has prompted fears of wider African spread “I am pleased to report that the preliminary laboratory results indicate that the sample is NEGATIVE for Ebola Virus Disease,” the Wajir county governor said in a statement. The suspected patient is a 20-year-old man with a travel history from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) through Uganda to Kenya. The other Kenyan patient who tested positive for the virus and subsequently died had travelled the same route. Kenya had reported its first-ever Ebola case on Tuesday after a citizen who became sick in the DRC died in Nairobi. The deadly strain of the Ebola virus has spread widely, starting in the DRC earlier this year. The DRC officially declared an outbreak in May. Kenya is the fourth country to record a case linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, the second-largest on record. The ongoing outbreak in the eastern DRC has killed at least 4,205 people out of more than 8,700 reported cases. The outbreak spread across the border to Uganda, which had about 20 cases before being declared Ebola-free in July. The strain behind the latest spread has been dubbed the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), believed to have spread from animals to humans through a new transmission route. No vaccine currently exists for Bundibugyo. The first case in Kenya drew scrutiny over the status of the virus in neighbouring Uganda and exposed lapses in Kenya’s border screening systems. The patient who died was able to pass through multiple airport temperature checks. The World Health Organization (WHO) is working with Kenyan authorities to trace contacts and strengthen checks for travellers entering the country.

events.title: OpenAI’s annualised revenue US$20 billion less than previously signalled: Report
events.summary: OpenAI told investors its revenue was approaching US$50 billion on an annualised basis at the end of September. OpenAI’s annualised revenue was about US$20 billion lower than previously reported, the Financial Times said, citing financial documents shared with investors. The company told investors revenue was nearing US$50 billion at the end of September, not US$70 billion as earlier media reports said. The gap came from different methods. Anthropic counts cloud partner sales, but OpenAI does not. A possible public listing could reveal more about both firms’ finances. OpenAI’s annualised revenue is about US$20 billion (S$25.6 billion) less than has been previously signalled, the Financial Times reported on Oct 8, citing financial documents shared with investors. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the report. The company has recently told investors its revenue was approaching US$50 billion on an annualised basis at the end of September, the report said, far short of the US$70 billion reported by media outlets, including Reuters, in late September. The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI’s own investors to produce a direct comparison with Anthropic’s annualised revenue, the FT reported, citing a person with knowledge of the matte The pair calculate the figure in different ways, with Anthropic including the revenue from sales via cloud partners such as AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not, the Financial Times report said Annualised revenue run rate is sometimes misleading sales metric, which often involves multiplying one month’s revenue by 12, but it has nonetheless become a popular metric commonly used by fast-growing Silicon Valley startups. OpenAI and its rival Anthropic are potentially preparing to go public, which could give Wall Street a clearer view of their finances, including the sustainability of their rapid revenue growth due to the AI boom. events.title: Hegseth says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be ‘public’
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections An official at the Pentagon told Al Jazeera that former US Army Major Nidal Hassan’s execution would be ‘livestreamed’. United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said the execution of a former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in Texas will be publicly available to watch. In an interview with the media outlet Real America’s Voice on Thursday, Hegseth was asked about President Donald Trump’s recent order to use a firing squad to execute Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of the 2009 shooting. list 1 of 3 Fort Hood shooting trial begins list 2 of 3 Trump approves firing squad execution for Fort Hood attacker Nidal Hasan list 3 of 3 Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad: All to know The secretary said he approved of the decision, calling it a “no-brainer”. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Hegseth told interviewer Jack Posobiec. “Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” Hegseth added that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on December 3 at 1pm US Central Time (19:00 GMT), the same time that the 2009 shooting took place. Hasan was sentenced to death in August 2013 after a military jury found him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted murder for the shooting. The former Army major walked into an army processing centre on the Texas base, shouted “Allahu akbar” (God is greatest) and opened fire on fellow military members waiting to get medical attention. Hasan’s execution required approval from Hegseth and Trump, who authorised the use of the firing squad on Monday. An official with the Defense Department told Al Jazeera that Hasan’s execution would be “livestreamed”, adding that more details would come soon. It is not clear from Hegseth’s remarks whether troops, spectators or US military officials would be present in person for the execution. US Army regulation states that at least two media outlets should be selected as witnesses. No state or federal execution has ever been televised in the US. The last public execution in the country took place more than 90 years ago in Owensboro, Kentucky, on August 14, 1936. The last time a US military execution was conducted by firing squad was in 1945, for desertion during World War II. When asked to comment on Hegseth’s remarks – and whether Trump would view the execution – the White House referred Al Jazeera to the Pentagon. The Trump administration announced it would add death by firing squad as an acceptable method for federal executions in April, along with gas asphyxiation and electrocution.

events.title: Ex-Warner Bros. CEO pockets US$600 million in sale to Paramount
events.summary: Co-chief executive officers of Skydance Corp. David Ellison (left) and Ynon Kreiz at the New York Stock Exchange in New York on Oct 8. - David Zaslav made about US$600 million from Warner Bros. Discovery’s sale to Paramount Skydance Corp., mostly through stock options. - Warner Bros. shareholders received US$31 a share in cash, about 25% above the April 2022 trading price, but below the S&P 500’s 76% rise. - The new Skydance Corp., led by David Ellison, now combines Paramount and Warner Bros. studios, TV networks like CBS and CNN, and streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max. NEW YORK – David Zaslav, the longtime TV executive who created Warner Bros. Discovery Inc. but ultimately failed to keep it going as an independent company, made about US$600 million (S$768 million) on the sale of the business to Paramount Skydance Corp. this week. Much of Zaslav’s compensation came in the form of stock options. Warner Bros. stockholders received US$31 a share in cash in the sale, a nearly 25% increase from when the stock first began trading in April of 2022. The S&P 500 rose 76% over that period. Many other Warner executives received large paydays, including streaming boss JB Perrette and strategy chief Bruce Campbell. A spokesperson said Zaslav doubled the number of employees overall who received stock awards. The new company, now called Skydance Corp. and led by technology scion David Ellison, is one of the largest media businesses in the world, comprising the century-old Paramount and Warner Bros. movie studios, dozens of TV networks, like CBS and CNN, as well as the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services. events.title: Man City charges: Mourinho jokes Premier League case will outlast him
events.summary: Jose Mourinho, one of most outspoken against Man City spending when United manager, jibes EPL appeal to outlast him. Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho joked that he may not live to see the end of Manchester City’s legal battle with the Premier League after the club appealed against a ruling that found it guilty of serious financial rule breaches. An independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of Premier League financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, as well as three of four charges relating to failures to cooperate with the investigation. City have denied wrongdoing and lodged an appeal . list 1 of 4 Prosecutors in Maradona death trial seek sentences up to 12 years list 2 of 4 CAS promises Senegal-Morocco AFCON title decision within days list 3 of 4 UEFA details FIFA presidential candidate criteria in bid to oust Infantino list 4 of 4 ‘Utmost respect’: Ronaldo pays tribute to Messi after Argentina farewell The Premier League said that City used “sham” commercial agreements to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.19bn) over nearly a decade, resulting in inaccurate financial reporting and breaches of spending rules. Mourinho managed Manchester United from 2016 to 2018 and led them to a second-placed Premier League finish behind Pep Guardiola’s City in 2017-18. “I would rather laugh about it,” Mourinho said when asked about the case in an interview with Italy’s Corriere dello Sport. “I think we will eventually get an ending, but we are both in our 60s, and we’ll need to be lucky enough to still be around when the final verdict arrives. “There will be a verdict, then appeals, then more appeals.” Mourinho has long maintained that one of his greatest achievements in football management was finishing second behind Guardiola’s side, given their spending power at the time. The Portuguese manager, now 63, said in 2024 that he had not given up on being awarded a winner’s medal for the 2018 season. “I think we still have a chance to win that league because maybe they punish Man City with points and maybe we win that league,” he quipped at a press conference ahead of a Europa League match against United with his then-club, Fenerbahce. “Then they have to pay me the bonus and give me the medal.” The appeal process will be conducted in private, and it remains unclear whether any sanctions would be imposed before it is heard, or whether any punishment would take effect immediately. City, seeking a sixth successive league win, are top of the Premier League with 15 points from five matches and travel to Liverpool on Sunday. Holders Arsenal entertain Leeds on Saturday, while United host Tottenham later the same day. Mourinho’s Real Madrid trail fierce rivals and La Liga leaders Barcelona by six points, with five wins and two defeats from their seven league matches this season. Both Barca and Real are in action on Saturday, with Getafe and Villarreal visiting, respectively.

events.title: Amex fined US$350 million for anti-money laundering lapses
events.summary: The US Federal Reserve announced a separate enforcement action against the New York-based company linked to its anti-money laundering programme. US regulators fined American Express US$350 million for anti-money laundering failures and said it missed about US$13 billion in suspected trade-based laundering over a decade. The OCC said Amex had “systemic breakdowns” in monitoring and reporting, while the Federal Reserve launched a separate action against its national bank unit. Amex said the penalty will not change 2026 or 2027 guidance, and chief executive Steve Squeri said the firm has made progress but “there is more work to do”. Federal regulators fined American Express US$350 million (S$448.2 million) for failing to catch and report money laundering in its system, one of the steepest penalties imposed by the financial authorities in US President Donald Trump’s second term. The US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) cited the bank for deficiencies in its compliance programmes, according to a statement on Oct 8 . The Federal Reserve announced a separate enforcement action against the New York-based company linked to its anti-money laundering programme, in particular at the firm’s national bank subsidiary. “The bank experienced systemic breakdowns in its suspicious activity monitoring and reporting processes, resulting in a failure to timely identify, evaluate, and sufficiently report approximately US$13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity that took place over the past decade,” the OCC said in its statement. Amex said in a regulatory filing that the penalty will not impact the full-year 2026 guidance it previously issued and the orders do no t impose an asset cap on the firm. Costs tied to fixing the issues are not expected to impact 2027 guidance either, the firm said. The fine contrasts with the deregulatory drive that has taken place under Trump’s second term. Watchdogs have largely worked to reduce the regulations that large US banks face, including by relaxing how much capital banks must hold as a buffer against potential losses, narrowing the scope of bank supervision and shrinking a Federal Reserve unit dedicated to bank oversight. Amex chief executive Steve Squeri said the firm identified areas for improvement in its compliance programmes through internal and external reviews. “We also investigated transactions that we identified being processed over our network by individuals misusing our products for the purchases of goods and services, reported that information to law enforcement, and took other appropriate action,” Squeri said in a separate statement. “While we have made meaningful progress, we know there is more work to do.” Amex is best known for its premium credit cards, including the Platinum card with its US$895 annual fee. The firm also has a national bank, which offers checking and savings accounts to customers. Amex shares dropped nearly 2% to US$302.10 at 5.22pm local time on Oct 8 in after-market trading. events.title: Anthropic is launching a ‘presidential engagement’ effort to advise candidates on AI policy ahead of the 2028 election
events.summary: Anthropic is setting up a “presidential engagement” program ahead of the 2028 elections, building an in-house team that will work directly with U.S. presidential candidates from both parties on AI issues, help Anthropic’s leadership set political strategy, and run the company’s political funding program. The effort—which is taking shape before the November midterm elections and an impending initial public offering that could value Anthropic at as much as $2 trillion—underscores the extent to which government policy, and the support of the White House in particular, have become critical to the AI industry. Anthropic is hiring a Political Programs lead to spearhead the effort and build the team. The person will “build and run Anthropic’s presidential engagement program for the 2028 cycle,” according to the job description that the company posted recently. The person in the role will “map the prospective fields in both parties, offer AI policy education to candidates and their advisors on equal terms, prepare Anthropic’s executives for those conversations, and plan ahead for the platform, convention, and transition periods.” “Decisions made over the next two years will shape the future enormously,” reads the job description. “We want every serious candidate and elected official, in both parties, to understand the technology and the case for governing it well.” Tech companies lobbying the government is established practice—and OpenAI is similarly hiring a U.S. Congressional Lead to advance its legislative priorities—but Anthropic’s plan to create a dedicated in-house program to engage with presidential candidates struck some experts as unusual. “Companies have relationships with presidential campaigns through their government affairs people. Corporate people can be involved on the fundraising side and on the policy side,” said Bruce F. Freed, the president of the non-partisan Center for Political Accountability. “But I’ve not seen such as formalized engagement through a presidential election engagement committee. My reading is this is an AI company effort aimed at shaping or staving off government regulation or oversight.” Anthropic did not immediately respond to our request for comment. Anthropic’s relationship with the Trump administration has been particularly rocky. In March, the Department of Defense designated Anthropic as a “supply chain risk” after the company clashed with the Pentagon over the ways its technology could be used by the military. Dario Amodei, the CEO and cofounder of Anthropic, has called for slowing the pace of the AI development in order to shore up safeguards and has been a vocal advocate for government regulation of AI. That view is not shared by President Trump, who has stridently rejected any regulation that could cause the U.S. to fall behind China in the AI race. Last week, Amodei attended a White House event with several other AI industry CEOs and signed an accord committing to self-regulation. “Consider this their start of developing relationships with whomever will be in the White House in 2029,” said Katie Harbath, founder and CEO of Anchor Change , a tech policy advisory firm, said of the Anthropic’s presidential engagement program. Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) said Anthropic’s search for a Political Programs lead is “a reminder that the companies building frontier AI models are also building political operations alongside their products.” While companies have a right to participate in the country’s democracy and to educate policymakers about how AI technology works, “education and influence are not the same thing, and the public deserves to know where one ends and the other begins,” Padilla told Fortune in a statement urging Anthropic to share more details about the program. “It’s important that the rules for AI be set by elected representatives accountable to voters, informed by industry and by independent experts, researchers, and affected communities, and not by whichever company has the best-resourced political program,” Padilla said. Politics is an open part of Anthropic’s DNA, while OpenAI’s influence is subtler Anthropic is already politically active, and sees itself as “equal parts research lab, policy think tank, and technology company,” according to the job description, which stresses that it political participation is bipartisan. In contrast to the Center for Political Accountability’s Freed, Harbath, the Anchor Change CEO, said that Anthropic’s Political Programs role did not strike her as unusual. “It sounds a lot like what my job at Facebook was and that a lot of other companies have,” said Harbath, who served as Public Policy Director at Facebook for 10 years. “What’s unusual about it is that it includes running the political action committee (PAC) money. Usually that was a separate thing.” In addition to candidate education and grassroots organizing, the role calls for running “the day-to-day of Anthropic’s political giving,” and helping employees who “choose to participate in politics do so in an informed way.” In April, Anthropic set up its first employee-funded political action committee (PAC), called AnthroPAC , which allows employees to contribute up to $5,000 per year, a legal cap. Other tech companies also have PACs, such as MetaPAC, and AmazonPAC. Individuals at tech companies can donate much more outside of their capped PAC contributions, and with Anthropic’s upcoming IPO, its employees will likely have even deeper pockets for political spending. In July, CEO Dario Amodei donated $1 million to a pro-AI regulation super PAC called Public First in July, Politico reports . Other employees have also given hundreds of thousands of dollars to Public First and other political advocacy groups. OpenAI does not have any employee-funded PACs, a company policy it highlighted in a June 2026 blog post . Instead, OpenAI leadership has made personal political donations and attempts to curry favor with the Trump administration. CEO Sam Altman donated $1 million to Trump’s inauguration fund in 2024. In early 2025, he posted on X that Trump “will be incredible for the country in many ways!” OpenAI president Greg Brockman donated $25 million to the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, although he cancelled his next planned $25 million donation after employee backlash , including employees setting up a rival super PAC to advocate for stricter AI safety laws. events.title: Mark Zuckerberg has an image problem - so why is Meta's business booming?
events.summary: Published 9 October 2026, 00:13 BST Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful. "Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make." Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists. It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company. For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users. That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case. And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him. This year Meta unveiled Muse, its AI companion app, alongside a Tamagotchi-like wearable device that allows users to talk to it His reputation is unlikely to be helped by The Social Reckoning, a film by Aaron Sorkin released this week. It's about whistleblower claims that Meta executives were aware of their products harming young people. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to a review in the Hollywood Reporter, "stoically arguing that even the slightest gesture of responsibility is anathema where money is concerned". Some speculate that this is Meta's "Big Tobacco" moment, with a consensus forming against the company, and the social media industry as a whole. But the truth seems to be more complicated. Despite months of bad press, in the real world Meta's products are doing better than ever. Use of its apps continues to rise, and users are already flocking to its new AI assistant. It raises the question: can anything really clip Meta's wings? Or is it now something of a 'Teflon' company, with scandals simply bouncing off it? It's certainly been a year of bad headlines for Meta. Last summer, Reuters revealed that Meta allowed its chatbots to "engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual", and provide false medical information to users. Meta has revised those policies and said that such responses should never have been allowed. And this year, bills have been mounting. In March, a jury gave $6m (£4.5m) to a 20-year-old California woman who claimed she suffered mental health harms related to her use of Meta's Instagram and Google's YouTube. Around the same time, New Mexico became the first state to succeed in a lawsuit against Meta over child safety issues. A jury found the company had failed to warn the public about the dangers its platforms posed to kids. Meta was fined a total of $942m. The judge called Meta a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution. Meta says it disagrees with the verdicts and is appealing both cases. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to one review of The Social Reckoning In May, Meta was among the social companies that avoided a trial by settling a case brought by a Kentucky school district that claimed their product design had led to a youth mental health crisis. Meta reportedly agreed to pay $9m, the most of any defendant. And this summer, Meta struck a high-profile $18bn settlement with 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Meta denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement, and during the five-day trial it maintained that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for young users, pouring resources into testing and research. As part of the deal, the firm promised to enact two-hour daily time limits for young users, along with night-time blocks on use, muted notifications during school hours, and other changes. The company faces other lawsuits too, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, also related to alleged social media addiction among young users. Meanwhile, several countries have moved to ban social media for children entirely, starting with Australia last December. Social media companies are broadly disliked, even while their products remain wildly popular. A Reuters/Ipsos survey suggests that 85% of Americans think social media can be addictive for children, and 61% support greater government oversight. Meta faces lawsuits over its handling of young social media users.

events.title: California threatens to worsen House Democrats' 2027 headaches
events.summary: More than half a dozen U.S. House districts in California will send a Democrat to Capitol Hill next year no matter what. Party leadership still has a lot riding on the outcome. Why it matters: Most of these Democrat vs. Democrat runoffs — a quirk of California's election system — are between an establishment candidate and an outsider vowing to make leadership's life hell. Democratic Reps. Mike Thompson, Doris Matsui and Jimmy Gomez are all facing well-funded challenges from younger, less establishment-aligned Democrats. There are also several Northern California races that feature a pro-leadership Democrat facing off against a more left-leaning rival. Sought for comment on this story, Justin Chermol, a spokesperson for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), told Axios: "Stop wasting our time with your irrelevant stories that have nothing to do with taking back control of the House of Representatives." 4th District: Rep. Mike Thompson vs. Eric Jones Thompson , a 75-year-old first elected in 1998, faces a challenge from 35-year-old former venture capitalist Eric Jones. "I don't think anyone in Democratic leadership today is really doing their job well," Jones said in an interview with Axios. Asked if he would vote for Jeffries as speaker, Jones replied: "As of today, I wouldn't vote for any member." Jones is trying to cobble together a populist, anti-establishment coalition consisting of both progressives and Republicans. He said he does not identify as progressive, telling Axios he prefers "no labels." He said that, if elected, he will "have the benefit of independence ... of not taking party money, and I'm not going to vote a party line." 7th District: Rep. Doris Matsui vs. Mai Vang Matsui, 85, is seen as particularly vulnerable after finishing second to Mai Vang in the jungle primary election in June. Vang, a progressive Sacramento City Councilmember in her 40s, has positioned herself alongside a new bloc of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-aligned candidates including Darializa Avila Chevalier, Chris Rabb and Melat Kiros. She previously signaled to Axios she won't vote for Jeffries as speaker, saying she "cannot support this kind of leadership" and that "we need new leadership and a new direction." 11th District: Scott Wiener vs. Connie Chan The fight between state Sen. Scott Wiener and San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan to succeed former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi has been particularly bitter. Chan has positioned herself to the left of Wiener, a longtime progressive who has come under fire from the pro-Palestinian movement for being insufficiently critical of Israel. Wiener told Mission Local he looks "forward to electing Hakeem Jeffries speaker." Chan told the outlet that "any candidate for speaker, including Hakeem Jeffries, will have to earn my vote." 14th District: Rep. Aisha Wahab vs. Melissa Hernandez Wahab , a progressive former state senator, defeated Hernandez, the more moderate former mayor of Dublin, California, in an August special election to replace former Rep. Eric Swalwell . The two are now duking it out for a full term. Wahab has already shown her willingness to buck leadership: She defied Pelosi and Jeffries by running in the special election instead of allowing a "caretaker" to run unopposed, according to The Sunday Times . The Wahab and Hernandez campaigns did not respond to questions about whether their candidates would vote for Jeffries as speaker. 34th District: Rep. Jimmy Gomez vs. Angela Gonzales-Torres Gomez has come under fire after the House Ethics Committee opened an investigation into him in August over allegations of sexual misconduct, which he denies. He has been a longtime target of the left, having survived three consecutive primary challenges from Democrat David Kim since 2020 by 2 to 11 percentage points. This time he faces a challenge from Angela Gonzales-Torres, a progressive local neighborhood councilor backed by many of the same left-wing groups that support Vang and Wahab. Gonzales-Torres , asked in an interview with Axios if she would vote for Jeffries as speaker, said she looks forward to "supporting leaders who are not nearly funded by corporate super PACs." Gonzales-Torres, pointing to her support from DSA, said she considers herself part of the "national slate" of progressive insurgents such as Avila Chevalier, Rabb and Kiros. "Right now [what] we are focusing on is winning this election and hopefully getting to be part of utilizing our bargaining power as this incoming class in Congress," she said. The bottom line: The larger the bloc of Jeffries skeptics that arrives on Capitol Hill in January, the worse a time Democratic leadership will have. That could be tempered to a large degree by the size of Democrats' potential majority, but, as Axios previously reported , many red-seat candidates are also maintaining their independence from leadership. Still, few Democrats think Jeffries will ultimately be denied the speakership. The fights that come after are more uncertain.
