events.title: Trump gives top US science awards to Elon Musk and other tech executives
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections The National Medal of Science is given annually to scientists and engineers for major contributions in their fields. United States President Donald Trump has awarded the country’s most prestigious honours in science and engineering to executives from top technology firms including SpaceX, Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia. On Thursday, Trump presented the National Medal of Science to billionaire SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Lisa Su of the semiconductor firm AMD. list 1 of 3 Trump, tech bosses sign voluntary pact pledging ‘robust’ AI safeguards list 2 of 3 What are the world’s biggest AI companies and how much are they worth? list 3 of 3 US suspends Microsoft and Adobe from visa programme amid fraud claims Two more recipients received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation: Michael Dell of Dell Technologies and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. At the award ceremony, Trump credited the honourees with “helping pioneer an incredible future for America”. “Because of these people here, we will always be on top. No one else can compete with us,” Trump said. Five of the six people receiving medals on Thursday were born outside the US. Four are among the 10 wealthiest people in the world, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. The award ceremony took place hours after the Trump administration announced it was suspending Microsoft and other top tech companies from using the H-1B visa system, which allows companies to hire skilled foreign workers and put them on a path towards permanent residency in the US. The suspension, officials said, was due to the companies allegedly using the system in a fraudulent manner. White House builds ties with Silicon Valley The medal ceremony was the latest example of what critics see as an increasingly close relationship between Silicon Valley tech executives and the second Trump administration. Powerful companies like Amazon, Meta and Nvidia contributed money to Trump’s second inauguration, and several high-profile industry leaders attended his swearing-in, including Musk and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. Trump, for his part, has pledged to slash regulations and position the US “as the world leader in artificial intelligence”. He has also touted self-regulation in the AI industry amid concerns about the safety of the technology. Several of the tech entrepreneurs honoured on Thursday have forged close ties to the White House, through political and business dealings. The South Africa-born Musk, for example, was the largest contributor to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign and has been a supporter of right-wing causes around the world, which he amplifies on his social media platform, X. He briefly served as a special adviser to the president during the first months of Trump’s second term, helping to lead the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and its efforts to downsize the federal government. Around the time he left DOGE, however, Musk and Trump had a public falling-out over the president’s tax-and-spending plans. The two have since reconciled. On Thursday, Trump hailed Musk as “our modern-day Thomas Edison” and an “industrial titan”, citing his work with the aerospace company SpaceX and the carmaker Tesla. “Few Americans in history have done more to advance America’s national interest than Elon in one field after another,” Trump said. Another honouree, Dell, has been a financial backer of the president’s efforts to launch Trump Accounts, a scheme to enrol American children born during Trump’s second term into government-backed investment accounts. Dell and his wife Susan Dell committed $6.25bn to the programme last year. Separately, the White House entered into a deal in August for the US government to take a 15 percent cut of any AI chip sales that Nvidia and AMD make with China. Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder, later invested in the struggling US tech firm Intel. He is reported to be among the donors financing Trump’s plans for a new White House ballroom. The National Medal of Science was first awarded in 1963 to Theodore von Karman, a pioneer in aerospace engineering who fled anti-Semitism in Europe during World War II. He went on to help found the Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology. Nominations for the award are solicited by the National Science Foundation, and the recipients are ultimately selected by a committee appointed by the president.

events.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
events.summary: Your browser doesn't support HTML5 video. Here is a link to the video instead. Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗 Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗 Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . With Astra, Jebens explored computer-aided design and tooling revisions for robots informed by simulation. The agent measured the available space and designed a wrench the robot could use to reach the suspension’s bolts. Jebens reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. This connects design and tooling decisions to disassembly results, offering a starting point for robot policy training. Explore the Onshape importer guide . Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗 Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗 A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Have a simulation idea?

events.title: Fears backpacker ballot will leave coastal towns short-staffed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Hospitality businesses seek designated area migration agreement to combat backpacker ballot There are concerns about how to fill jobs when the backpacker ballot begins. ( Flickr CC BY-NC-ND 2.0: Jo Christian Oterhals ) Hospitality experts say the backpacker ballot could create significant workforce shortages in holiday towns that rely heavily on seasonal workers. North Coast Hotel Group director Harry Barry says his business hires backpackers because of a local workforce shortage. Business leaders along the NSW coast are looking to negotiate a federal agreement to help fill roles in the regions. For publican Harry Barry, backpackers are the lifeblood of his business. But he says many of his employees are considering returning home after the federal government announced a backpacker ballot , which would effectively cap second-year backpacker visas. "The incentive was a guarantee they could extend their visas by another 12 months," he said. "A lot of them are deciding that there is no guarantee that [they're] going to be earning enough money to pay [their] way. Harry Barry says a designated area migration agreement could help the Coffs Harbour region. ( ABC Coffs Harbour: Claudia Jambor ) The new backpacker ballot will cap annual places at 45,000 for second-year visas if the standard 88 days of regional work are completed. Even fewer third-year places are available. About 57,000 people qualified last year . Mr Barry is among a number of business owners concerned about how the cap will impact their staff. The director of the North Coast Hotel Group runs pubs from Grafton to Taree that employed 80 backpackers over the past two years, with 20 still on his books. "If we're employing 80 backpackers, we're doing it for a reason , and the reason is we can't find local workers to fill the slots," he said. Harry Barry believes the new backpacker ballot will negatively affect the Mid North Coast. ( ABC Coffs Coast: Claudia Jambor ) According to jobs website Seek, there were more than 130 vacancies in the Coffs Harbour region in the industry on Wednesday. To fill the gap left by backpackers leaving, Mr Barry is backing a push to establish the region as a priority area for semi-skilled migrants, also known as a Designated Area Migration Agreement (DAMA). The DAMA is an agreement between the federal government and a state or regional authority that assists regional areas to fill roles that would otherwise remain empty. It allows skilled migrants, in industries of need, to move to the area for work. Industries include skilled roles in hospitality, agriculture, engineering and more. The agreements are usually in place for five years before they are reviewed. Backpackers help pick fruit across regional NSW. ( ABC Rural: Stephanie Anderson ) There are 13 DAMAs in place across Australia, with one operation in New South Wales; two in South Australia; five in Western Australia; one in the Northern Territory; two in Victoria; and two in Queensland. Regional Development Australia Mid North Coast CEO Madeleine Lawler said the DAMA was not about filling jobs with migrants that could have otherwise employed locals. "The DAMA requires businesses to be able to substantiate that they have been seeking Australians for a long period of time and have not been able to fill these positions with Australians or people locally," she said. A similar agreement in Townsville, in Northern Queensland, brought in an additional 480 workers over three years to fill a skills shortage. Holiday hotspot Cairns has held a DAMA for the past seven years. The agreement, according to the Cairns Chamber of Commerce, was key to keeping the region thriving. CEO Patricia O'Neill said there was a hotel on Thursday Island, which was included in the Cairns agreement, that would shut down without DAMA workforce. Patricia O'Neill says the DAMA has been a lifeline for the Cairns region. ( ABC News: Conor Byrne ) "Government go to [Thursday Island] regularly; there is only one hotel in the place. If they weren't able to apply to attract a chef, that hotel would need to close [because] it can't feed anyone," Ms O'Neill said. "That's how critical a DAMA is to certain parts of an economy up here. "Without having the Far North Queensland DAMA, we would not have a thriving economy; we would not have a workforce to take up jobs." Each area with an agreement has a list of specific jobs, tailored to the region's needs, that can be filled by overseas workers.

events.title: The staggering cost of winning a Senate seat in 2026
events.summary: Source: AdImpact, Census.gov Note: AdImpact data includes dollars spent on video advertisements on broadcast, cable and social media as well as spending estimates on streaming platforms. Chart: Stef Kight/Axios Every voting-age Mainer could get a $167 voucher for home heating oil with what Democrats and Republicans are spending on ads in the Senate race, according to an analysis of AdImpact data. Why it matters: Every senator gets one vote, but Senate seats aren't created equal — and they don't cost the same. Zoom in: Like two years ago , the less-populated states have a dramatically higher dollar-per-voter ratio in 2026. Maine is in first place, followed by Alaska, which is scheduled to be hit with $76 million in ads — enough to suck up most of the state's inventory. Between the lines: Ohio is only in fifth place on the dollar-per-voter metric, but it's on track to host the most expensive Senate race in the country — for the second cycle in a row . Sherrod Brown's comeback bid is proving more expensive than his 2024 race, when he was ousted by now-Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). And in New Hampshire, where Democratic Senate nominee Chris Pappas has been warning that his race is actually quite close, both parties are spending heavily to reach the state's voters. Data: AdImpact Note: AdImpact data includes dollars spent on video advertisements on broadcast, cable and social media as well as spending estimates on streaming platforms. Chart: Stef Kight/Axios The big picture: Both chambers are likely to come down to a handful of races. All year, Republicans warned that Texas would get really expensive if Attorney General Ken Paxton won the primary. They were right. Outside GOP groups spent a mind-blowing $131 million in just 17 days trying to rescue Paxton. And tens of millions more could be on the way. But in North Carolina, where Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), predicted the race could cost $1 billion , the contest looks like it will come in under $200 million. Republican super PACs are abandoning the Senate race there as they reallocate money to redder states. The bottom line: Republicans have a spending advantage, especially when it comes to how many eyeballs they're actually reaching in Texas and Ohio . But neither side has really figured out how to play moneyball and find a way to reach voters with a dramatically smaller budget.

events.title: Pretend you’re sitting at Elizabeth Holmes’ desk on this weirdly detailed website
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. With over a thousand emails, slides, texts, and documents unveiled during the United States v. Elizabeth Holmes trial, Extend engineer Bo Lau created a website that simulates what it might have been like to be the chief executive of Theranos before everything came crashing down. (Every day, I am grateful to the American legal system for making the discovery process public.) i built a website where you can sit at elizabeth holmes’ desk open her macbook, scroll her iphone, run the theranos edison machine her texts, emails, slides, documents, and theranos machine records are real, sourced from exhibits in the united states v. holmes criminal trial pic.twitter.com/5At9T5m3UV — bo lau (@bolau_) October 8, 2026 The environment that Lau created is ambitiously detailed, taking you right back to 2016, a time when iPhones had home buttons, and you had to slide your finger across the screen to unlock it. Even the MacBook Air is running OS X El Capitan. You can click around the environment, which lets you look through the documents made public from the court case on Holmes’ iPhone and laptop screens. You can even run the Theranos Edison machine, the company’s ill-fated device that was supposed to be able to extract large amounts of health data from one drop of blood. The project seems like it was mostly made for laughs, but it’s actually an interesting way to peruse the documents from one of the most infamous court cases in tech history — it’s a lot easier to navigate this than to source thousands of PDFs from court websites. There’s another agenda, though. Lau is promoting a watch party that her company is throwing for Nathan Fielder’s upcoming documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, “ You Can See Everything .” Also, of course, she’s promoting the company itself. So, what exactly does Extend do? Apparently, it can “parse, extract, and split your hardest documents with unmatched accuracy.” (I’m not really sure what that means, but if it makes something like this Holmes desk simulator possible, then I guess that means I’m bullish on B2B SaaS.) events.title: How to get friends to share expenses during group holidays
events.summary: Most people make the mistake of not talking about spending limits and repayment plans before a trip. When Stasia Maltseva went to Thailand and Cambodia with six friends, everyone paid in cash and with no system to record expenses. The cost of street food, souvenirs, group massages and tuk-tuk rides disappeared into an untraceable pit. They assumed they’d figure out the IOUs when the two-week trip ended. But when it came time to even out the books, “no one had the slightest idea” how much each person had spent, said Maltseva, a 36-year-old content manager from Amsterdam.

events.title: Satya Nadella had an awkward White House day
events.summary: Satya Nadella and Donald Trump were all ... smiles? Win McNamee/Getty Images It was a roller coaster Thursday for Microsoft. JD Vance called out Microsoft during a press conference about visa crackdowns. Hours later, Trump honored CEO Satya Nadella as a "key figure". Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella had a bizarre day. On Thursday morning, Vice President JD Vance hosted a press conference to announce that the US would suspend a major visa program for Microsoft's workers . Though several tech companies were targeted, Vance called out Microsoft by name, alleging that "no company in the United States" abused the Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) worse. "If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one-and-a-half foreign indentured servants," Vance said. "Now that is a scandalous system that we've allowed in this country for far too long." Huge banners behind the veep declared "PROTECTING AMERICAN WORKERS" and "FIGHTING VISA FRAUD." But hours later, Trump was singing Nadella's praises. At a White House event honoring "a new golden age" for science, Nadella walked up to the president — whose administration had just accused his company of visa fraud, mind you — and received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. "For more than three decades, Satya Nadella has been a key figure in the transformation of Microsoft — revolutionizing the company and empowering businesses, students, and consumers from all over the world with some of the most capable software ever built or ever even conceived," Trump said at the event, before the two posed for a photo op. Nadella, for his part, thanked Trump for the "incredible honor" in an X post , which didn't mention Vance's accusations. A Microsoft blog post shared by a spokesperson to Business Insider said 80% of the company's roughly 6,000 H-1B visa applications were for existing employees, not new hires. "Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," the company wrote. It also said the "vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." Thursday's awkwardness was the latest example of Trump putting business leaders in tricky situations as he takes a far more active role in business dealings than his presidential predecessors. Trump has used his executive influence to encourage business leaders to back a variety of his initiatives, like his Trump Account savings program for American children. At the same time, he's lashed out at opposition, including on Thursday when he said that anyone who wasn't on board with his official declaration to rebrand artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" would be considered an "enemy" of the White House. events.title: America shut out Chinese EVs. Britain welcomed them — and now faces a difficult choice
events.summary: Britain faces a finely balanced choice over whether to follow the EU in imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs, as it seeks closer post-Brexit ties while risking retaliation from Beijing. Chinese automakers are rapidly gaining ground in Britain. Analysts warn EV tariffs alone may not curb China’s advance, with hybrid sales also surging and Chinese brands benefiting from advantages in cost, supply chains and product development. The U.K. broke with the U.S. by opening its doors to China's electric vehicle juggernaut . Chinese EVs face only a 10% standard import duty in Britain, one of the largest major overseas markets without additional China-specific tariffs. Japan and Norway also lack them. It's in contrast to the U.S., where a 100% tariff effectively shut Chinese EVs out. The European Union , the U.K.'s biggest trading partner, has manufacturer-specific duties on Chinese EVs of up to 35.3%, in addition to a standard 10% import duty on all foreign cars. Now, the U.K. faces a difficult choice, as EU proposals may force it to impose tariffs to match the bloc's. At the weekend, The Sunday Times reported that U.K. Business Minister Jonathan Reynolds is considering matching the EU's levy on Chinese EVs to avoid the pain of so-called Made in Europe proposals, which could hurt domestic companies selling into the EU. A U.K. government spokesperson reiterated to CNBC that it had not imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs but added, "We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector's and UK's national interests." The Made in Europe legislation, part of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act , is designed to protect the bloc's industries from unfair international competition by prioritizing European-made goods. An EU official told the Financial Times in September that London would need to raise tariffs on Chinese EVs and align more closely with EU trade policy to avoid "Made in Europe" barriers. The decision is finely balanced, given Prime Minister Andy Burnham's desire to reset relations with the EU , which the U.K. formally left in 2020, and the likelihood of China responding with retaliatory measures. A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said it had expressed "serious concern" to Britain about the reports about potential tariffs. "China is firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products," a spokesperson said Tuesday. "We will continue to follow developments and respond accordingly," they said. Chinese automakers rapidly made inroads in the U.K. Chinese car brands have swiftly captured market share in the U.K. Analysis by Jato Dynamics found that registrations of Chinese automakers, or original equipment manufacturers, across both battery-electric and hybrid powertrains, rose to 519,424 between the start of January and the end of August, lifting their total market share to 28.1%. That's up sharply from 12.9% in the same period in 2025. Hybrids accounted for the larger increase, adding 62,655 registrations versus 32,565 for battery-electric vehicles. "That matters for policy," Paul Hilton, head of retail at Jato Dynamics, told CNBC by email. "Tariffs aimed only at Chinese-built battery EVs could slow one part of the expansion, but would not address hybrid growth, vehicles made outside China or the underlying advantages in cost, product cadence and supply chains," Hilton said. "A durable UK response should pair any evidence-based trade remedy with incentives for local production, competitive energy and battery costs, charging infrastructure, skills and alignment with European market-access rules." The bestselling car in the U.K. last month was not a Tesla or a Ford — but the Jaecoo 7 from China. The mid-size SUV, nicknamed the “Temu Range Rover,” starts at about £29,000 ($38,350) in the U.K., compared with roughly £45,500 for a Land Rover Discovery Sport. The Jaecoo 7's nationwide sales climbed to 10,814 in September, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, outpacing the Tesla Model 3, Ford Puma and Kia Sportage. Rico Luman, senior sector economist for transport and logistics at ING, said the growing policy gap between Britain and the EU is leaving the U.K. with limited options, besides tariffs, if it wants to maintain a level playing field with the bloc. Speaking to CNBC by email, Luman said exclusion from the Made in Europe initiative could have “significant consequences” for existing businesses, making closer alignment with EU trade policy increasingly difficult to avoid. "It's generally quite remarkable that batteries from China are exempted from EU tariffs," Luman said. "At the same time this is logical as production in Europe isn't up to speed and Europe lacks the rare earth minerals and refinery capacity behind it," he added.

events.title: South Africa protests turn violent amid rage over asylum ruling
events.summary: Several cars torched and foreign-run businesses forced to shut in Johannesburg’s Soweto and coastal city of Durban. Anti-migrant protests in two cities in South Africa have turned ⁠violent, with the government blaming disinformation about a court ruling on asylum seekers. Violence erupted on Thursday in Johannesburg’s Soweto township and the east coast port city of Durban, with two dozens cars set ablaze and foreign-run businesses forced to close, police said. list 1 of 3 Refugees in South Africa fear new attacks as September 30 deadline looms list 2 of 3 Dozens killed in two mass shootings in South Africa list 3 of 3 South African police discover body of 11th woman near Johannesburg The unrest followed demonstrations demanding that refugee centres stop processing asylum applications. Acting National Police Commissioner Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane on Thursday said 10 vehicles were torched in Johannesburg and 14 in Durban, where three people were arrested. In Soweto, a Reuters reporter saw residents carrying groceries out of a shop they said was owned by a person from Somalia, whom they chased away. Those residents fled after police arrived. In Durban, a Reuters reporter saw cars torched in the urban centre, where foreign-owned shops were also looted. AFP reporters in the city said police opened fire with rubber bullets to disperse protesters who reportedly set alight a business run by foreigners. The protesters are opposed to a July Constitutional Court decision that removes procedural barriers to seeking asylum, including for people who entered South Africa irregularly, lacked asylum transit visas, or missed reporting deadlines. On Thursday, the government’s Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration held an urgent briefing to address overcrowding at asylum offices after implementing the ruling. A day prior, the committee said all its offices were overwhelmed by the number of incoming applications. Government spokesperson William Baloyi said ‌the violence was triggered by people spreading deliberately false information about the constitutional court ruling. Baloyi said the court decision had been widely misrepresented, and that it did not automatically grant refugee status, permanent residence or other legal rights to undocumented migrants. “We are ⁠deeply concerned by what is going on now,” he added. Months of protests by populist, anti-immigrant groups against undocumented foreign nationals, demanding they leave South Africa, have led tens of thousands to flee, some repatriated by their governments. Three decades since apartheid ended, South Africa remains deeply unequal and about a third of people are out of work. Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fuelling crime and straining public services, although such claims are not supported by evidence.

events.title: ‘We are so excited to be back’: SpaceX’s recovery ship brought back four astronauts to Earth after an eight-month mission
events.summary: Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew. SpaceX brought the U.S., French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles. NASA’s Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France’s Sophie Adenot and Russia’s Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew’s homecoming. They couldn’t wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports. “We are so excited to be back on Planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station,” Meir radioed moments after splashing down. While still in orbit, she said the crew had “a lot of mixed, swirling emotions” and would miss the “extraordinary views of our home planet.” All four were out of their capsule within an hour, waving and pumping their fists in the air aboard SpaceX’s recovery ship. After a helicopter ride to shore, they were going to head for Houston. Meir and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them — NASA’s Mike Fincke, now retired — fell ill. It was NASA’s first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight. The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States’ 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert. Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost. In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef’s toque. Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy mustache — a space rarity — groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style mustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honor his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew mustaches in solidarity. Will his mustache disappear now that his mission is over? “It’s kind of become a little bit of my brand up here,” Hathaway said in August, “so I don’t know if it’ll go away right away or I’ll end up keeping it for a while.” Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the U.S., Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA’s count. ___ The Associated Press’ health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. events.title: 'Consumers should feel ripped off': How coffee brands have changed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Coffee manufacturers quietly change marketing after price squeeze Coffee brands are changing their marketing due to price pressures. ( ABC News: Brandon Long ) Major supermarket coffee brands have changed their marketing in response to bean prices surging to almost 50-year highs. Some companies no longer label their products as "100 per cent arabica" but instead as "coffee", or mix the more expensive arabica beans with cheaper robusta beans. Experts and consumers want companies to flag recipe changes to buyers. Major supermarket coffee brands have quietly changed their marketing in response to bean prices surging to almost 50-year highs. Labelling of premium arabica coffee beans, prized for their sweeter, more complex flavour, has switched in some cases from "100 per cent arabica" to being described as "coffee", or as a blend with robusta, a more bitter variety of the plant. While the change is legal and does not necessarily mean the coffee is worse, experts say consumers deserve to know when changes are made. Cairns pensioner Brian Rantzau said price was his most important consideration when buying coffee, but he also wanted clear information about changes to the product. "As a pensioner, you've got to mind every dollar," Mr Rantzau said. "It should really tell us what's in it, right?" Coles's Organic Fairtrade Gold Freeze Dried Coffee has doubled in price since 2024. ( ABC News: Brandon Long ) The price of Mr Rantzau's preferred Coles's Organic Fairtrade Gold Freeze Dried Coffee has doubled since early 2024, jumping from $4 per 100 grams to $8. Earlier this year, the product's "100 per cent arabica" description was also changed to simply read "instant coffee". Both versions may appear on supermarket shelves at the same time as stores gradually phase out the old recipe. Coles is phasing out 100 per cent arabica from the label of its Organic Fairtrade Gold Freeze Dried Coffee. Its website currently shows the old and new labels. ( Supplied: Coles ) Gold Coast mother Vicki Jarvis said she stopped buying the product. "It just kept going up, and now it's $8 a jar, and I just would not pay that," she said. "[But] if they've gone and changed what is actually in it, it should be written on the front of the label to let people know." A Coles spokesperson said product formulations may need to change occasionally in response to ingredient availability and supply conditions. "We work closely with our suppliers to ensure our products continue to meet our quality standards and provide great value for customers," the spokesperson said. Australian food labelling rules do not require coffee companies to identify the species of bean unless they make a specific claim about it. University of Queensland sensory scientist Heather Smyth said consumers had every right to feel ripped off. Heather Smyth says robusta is not a bad bean, but it is more bitter. ( Supplied: UQ ) Professor Smyth said consumers should be told when a product they had previously chosen for a key ingredient had changed. Jason Lilienstein runs a specialty roaster in Toowoomba, Queensland, and has only ever used arabica beans, bought directly from Colombian farmers he has met personally. "Arabica has always been the preferred, high-quality bean," he said. Jason Lilienstein runs specialty roaster Six Of One in Toowoomba. ( ABC News: Brandon Long ) Robusta is not necessarily bad, he said, but he has not found one good enough for his blends. "I haven't found it of sufficient quality to put in any of our coffee at this stage." He said his customers tended to focus less on the species of bean and more on its flavour and origin. Coffee prices have soared recently, with arabica prices reaching $15.40 a kilogram, while robusta hit $8.73 a kilogram — levels not seen since 1977 — piling pressure onto manufacturers. While prices have fallen about 35 per cent from their peak ahead of what is expected to be a record Brazilian harvest, some say consumers may not see lower prices as other costs continue to rise. Some coffee manufacturers have responded by adjusting the composition of their blends. Australian-owned coffee manufacturer Vittoria's website once prominently promoted its coffee as "100 per cent arabica", stating in 2020: "At Vittoria coffee, we make no excuses, all our coffee is 100 per cent arabica". The Vittoria website compares arabica to robusta beans in 2020. ( Supplied: Wayback Machine/Vittoria ) And in mid-2025, the company's website described robusta as an "inferior quality bean". But a few months later, that message had changed.

events.title: How the cast of 'The Social Reckoning' compares to the real-life people they're playing
events.summary: Jeremy Allen White, Mikey Madison, and Aaron Sorkin attend the Paris premiere of "The Social Reckoning." Yaro Roland/Getty Images Aaron Sorkin's new film "The Social Reckoning" is about the 2021 Facebook whistleblower scandal. Jeremy Strong stars as Mark Zuckerberg opposite Mikey Madison as the whistleblower Frances Haugen. Jeremy Allen White plays Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz. Aaron Sorkin's " The Social Reckoning " sees Jeremy Strong portray Mark Zuckerberg during the 2021 Facebook whistleblower scandal. The new film, which hits theaters on October 9, is the much-anticipated follow-up to 2010's "The Social Network." It also stars Mikey Madison as the whistleblower Frances Haugen and Jeremy Allen White as the award-winning technology reporter Jeff Horwitz. Here's how the cast compares to the real-life people they're playing in "The Social Reckoning." Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg, Facebook founder and Meta CEO. Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Reckoning." Sony; David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Jesse Eisenberg , who played Zuckerberg in "The Social Network," told Variety that he was asked to reprise the role for "The Social Reckoning," but declined. "I just told him I'm moving in different directions in my life," Eisenberg said of Sorkin, who wrote and directed the new film. "I don't want to be associated with that character, but all of my reasons for not wanting to do the movie have nothing to do with how wonderful the movie is, and will be, and I'm sure is already." Instead, Jeremy Strong was cast as the adult version of Facebook's founder. As he did while playing Kendall Roy in HBO's billionaire-family drama "Succession," Strong went method for the role, according to Sorkin. "Jeremy does a lot of his own work," Sorkin told NYT's "The Interview." "I told all the other actors in his scenes: 'Guys, he's not going to be hanging out with you at craft service. He's not going to be yucking it up with you between takes. He's probably not going to speak to you at all." "He is going to treat you the way he imagines Mark treats the people around him.' And that's what happened," he continued. "You cannot argue with the results." Mikey Madison plays Frances Haugen, also known as the "Facebook whistleblower." Mikey Madison plays Frances Haugen in "The Social Reckoning." Sony; Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Frances Haugen is a data scientist and former product manager on Facebook's civic misinformation team, also called the civic integrity team. In 2021, Haugen became known as the "Facebook whistleblower" when she leaked tens of thousands of internal Facebook documents to reporters and lawmakers. She testified at a Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection that Facebook's algorithm prioritizes divisive and extremist posts , and she advocated for governmental regulation and stronger oversight. Haugen told The Hollywood Reporter that she didn't get a chance to meet Mikey Madison, who won the 2025 best actress Oscar for "Anora," before Madison stepped into the whistleblower role for "The Social Reckoning." "She was extremely busy that year because she'd won the Oscar just a few months before," Haugen said. Still, Haugen said she hopes that Zuckerberg will watch the film. "When I sat there for two hours and watched it, I was like, 'Wow, this is a thing that has really impacted the course of my life, and I have done a wonderful job of being in denial about that,'" Haugen said. "I hope if Mark watches the movie, he has the same experience." "He should be reminded that, hey, you are making choices," she continued. "You don't have to be the head of Meta forever. You don't have to play this role in society." Jeremy Allen White plays Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz. Jeremy Allen White plays Jeff Horwitz in "The Social Reckoning." Sean Zanni/Getty Images for Sony Pictures Entertainment; Sony Jeff Horwitz, a former technology reporter for The Wall Street Journal, is now a San Francisco-based reporter for Reuters. Horwitz won several journalism awards for " The Facebook Files ," a 2021 investigative series based largely on the internal documents provided by Haugen. Jeremy Allen White, who previously helmed the 2025 Bruce Springsteen biopic  "Deliver Me from Nowhere," recently  told The Independent  that he was initially hesitant about taking on the role in "The Social Reckoning." "I was really nervous about playing another real person," he said. "I didn't know if I wanted that responsibility entirely." Bill Burr plays Charlie, a character inspired by Facebook investor Roger McNamee. Roger McNamee in 2012 and Bill Burr in "The Social Reckoning." David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Sony Sorkin told Vanity Fair that, due to potential legal concerns, he didn't name Bill Burr's character in "The Social Reckoning" after Roger McNamee , a venture capitalist and early Facebook investor . In 2019, McNamee published a scathing book about Zuckerberg, titled "Zucked: Waking Up to the Facebook Catastrophe," which is listed in the movie's credits — along with Haugen's memoir and Horwitz's book, "Broken Code" — as additional research materials. Sorkin said he spoke to all three "a lot" while writing the script. Sorkin described McNamee as "a kind of consigliere to Mark until they had a big falling out over the direction of the company." "Originally, it was made clear to me that I couldn't call Bill Burr's character Roger McNamee, not because there was going to be a problem with Roger, who was on board, but because there might be a problem with Facebook and the situation that I have Mark and Bill Burr's character in the movie," Sorkin told Vanity Fair. "So that character had to become inspired by Roger McNamee, which is what it is now." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A FEMA administrator created the Waffle House Index after looking for a place to eat during hurricane clean up and only Waffle House was open
events.summary: Golden hash browns, gravy-smothered biscuits and crispy waffles with a hearty helping of syrup are among the classic Southern comfort foods. But when hurricanes tear through Southeastern towns, the hot meals and bold yellow signs of the local Waffle House provide another kind of comfort. If a Waffle House stays open in town, even in a limited capacity, neighbors are reassured that the coming storm is unlikely to cause devastation. A closed location of the dependable diner chain has come to indicate impending disaster. The metric is known as the Waffle House Index. What might sound like silly logic has become one of the most reliable ways for Southerners — and even federal officials — to gauge a storm’s severity and identify communities most in need of immediate aid. What is the Waffle House Index? The South’s favorite disaster authority provides an informal measure of how significantly a storm will affect or has affected a community. A map of the chain’s over 1,900 locations, concentrated in the Southeast and mid-Atlantic, helps residents of storm-prone states assess whether they’re likely to lose power, experience severe flooding or endure other extreme conditions that might cause a resilient restaurant to close its doors. For some, it’s a telltale sign of whether they need to evacuate. Waffle House is known not just for serving breakfast 24/7, 365 days a year, but also for its disaster preparedness. For decades, people across the South have noticed that the local Waffle House seemed to be the only business still open during a storm or the first to reopen after it passed. The restaurant chain’s reputation for remaining open when people desperately needed a place to warm up, charge devices and grab a hot meal became a fairly reliable — albeit amusing — resource to help track recovery efforts. The company even operates its own storm center. How does the index work? Waffle House’s social media shares color-coded maps of its restaurant locations in certain regions that will soon be hit or are recovering from storm damage. The Federal Emergency Management Agency also offers some live tracking. Green means the location is serving a full menu, indicating minimal damage in the surrounding area. The lights are on and the syrup is flowing. Yellow means the restaurant is serving a limited menu, a signal that it’s pulling power from a generator and might have a low food supply. The area might not have running water or electricity, but there’s enough gas to fry up bacon for hungry customers. Red means the location is closed, a sign of unsafe operating conditions and severe destruction to the restaurant or nearby communities. How did the index start? Former FEMA Administrator Craig Fugate has said he thought up the Waffle House Index while leading Florida’s emergency management efforts in 2004. He had been searching for something to eat while surveying the devastation left by Hurricane Charley and was only able to find a Waffle House serving a limited menu. His team began to notice other open Waffle Houses in communities without power or running water. The restaurants eventually became a key feature on a color-coded map that his team provided to help the public and local officials identify where storm damage was most severe. Fugate continued to use his color-coded map when he joined FEMA under President Barack Obama. He was the agency’s administrator in 2011 when a deadly tornado tore through the town of Joplin, Missouri. Both of the town’s Waffle Houses reportedly stayed open. The restaurant chain’s disaster readiness is no coincidence. Seven locations were destroyed and 100 more shut down in 2005 during Hurricane Katrina, but company executives saw business skyrocket at restaurants that reopened quickly. They soon embraced a business strategy centered around keeping their restaurants operable during and after a disaster, according to the company’s website. The chain said it has invested in portable generators, bought a mobile command center and trained employees on what they can still serve if they lose electricity. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Average long-term US mortgage rate rises to highest level in nearly 3 years
events.summary: Mortgage rates marched higher for the seventh week in a row, driving the average long-term U.S. home loan rate to its highest level in nearly three years Mortgage rates marched higher for the seventh week in a row, driving the average long-term U.S. home loan rate to its highest level in nearly three years. The benchmark 30-year fixed-rate mortgage climbed to 7.40% from 7.28% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.30%. The average rate is now the highest it’s been since Nov. 16, 2023, when it was at 7.44%. The housing market has been stuck in a rut this year in large part because of rising mortgage rates, which can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power and prompting many to put off buying a home. Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also rose this week. That average rate increased to 6.73% from 6.60% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.53%. Mortgage rates have been climbing in the months since the start of the U.S. war with Iran in late February. The recent run-up in rates also reflects heightened bond market volatility as surging oil prices due to the war fuel inflation worries. Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen to its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation , big government debt loads and other factors. The yield was at 5.29% at midday Thursday on the bond market. That's well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran began. Iran live updates: Trump says US won't attack Iran again ahead of midterms Mortgage rates hit highest level in nearly 20 months Why are gas prices still high even as traffic improves in the Strait of Hormuz? In late February, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage briefly dipped to 5.98%, its lowest level going back to late 2022. The 1.42 percentage point increase in the rate since then translates roughly into an additional monthly cost of $376 for a borrower financing a $400,000 home loan at the current average rate. Depending on a borrower’s income, credit and other factors, they may qualify for a rate on a 30-year mortgage that is below or above the current average. The U.S. housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. Last month, the National Association of Realtors said that existing home sales fell 2% in August from July to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.98 million units. That was their slowest annual pace in more than a year. The sharp rise in mortgage rates has many would-be homebuyers putting their home shopping plans on hold. Mortgage applications, which include loans to buy a home or refinance an existing mortgage, fell for the fifth week in a row last week as mortgage rates kept climbing, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Higher rates are also keeping many homeowners from refinancing their existing mortgage. Home loan refinance applications fell last week to their lowest level since January 2025 and were less than half last year’s pace, according to the MBA. events.title: Vance says the US is suspending permanent visa residency program for Microsoft
events.summary: Vance announced the visa changes at a press conference Thursday. Alex Wong/Getty Images The Trump administration says it's suspending Microsoft and Adobe from a federal program used to sponsor foreign workers. JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” the VP said. The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft and Adobe from a federal program that companies use to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said Thursday during a press conference. Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM. The program is an initial step that employers generally must complete before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based green card, requiring them to show that no qualified and available US workers could fill the role. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said. Microsoft filed more certified PERM applications than any other employer in the first three quarters of this fiscal year, with 1504, according to a Business Insider analysis, and an additional 174 were filed for subsidiaries LinkedIn and Activision. Adobe filed 168 in the same time period. The announcement came just over a week after Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella sat two seats away from Vance at President Donald Trump's White House "Super Intelligence" luncheon, a gathering of tech executives focused on AI. A Microsoft spokesperson pointed Business Insider to a blog post the company published Thursday, which said “the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans.” Microsoft wrote that roughly 80% of the about 6,000 H-1B visa applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees, rather than to hire new people. It said the remaining applications were for people already legally in the US and amounted to 1% of its US workforce. Adobe did not respond to Business Insider's request for comment. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the administration was also suspending Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini from the program. The IT companies are among the largest users of PERM and other employment-based immigration pathways in the US. Vance also said the administration would investigate nine universities, including Harvard, Yale, and Stanford, over allegations that they used J-1 exchange visas to undercut American wages. Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served. The announcement is the latest escalation for the administration against companies that rely on highly skilled foreign workers, particularly through the H-1B visa system . Microsoft is one of the biggest employers of H-1B workers in the US. It was not immediately clear how long the suspension would last or what it would mean for Microsoft employees whose permanent-residency cases are already pending. The process is already slow: The Labor Department says PERM applications took an average of 336 calendar days to process in August. Correction: October 8, 2026 — An earlier version of this story misstated who announced Adobe's suspension. It was Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Sports gambling seeps even deeper into Wall Street's world as hundreds of pro team ETFs emerge
events.summary: Prediction markets have blurred the line between financial trading and gambling, and now fund companies have filed for hundreds of ETFs that track individual NHL and MLB teams through futures tied to single-season team performance metrics. There are sports ETFs that hold publicly traded shares of companies that own teams, a conventional investment approach allowing for balance sheet analysis, including Gabelli Funds' GOLS and Amplify Funds' planned PROS ETF. But investing experts put the individual team funds, none of which have yet launched, closer to wagering than investing, while issuers say they offer a transparent way for fans to put money behind their teams. In 1989, all-time hits leader Pete Rose was banned from Major League Baseball for life because of his gambling activities. He wasn't reinstated until last year, months after his death in 2024. Fast-forward to today, and Pete Rose's gambling might seem like just another day on Wall Street as financial firms expand the ways fans can put money behind their teams, beyond a beer and a $15 hot dog. You may soon be able to buy a ticker for your favorite hockey team, and it isn't a stake in the franchise. Multiple asset managers have filed to launch dozens of ETFs, one for every NHL team, with MLB baseball team funds filed as well, all built on new futures contracts that track a team's season statistics. None has begun trading but in all, hundreds of ETFs that track the single-season performance of one professional team across a mix of statistical categories have been filed at the SEC for approval. Some finance experts see the development as lacking any nuance whatsoever. "The line between gambling and investing has not simply been blurred, it has been erased," said Robert Johnson, a professor of finance at Creighton University. Among fund companies getting in on the novel trend are VolatilityShares , LeagueShares, Roundhill Investments , and Rex Financial . None of the four companies responded to requests for comment. Asset managers typically cannot publicly comment during the period between when funds are filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission for approval and when they become effective, if approved. Rex, a Miami-based ETF issuer, announced Sept. 21 that it was launching Alpha Sports Holdings, a new subsidiary built to turn team performance into exchange-traded funds. REX has filed with the SEC for BaseballShares and HockeyShares, suites of ETFs that would track Major League Baseball and National Hockey League teams through futures contracts that CME Group, the derivatives exchange, lists on indexes built by FutureSports, an index company. The underlying CME futures , which began trading for NHL teams in late September, need to first establish a trading history. MLB team futures are scheduled to launch on the CME on Oct. 12. Each team's index opens the season at a set number and moves as the team racks up statistics, including runs scored, stolen bases and strikeouts for baseball, then resets in the offseason. "The sports industry generates hundreds of billions of dollars a year, but there has never been a liquid, transparent investment product tied directly to what happens in live games," said Greg King, CEO of Alpha Sports, in a press release. "Alpha Sports exists to build that product for passionate investors who want to participate in the fortunes of their favorite teams." Johnson, though, said the sports-themed ETFs are far more gaming than investing. "I thought that the ETF world had jumped the shark with the introduction of the 2X and 3X leveraged and inverse ETFs. In my mind these were simply vehicles for short term speculators. But, at least these vehicles were based upon assets. The new structures — and I call them structures, not assets — are simply gambling dressed up as investing," Johnson said. In fact, the proposed team ETFs include in some cases leveraged versions of trades on single-team performance. The boom in prediction markets is already blurring the lines between sports wagering and market trading, with regulatory battles intensifying over the distinction — CNBC reported on Thursday that the NFL is pushing for prediction markets to be regulated by state gambling authorities. Unlike prediction markets contracts, the sports team ETFs are tracking futures off an index rather than a single event (e.g. win or loss). But while structurally contracts in this market have a role to play for investors, in the case of sports performance, Johnson says the case is weak. "They have societal value in that parties are able to hedge natural positions and transact with other speculators willing to bear that risk. This allows a more optimal allocation of risk," Johnson said. But he added that is not the case when individual investors are making bets on the performance of sports teams they follow. "There are no natural positions being hedged. In the aggregate, they destroy wealth," Johnson said.

events.title: There can be only one: Google Cloud casts Gemini as your enterprise AI hero
events.summary: Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said that Gemini will be "your new single, universal agent for work," a declaration as unassailable as Google's history of consistency, customer service, and long-term product support. Long-term here means a median lifespan of about 4.1 years and a mean lifespan of about 5.4 years across 308 discontinued products and services. That doesn't include enduring successes like Gmail and Search. Perhaps Gemini is destined for that level of longevity. In a blog post adapted from the prepared remarks he spoke at the Gemini at Work 2026 event – and what could be more appropriate for Google than to herald Gemini with a derivative work? – Kurian laid out his vision for an AI service known as Bard only two years ago. Gemini, he said, has your business context – which is to say, data – and thus can be used for various tasks like question answering, content creation, and coding. "It plans the work, uses skills and tools, connects to your systems, and brings back something finished — inside the documents, the inbox, and the developer environments you already work in," Kurian said. "It chooses the best model for the job, has built-in cost controls, and most importantly, has the security, administration, and governance required by your company." Kurian's actual remarks at the event were more succinct. "Today, Gemini became an agent," he said. "You give it objectives, not just instructions. It plans the work, uses custom skills and tools, connects to your systems and brings back something finished." You might wonder what role you play in all this as a Google Enterprise customer, when Gemini is planning, executing, and delivering. There's always Minesweeper and hunting for a job that involves physical labor and human dignity. Sundai Pichai, CEO of Google parent Alphabet, opened the Google Cloud event with the Recitation of Self-Reported Statistics, a common ritual in the technocratic liturgy. "Enterprise adoption is moving faster than most people realize," he said. "Nearly 80 percent of Google Cloud customers are using our AI products. And they are not just using it, they're using it intensely. Nearly 500 enterprise customers have each processed over 1 trillion tokens on our platform in the last year." Pichai took time to praise Google's latest model, Gemini 4 Argon, noting that it outperforms rival models Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, and GPT-6 Astra on the DeepSWE v1.1 coding benchmark with a score of 77.9 percent. And within Google, he said, Gemini 4 Argon has reduced post-submit code rollbacks by 30 percent while increasing agentic code submissions from employees by 35 percent. Kurian then continued the customer success report by citing various claimed productivity gains from Google Cloud customers. Japanese telecom biz NTT Docomo, he said, has saved 450,000 hours annually using data agents. Your mileage may vary. But Kurian's emphasis on the solipsism of Gemini isn't entirely accurate. Gemini is unified in theory. It works within Gmail, Dive, Docs, Slides, Sheets, Chat, and Calendar as a single surface. It can be accessed across iOS, Android, Windows, and Mac desktops, not to mention third-party applications where enabled or during headless operations. It resides in Google Cloud so it retains contextual info. But no agent is an island. Just like the stellar twins for which it's named, Gemini has more than one moving part. "It can dynamically create a roster of sub-agents — temporary, job-specific agents, each with their own identity — to tackle multi-step tasks," said Kurian, perhaps overestimating the appeal of naming spawned processes. And the Gemini agent is distinct from the various models it may call upon, even if one of those might be Gemini 4 Argon. "It runs each job on the model that fits best — orchestrating across our Gemini family of models and Claude models from Anthropic today, and other leading private and open models in the future — to deliver optimal quality and lower your costs," Kurian explained. During the event, Kurian highlighted how Gemini inherits existing enterprise controls. "Every Gemini agent has an identity of its own, separate from your identity," he said. "Your policies reach it the very same way they reach your people: set the policies once, apply them everywhere rather than agency by agent. You set its budget before it starts and that budget covers the whole cost of the work." That's the promise, but of course the very existence of enterprise cost control mechanisms suggests costs can get out of hand. It was only two months ago that Google introduced flexible billing and cost controls for agents. Managing AI spending, however, remains an unsolved problem. As noted by the Wall Street Journal recently, "Spending on AI Is Becoming Almost Impossible for Businesses to Budget." Back in July, AI cost management company Coworker AI observed there were two Gemini Enterprise products that could easily be confused. Now we're told there's just one. Enjoy it while it lasts. ®

events.title: Major League Baseball proposes shortening its regular season as it pushes for a salary cap
events.summary: Major League Baseball proposed shortening its regular season to 154 games from 162 as it tries to convince players to approve a salary cap in the league's next collective bargaining agreement. The new shortened regular season schedule would begin in 2029. The Major League Baseball Players Association responded to the proposed changes in a statement that said, "Players will weigh in on these proposals and we will respond at the bargaining table." Major League Baseball proposed shortening its regular season to 154 games from 162 as it attempts to convince players to approve a salary cap in the league's next collective bargaining agreement. The new shortened schedule would begin in 2029. MLB's CBA expires Dec. 1, after the conclusion of this season's World Series. The most contentious issue is the introduction of a salary cap on players. MLB is the only major American sports league without a cap. The league has failed to convince the players' union to adopt one in several previous CBA negotiations. A 154-game season was used between 1904 and 1960, except for 1918 and 1919 when the schedule was abbreviated because of World War I. For the past 66 years, 162 regular season games has been the standard, though some seasons have been shortened. Lopping off eight games "is good for player health, while also creating a new national broadcast window to showcase our most exciting teams and players," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "A shorter regular season unlocks making October even better for our fans — with fewer weekday afternoon games, a longer Division Series, and more opportunities to see the game's best pitchers on the biggest stage." As part of the proposal, MLB wants to cement Monday as an exclusive broadcast window for one or two games to "increase national exposure for the sport." The league could conceivably sell a package of Monday-only games to a streaming service looking to increase subscriber and advertising revenue. Every team not playing in the national game or games would have an off day. Teams that play Monday would be off on Thursday, MLB said. In addition to lowering the number of regular season games, MLB would extend the divisional round of the playoffs to seven games from five and would allow the higher-seeded teams in both the wild card round and in the divisional round to choose their lower-seeded opponent. The Major League Baseball Players Association responded to the MLB's proposed changes by claiming the league "once again made clear that all of its proposals are contingent on players' agreement to a salary cap, a system that guts player rights and compensation, as well as its other anti-player proposals." An MLB spokesperson confirmed that Thursday's proposed changes are contingent on adopting a cap – and a salary floor, which would force teams to spend a certain amount on players. Still, the MLBPA said it would review the proposed changes. "Players will weigh in on these proposals and we will respond at the bargaining table," MLBPA said in a statement. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Space agency claims steady progress on lunar reactor plans, but offers little evidence to back it up Margaret Hamilton, software pioneer who helped put humans on the Moon, dies at 90 11 hours ago Google teams with nuclear power giant to give reactors a tune-up 2 days ago Scientists find planet made on new matter recipe, and it formed after a Red Giant ate a solar system 2 days ago Google launches first datacenter satellite and research that finds orbiting bit barns can work 6 days ago Boeing's Calamity Capsule gets another shot at the ISS taxi business 9 days ago NASA and the Department of Energy have agreed to expand their collaboration on the space agency's nuclear ambitions, as administrator Jared Isaacman pushes ahead with a tight deadline to launch a fission-powered spacecraft to Mars. “We are entering the ‘Nuclear NASA-era,’” Isaacman said at a signing ceremony where he and Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed a joint memorandum of understanding. The MOU, the full text of which doesn’t appear to have been published, establishes a framework for collaboration on space nuclear technology. Per NASA, the agreement “unites both agencies” in pursuing its objectives, with work to include research and fuel production, testing, launch integration, and operations. “Nuclear power will allow us to go farther, operate longer, and field more capable spacecraft and instruments than ever before,” Isaacman added. “The work we’re doing today is laying the foundation for the fission-poweuing NASA’s objred spacecraft of tomorrow and opening an entirely new frontier for exploration and discovery.” NASA has been making big plans to launch nuclear reactors into space since earlier this year when the agency paused work on the orbital Lunar Gateway station in favor of a base on the Moon’s surface. Those plans include a nuclear reactor to power said base , which NASA said on Thursday it intends to have ready for launch by 2030, giving the agency precious little time to meet such an ambitious goal. NASA has provided little evidence the initiative is on track, aside from noting in Thursday's announcement that it is “making steady progress” on Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1), the unit it wants to use to power its Moon base. Before then, however, NASA faces an even tighter deadline for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1), which it intends to use to power a nuclear-propelled spacecraft scheduled to launch in December 2028. That’s just over two years away, mind you, and NASA has provided little public evidence of progress on the spacecraft, which it has dubbed "Freedom." NASA provided details [PDF] for SR-1 back in March when it paused work on the Lunar Gateway, describing the spacecraft as being mostly constructed from a repurposed spacecraft bus that NASA had almost completed for a previous project. The reactor would produce more than 20 kilowatts of electricity to power Freedom's electric thrusters on its journey to Mars, where it would deliver three Ingenuity-class helicopters to survey potential future human landing sites. Whether that’ll happen on any sort of timeline that resembles the current one is anyone’s guess, but let’s face it: NASA doesn’t exactly have a great track record for getting things done on time. The Government Accountability Office has been watching NASA’s lunar return ambitions for years, and has been noting for nearly a decade that its timelines were more fantasy than reality. In the past couple of years, the GAO has noted that existing NASA timelines were tight enough that any one mishap could push them back considerably, and massive workforce reductions under the second Trump administration haven’t helped matters. The Artemis missions to return humans to the Moon have also suffered a few hitches. Artemis I and Artemis II faced multiple delays, and NASA has since changed Artemis III's objectives, turning the planned 2027 lunar landing into a demonstration mission in low Earth orbit, in part to address concerns about the readiness of lunar landing systems, including SpaceX's Starship.
