events.title: A timeline of former Prince Andrew's ties to Jeffrey Epstein, from the Virginia Giuffre lawsuit to his arrest in 2026
events.summary: Prince Andrew in December 2023. Adrian DENNIS / AFP via Getty Images Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office. On Thursday, a judge said that the search warrants used to search his homes were unlawful. The arrest followed years of public scrutiny over Mountbatten-Windsor's ties to Jeffrey Epstein. The investigation into Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor received a setback. Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, was arrested by Thames Valley Police , the local force for southeast England, at a royal home on suspicion of misconduct in public office related to his ties to Jeffrey Epstein in February 2026. On Thursday, a judge said that search warrants issued at the time of his arrest were unlawful. Still, the Thames Valley Police's investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor's ties to Epstein continues. Mountbatten-Windsor has repeatedly denied any involvement with Epstein's sex-trafficking crimes. However, his relationship with Epstein has been under scrutiny for over a decade, as Virginia Giuffre named him in a lawsuit she filed against Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell in 2015. That scrutiny only intensified after the release of documents in the Epstein files in early 2026. According to emails released, the former prince appeared to forward reports related to his work as UK trade envoy to Epstein in 2010 and 2011. King Charles said in a statement at the time of the arrest that "the law must take its course" and that the authorities had the royal family's "full and wholehearted support and co-operation." Here's a timeline of Mountbatten-Windsor's connection to Epstein. 1999: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and Jeffrey Epstein reportedly met through Ghislaine Maxwell. Melania Trump, Prince Andrew, Gwendolyn Beck, and Jeffrey Epstein at a party at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach in 2000. Davidoff Studios/Getty Images As the BBC reported , Ghislaine Maxwell introduced Epstein to Mountbatten-Windsor in 1999. The trio remained friends throughout the early 2000s, with Epstein and Maxwell attending parties at Windsor Castle and Sandringham. The three were also photographed together at events, including a 2000 party at Mar-a-Lago with Donald and Melania Trump and the 2000 Royal Ascot. Epstein and Maxwell were also photographed at Princess Beatrice's 18th birthday party in July 2006, the BBC reported . In 2008, Epstein pleaded guilty to solicitation of prostitution and solicitation of prostitution with a minor under the age of 18, and was sentenced to 18 months. Mountbatten-Windsor visited Epstein in New York in December 2010, just four months after Epstein's release. Mountbatten-Windsor said it was a "mistake and an error" to visit Epstein after he was convicted of the sex crime in a statement released by Buckingham Palace in August 2019. April 2015: Virginia Giuffre sued Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell for defamation, naming Mountbatten-Windsor in the suit. Prince Andrew and Virginia Giuffre, then known as Virginia Roberts, along with Ghislaine Maxwell. This photo was included in an affidavit where Giuffre claimed Prince Andrew directed her to have sex with him. Florida Southern District Court In 2015, Virginia Giuffre brought a defamation case against Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell , alleging that the pair had sex-trafficked her starting in 2000, when she was known as Virginia Roberts. Giuffre alleged that Epstein forced her to have sex with Mountbatten-Windsor in his New York mansion, in London, and on Epstein's private island in the US Virgin Islands in 2001 when she was 17.  However, the allegation was thrown out and struck from the record by a judge, who said it was "immaterial and impertinent to the central claim" in the case at the time. August 2019: Giuffre's allegations were made public when documents from the 2015 case were unsealed. Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor at he funeral of Britain's Prince Philip in April 2021. Chris Jackson/Pool via Reuters Further details about Giuffre's allegations against Mountbatten-Windsor were made public in 2019, after documents from the 2015 defamation case were unsealed . In the documents related to sex-trafficking charges against Epstein, witness Johanna Sjoberg told investigators about a sexual incident that she said happened, and involved herself, Maxwell, Mountbatten-Windsor, Giuffre, and a puppet of the prince. "Andrew and Virginia sat on the couch, and they put the puppet ... on her lap," Sjoberg was quoted as saying in the documents. "I sat on Andrew's lap, I believe on my own volition, and they took the puppet's hands and put it on Virginia's breast, and so Andrew put his on mine." Buckingham Palace denied Mountbatten-Windsor's alleged involvement with Giuffre in a statement at the time. "It is emphatically denied that The Duke of York had any form of sexual contact or relationship with Virginia Roberts," the palace's statement read. "Any claim to the contrary is false and without foundation." August 2019: Giuffre said Mountbatten-Windsor "knows exactly what he's done" after the royal denied involvement in Epstein's sex-trafficking operation. Prince Andrew, left, and Jeffrey Epstein, right. AP/Sang Tan, Patrick McMullan via Getty Images Mountbatten-Windsor made a statement after Epstein was found dead in his Manhattan jail cell on August 10, 2019, saying he sympathized "with everyone who has been affected and wants some form of closure." Mountbatten-Windsor added that during the time he knew Epstein, he did not witness or "suspect any behavior of the sort that subsequently led to his arrest and conviction." Giuffre responded with a statement of her own. Speaking to reporters outside a Manhattan court at the time, she said the prince "knows exactly what he's done, and I hope he comes clean about it." November 2019: The then-prince stepped down from his royal duties days after a disastrous BBC "Newsnight" interview. BBC News/YouTube Discussing the allegations in a BBC "Newsnight" interview with host Emily Maitlis on November 16, 2019, Mountbatten-Windsor suggested that a photo appearing to show him with his hand around Giuffre's waist  was fake. He also said during the interview that on the night Giuffre alleged they had dinner, partied at a club in London called Tramp, and later had sex, that he was at home with his daughters, Beatrice and Eugenie. The interview was perceived negatively and labeled a "car crash" by much of the British media. Following the interview, a string of charities, businesses, and universities cut ties with Mountbatten-Windsor , and on November 20, 2019, the duke announced he would step back from his royal duties. events.title: Trump Administration Cuts Off Access to a Major Immigration Program for Workers at Microsoft and Adobe
events.summary: The Trump administration will no longer allow Microsoft and other tech companies to participate in a program that allows H-1B visa holders to apply for green cards, one of the most common pathways for skilled foreign workers seeking permanent residency in the United States. In addition to Microsoft, administration officials said on Thursday that software giant Adobe and IT companies including Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata will be suspended from the PERM program, the Labor Department's permanent labor certification program. PERM is a key step for H-1B visa holders to gain permanent residency, requiring employers to prove that there are no American workers who would be suitable for the applicant's permanent job opportunity. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said that the agency is investigating whether these companies committed fraud, undercutting American workers by hiring foreign employees. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, singled out Microsoft. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance said during a press conference. In a statement provided by Microsoft representative Kaitlin Haskins, the company said it “only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," adding that it develops its workforce by "strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world." Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment. The suspension marks a victory for tech workers who have complained about unfairly losing out on jobs to immigrant workers. Jobs Now, an advocacy group composed of US citizens working in big tech, celebrated Vance’s announcement on its X account with a video of dancing crabs. The group publicizes otherwise difficult-to-find PERM job postings and says it helped Americans apply to nearly 500,000 jobs across 7,000 employers between last January and this past July. The organization and its members have also filed complaints against tech companies about alleged abuse of the PERM system, and have called for a number of changes to the employment immigration system. “Every job in America should be offered to an American first, no exceptions,” the group told WIRED in an unsigned statement. This isn't the first time tech companies have been targeted over PERM. Earlier this year, OpenAI and a company it acquired agreed to settle accusations from the Trump administration about violating rules for the program. Apple reached a similar deal in 2023. The administration's disparagement of H-1B visas—one of the most common work visas in the US—has sent waves of panic through Silicon Valley since Trump's reelection. Tech companies are some of the H1-B program's biggest users: So far in the fiscal year 2026 , the top three employers with the most visas approved are Amazon, Tata, and Infosys. Microsoft is No. 5, with 3,688 visas approved in 2026; in 2025, 6,258 visas were approved. According to the company, 80 percent of last year's visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees, not to hire new people. "The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our US workforce," Microsoft’s statement said. It's unclear if Thursday’s announcement would affect the ability of employees at these companies to apply for H1-B visas themselves. The Office of the Vice President and the Department of Labor did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for clarity on if the suspension would impact those seeking H-1B visas. "It's one thing if you want to bring in someone like Elon Musk" who aims to "build something great in America," Vance said on Thursday. He equated the current state of the H-1B program to bringing "indentured servants" into the US, taking jobs away from American workers. (Musk, who was born in South Africa, came to the US via Canada to pursue a bachelor's degree at the University of Pennsylvania.) The announcement came shortly before Trump was set to award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. When asked about the upcoming event, Vance said, "We’re going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we’re also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first.” Vance also said that the administration is investigating nine universities to see if they might be committing fraud with the J-1 visa program, which allows international candidates to study and conduct research in the US.

events.title: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
events.summary: Jorge Moreno (left) says "vulture funds" are hiking up rents, while Pierina Nicuray points out that there is "a lack of homes" in Spain Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square. Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis , she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause. "It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes." She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb." Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees. "There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own. "They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home." His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government. On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate". Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month. Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay. Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday . Protesters at Pueta del Sol have been paying tributes to Maricarmen Abascal Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market. Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years. When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent. "When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security." Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista. In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%. Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern. A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market. Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes. Carmen Pérez says high rental costs have affected her health However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation. He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies. Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain. "When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years." The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes. The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million. There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs. Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.

events.title: Veterans sue government over 'mass and routine' medical data sharing
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Veterans sue Australian government over sharing of medical data Alan Ashmore said he was "staggered" by the volume of information transmitted to UniSA. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) A new class action alleges the federal government breached privacy laws by disclosing thousands of ex-ADF members' medical records to an Australian university. The MATES healthcare program was shut down by the Veterans' Affairs Minister in 2024. The case will be heard in the Victorian Supreme Court and the Department of Veterans' Affairs declined to comment while proceedings are underway. A class action has been launched against the federal government over allegations of "mass and routine sharing" of veterans' medical records over 20 years. On Wednesday, Gordon Legal served the Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) with a privacy breach claim, following a two-year investigation into a health program which accessed thousands of Australian military veterans' data. Medicines Advice and Therapeutics Education Services (MATES) was administered by the now-defunct University of South Australia (UniSA) under contract from 2004 to 2024, when the Veterans' Affairs Minister shut it down after an ethics review. Gordon Legal partner Seb O'Meara, who worked on the Robodebt class action settlement, said anyone who used a DVA healthcare card while MATES operated — around 300,000, including bereaved spouses – could register for the lawsuit. Lawyers for the plaintiff will alleged most veterans were "not aware of the MATES program" and "did not provide consent … for the disclosure of their personal information". The firm will seek damages for breach of confidence in the Victorian Supreme Court. Gordon Legal estimated more than 300,000 veterans and family members with DVA healthcare cards had been auto-enrolled in MATES. ( AAP: Tracey Nearmy ) Case about 'what government can do with our information' DVA's website said MATES was about "preventing adverse health outcomes, such as hospitalisations or unwanted side effects, for veterans who take multiple medications". Their DVA healthcare card payments — equivalent to Medicare data — were periodically sent to UniSA, including their name, address, accepted medical conditions and treatments. The patient's identity was initially obscured, but if health risks were found, "a restricted and small number" of staff identified them and contacted their GP. "In these instances, the data accessed was limited to the veteran's name, address and targeted patient feedback … this may have included prescribed medicines, prescriber details and potential risk factors," the website said. Mr O'Meara said the legal issue was that DVA enrolled participants without seeking their informed consent about who would see their personal information and where it would be stored. Seb O'Meara said at least 6,000 people have expressed interest in joining the class action. ( ABC News: Billy Draper ) "At the heart of this case is what our own government can do with our personal information, and in particular … of a reasonably vulnerable cohort of people," Mr O'Meara said. "A lot of these people have pretty complex medical histories. "They include complex psychiatric and psychological conditions, and for many of them, learning of the disclosure … has caused them pretty significant distress." A DVA spokesperson said it was aware of the class action but it would "not be appropriate to comment" while the matter is before the courts. "Throughout its operation, the program was conducted under ethics approvals and formal contractual arrangements, including data security requirements," they said. "As this matter is the subject of active legal proceedings, it would not be appropriate to comment further on questions relating to program governance, consent arrangements, data handling processes, or allegations made by parties." DVA previously said MATES prevented 930 hospitalisations and 140 deaths. Adelaide University, an institution created during a merger between UniSA and University of Adelaide, declined to comment. Vietnam War veteran Alan Ashmore, who has "significant health issues" stemming from deployment, is among at least 6,000 who have expressed interest in joining the action. Mr Ashmore, of Melbourne, is helping others use Freedom of Information to access their MATES files, following a recent swell of interest. Alan Ashmore was sent to Vietnam as part of his national service. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) He was "staggered" to discover his own contained 25 pages, including health conditions and prescribed medications.

events.title: 'Got to be more careful': Paxton leaks prompt Republican handwringing
events.summary: The News Three is a trend, and the leaks about Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton’s campaign have more than hit that threshold. On Thursday the Texas Tribune published audio of Paxton saying the US needs to “suck it up” and cut federal programs, more drips from the same fundraiser that elicited Paxton’s complaints about gas prices , lack of control over his own campaign, and the Republican midterm convention depressing his numbers. “Paxton has always relied on his base and a strong statewide ticket to carry him across the finish line. He’s never played anywhere near this level and doesn’t understand the magnitude of effort being expended on his behalf to try to win this race,” Steven Law, former leader of the Senate Leadership Fund super PAC, told Semafor. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, said of Paxton: “Got to be more careful when you run with the big dogs.” Republicans don’t see any of Paxton’s remarks as politically fatal to Paxton’s campaign, but the leaks are not helpful — they only contribute to perceptions of GOP disarray in a tight Senate race. National Republican Senatorial Campaign spokesperson Joanna Rodriguez told Semafor that Republicans need to “put your jersey on and fight with us or go sit in the stands enjoying tofu with the Talafreakos.” Know More Polls this week have continued to show Democratic nominee James Talarico with a slight lead or tied with Paxton, a harrowing result for the GOP in the home state of the modern Republican Party. President Donald Trump rallied with Paxton on Wednesday night, then offered Paxton up for a debate with Talarico — prompting the Democrat to quickly agree and say: “I agree. Ball’s in your court, Ken.” Republicans saw all this coming from a mile away, of course, spending huge sums to help Cornyn defeat Paxton in the primary, reasoning that the general election would be a relative layup for Cornyn. But that didn’t happen, Trump endorsed Paxton, and now Republicans say they need to act like the entire majority is on the line in Texas — because it very well might be. “There are only two teams fighting for Texas’ future: the one with vegans and radicals who want to ban meat, reopen our borders, and transition your kids or the Republican team with a proven record fighting everything the other stands for,” Rodriguez said.

events.title: Mikey Madison plays a Facebook whistleblower in 'The Social Reckoning.' Here's where the real Frances Haugen is now.
events.summary: Jeremy Allen White and Mikey Madison in "The Social Reckoning." Sony Mikey Madison plays Frances Haugen in Aaron Sorkin's new film "The Social Reckoning." In real life, Haugen is a former Facebook product manager-turned-whistleblower. Haugen testified before Congress in 2021 that Facebook was knowingly causing harm. Much like its acclaimed predecessor, Aaron Sorkin's new film "The Social Reckoning" examines and dramatizes the real people in Mark Zuckerberg's orbit . Billed as a companion piece to the 2010 hit film "The Social Network," which told the story of Facebook's early-aughts founding and rapid climb to a multibillion-dollar valuation, "The Social Reckoning" stars Jeremy Strong as a grown-up Zuckerberg in the throes of wealth, power, and scandal. "The Social Reckoning" also stars Oscar winner Mikey Madison as Frances Haugen , better known as the "Facebook whistleblower." Starting in September 2021, The Wall Street Journal published " The Facebook Files ," an investigative series made possible by Haugen, a data scientist and former product manager on Facebook's civic integrity team. Haugen leaked tens of thousands of internal documents after leaving the company, sharing many with reporter Jeff Horwitz (played by Jeremy Allen White) to expose its harmful policies and prompt change at the company. Here's everything to know about the real-life woman who inspired Madison's character. Frances Haugen began her career at Google in 2006 Aaron Sorkin and Mikey Madison on the set of "The Social Reckoning." Sony Born and raised in Iowa, Haugen studied computer engineering and later earned a master's degree in business from Harvard. In her 2023 memoir, "The Power of One," Haugen writes that when she arrived in Silicon Valley in 2006, it was very much a boys club. She felt like an outlier. "Blonde women were on the sales team or were marketers," Haugen writes. "They did not code — but I did." On that note: Sorkin told Business Insider's Jason Guerrasio that Madison was keen to dye her hair blonde, but he dissuaded her from the idea. (They did, however, agree to give Madison a shorter haircut.) "I didn't want her worried about that in the performance," Sorkin said. "I always worry, like for instance, if I cast a British actor and they need to do an American accent, is that going to be your concern every moment of every day? Are you going to be able to do what I need you to do in terms of getting into the text if all you're thinking about is the American accent?" In "The Social Reckoning," Haugen is shown dealing with dismissive comments from male colleagues, like one who tells her to join a dating app because she would "benefit from loosening up." Haugen spent the first eight years of her career working in various positions at Google. She resigned from the company in 2014, largely due to health issues. She was diagnosed with celiac disease and later with non-occlusive temperature-sensitive vasoconstrictive disorder, a rare condition that causes chronic pain and inflammation in cold temperatures. Haugen was hired by Facebook in 2019 to work on the civic integrity team After Haugen's health improved, she worked at other major tech companies, including Yelp and Pinterest, before being recruited by Facebook in 2019. She has said she agreed to work at Facebook on the condition that her role would be in detecting and combating misinformation on the platform, motivated by a former friend who'd become obsessed with conspiracy theories. "It's one thing to study misinformation, it's another to lose someone to it," she told The Wall Street Journal . "A lot of people who work on these products only see the positive side of things." Haugen was assigned to monitor Facebook's impact on international elections and protect against election interference, and later said she was shocked by the "horrifying magnitude of the danger that we were facing." Haugen said her breaking point was when the civic integrity team was dissolved in the wake of the 2020 presidential election , and she quit in May 2021 — but not before secretly copying about 22,000 internal documents, many of which she shared with Horwitz and federal law enforcement. (At the time, Facebook said the civic integrity team wasn't dissolved, but "integrated into a larger Central Integrity team.") Haugen, then 37, sought federal whistleblower protection with the Securities and Exchange Commission. She then publicly revealed her identity during a "60 Minutes" interview with Scott Pelley. "When they got rid of civic integrity, it was the moment where I was like, I don't trust that they're willing to actually invest what needs to be invested to keep Facebook from being dangerous," Haugen told Pelley. Haugen said the root of Facebook's problems is how it optimizes for engagement: Posts that contain divisive language and misinformation are more likely to elicit likes, comments, and shares, so the algorithm amplifies them . "Facebook has realized that if they change the algorithm to be safer, people will spend less time on the site, they'll click on less ads," she said. "Facebook makes more money when you consume more content." Haugen added that, in her view, Facebook routinely prioritizes "profit over safety." The documents obtained by Haugen included a range of internal reports and studies showing, in part, that Facebook's algorithm had encouraged political parties around the world to embrace extremist ideas; that drug traffickers and human traffickers openly used Facebook's services; and that Instagram, acquired by Facebook in 2012, increased rates of depression and eating disorders among its users, especially teenage girls , more so than other social media apps. Haugen testified before Congress in October 2021 Frances Haugen testified before Congress in 2021. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Haugen testified before the Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection that Facebook not only causes harm but does so knowingly , while hiding its research from the public. In her opening remarks, Haugen said that Facebook is used to "deepen divides, destabilize democracies, and make young girls and women feel bad about their bodies." Haugen also stressed the need for government regulation , telling the lawmakers, "There is no one currently holding Mark accountable but himself." "When we realized tobacco companies were hiding the harms it caused, the government took action. When we figured out cars were safer with seat belts, the government took action. And today, the government is taking action against companies that hid evidence on opioids," she said in her written testimony . "I implore you to do the same here." Haugen's testimony received bipartisan support, and Sen. Ed Markey, a Democrat from Massachusetts, called Haugen "A 21st-century American hero." Zuckerberg said in a statement that Haugen presented a "false narrative" about the company. Where is Haugen now? Frances Haugen photographed in Australia

events.title: Oil prices jump as Iran steps up tanker attacks, hurricane threatens U.S. Gulf production
events.summary: Iran is ramping up tanker attacks while Houthi militants fired ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh. Oil prices came off their session highs after President Donald Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections. Oil companies shut in about 500,000 barrels per day or 25% of production in the Gulf of Mexico in response to Hurricane Isaias. Crude oil prices rose sharply Thursday, as Iran ramped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and Hurricane Isaias threatened U.S. offshore production in the Gulf of Mexico. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, gained 4% to close at $104.28 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures advanced 3.6% to settle at $91.49 per barrel. Nine tankers have come under attack in and around Hormuz over the past week, jeopardizing the recent recovery in crude oil flows through the strait Oil prices backed off session highs after President Donald Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections. NBC News, citing unnamed sources, reported earlier that Trump and his national security team were considering renewing strikes in the coming weeks. Some 9.5 million barrels per day exited Hormuz during the week ended Tuesday, about 30% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to Kpler data. Crude flows from the Middle East, including pipeline workarounds, stood at 16.4 million bpd which is nearly equivalent to prewar levels. In the Gulf of Mexico, oil companies have shut in about 500,000 bpd, or 25% of offshore production in the region, as Hurricane Isaias churns toward the coasts of Alabama, Mississippi and the Florida panhandle. Tensions are sharply escalating in the Middle East. Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen fired missiles at airports in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and the city of Abha on Tuesday and Wednesday. Three people died and 36 were injured, according to the state-owned media outlet Al Arabiya. The Saudis intercepted another volley of ballistic missiles fired Thursday at Riyadh and Khamis Mushait, a spokesperson for the kingdom's military said. "While flows from the region have largely normalized, the need for US navy escorts, increased costs and logistical frictions and constant risk of being attacked call into question the longer-term feasibility of the flows," said Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities. "This ultimately warrants a sticky risk premium to remain in pricing," McKay told clients in a Thursday note.

events.title: Exclusive: Anthropic's plan to protect critical infrastructure
events.summary: Anthropic is launching a new cybersecurity initiative designed to bring its most powerful AI models and engineers to companies protecting power grids, water utilities and other critical infrastructure, the company first shared with Axios. Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are struggling to secure aging, complex systems as AI threatens to make cyberattacks faster and cheaper to execute. Driving the news: Under its new Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, Anthropic will provide its frontier AI models, on-site engineers and threat research to companies already responsible for securing critical infrastructure systems. Participating companies will use these resources to identify and fix vulnerabilities in their customers' systems. The program's founding partners include Accenture, Booz Allen Hamilton, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC and Rockwell Automation. Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers do the same. Zoom in: Anthropic is also launching a free AI-powered vulnerability scanning service for open-source software projects, called OSS Scanner. Participating projects will receive periodic scans from Claude, along with automated reports detailing vulnerabilities, how they could be exploited and suggested fixes. The reports won't undergo human review before being sent to software maintainers, meaning some findings could be inaccurate. The big picture: Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI developers are looking for ways to put their most powerful models in the hands of cyber defenders as hackers gain access to similar capabilities . Anthropic's new initiative builds on lessons from Project Glasswing, which gave vetted organizations access to its most capable AI models to identify security vulnerabilities. The company said the project demonstrated how quickly AI can uncover vulnerabilities, but also how difficult it remains to verify and fix them. Yes, but: It's unclear how participating companies will safely test and deploy fixes without disrupting utilities' operations, one of the biggest challenges in securing critical infrastructure. Anthropic also didn't specify whether partners will receive free model access or who will cover the computing costs associated with using its AI tools. events.title: I always thought I'd settle down in Canada. Living in Japan for a year changed my mind.
events.summary: Living in Japan changed my plans for the future. Alessa Hickman After spending most of my life in Ottawa, I moved to Japan expecting to head home after one year. Living abroad showed me how much I value spontaneity, travel, and a life that feels like my own. Now, I'm heading back to Canada with a different perspective on what I want from my future. I was born and raised in Ottawa, and aside from a handful of vacations abroad and summer road trips to nearby Canadian cities , it's where I spent almost all of my time. Most of my family lives there, and the relatives who don't are only a few hours away. Growing up, the path modeled to me was pretty straightforward: Stay close to home, take vacations when you can, and build your life nearby. As I got older, though, I felt a growing need to see what else was out there. I was also feeling the pressure of rising costs in Canada , and my apartment lease was ending, so the timing felt right for a change. I'd visited Japan a couple of years earlier and loved it, so when I found out about the yearlong Working Holiday Visa program, it felt like the perfect fit. I assumed that once the year was up, I'd just come back home and sign another lease nearby. However, after my first night out in Tokyo, I was already looking into how I could stay away longer. Living in Japan has been better than I ever imagined I've missed Canada at times, but Japan has felt like home in a way I didn't expect. Alessa Hickman For most of my life, I've craved adventure. I grew up hiking, taking little road trips with my mom, and looking for any excuse to get out of the city for a day. I've always loved novelty, and living in Japan has given me so much of it. Since moving here, I've lived in multiple places, including Tokyo and Osaka . I've traveled to over a dozen more cities and towns, tried countless new restaurants, and met people from all over the world. It feels like there's constantly something new to see or explore. The train system here makes it so easy to lean into that spontaneous side of myself. I love being able to visit a new city on a whim, whereas in Ottawa, doing the same thing would usually require a little more planning and a lot more money. The more I've experienced this kind of lifestyle, the harder it is to imagine giving it up. I don't necessarily want to spend my life in one place just because it's where I'm from, and now, I know a future filled with new places and experiences is available to me. I'm going home, but I'm not done exploring Now, I know I want to see more of the world. Alessa Hickman Going back to Canada is the next logical, short-term step for me. My visa's coming to an end, and making a permanent move abroad would take a lot more planning and paperwork. This doesn't mean I'm done exploring the rest of the world, though. After I leave Japan in a couple of months, I'm planning to spend some time in Southeast Asia — and if I can, I might squeeze in a couple more stops on my way home. Once I'm back in Canada, I'm sure I'll jump into planning another trip, or maybe I'll start looking into another yearlong visa. I can see myself living abroad again, or at least spending more time traveling internationally, whether that's in Japan or somewhere completely new. For now, though, I don't plan to settle back into life in Ottawa the way I once thought I would. While I'm in this up-in-the-air phase, I'd love to move (or drive!) across Canada and see where life takes me from there. I'm looking forward to exploring more of my home country. Since moving to Japan, I feel like I've changed, too — and I've reflected on how little of Canada I've actually seen. I'm excited to experience my home with a new perspective. I'm still in my 20s, so I feel lucky to have the freedom to keep figuring things out as I go. And living in Japan didn't give me all the answers, either. If anything, it gave me more questions. As I head home, I'm taking everything I've learned and felt this year in Japan with me — and I'm so excited to see where I'll go next. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Trump: Anyone saying "AI" is "THE ENEMY!" The White House uses it
events.summary: President Trump on Thursday called anyone who uses "Artificial Intelligence" instead of "Super Intelligence" "THE ENEMY!" — even as the White House continues using the term "AI." Why it matters: Trump's push to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" clashes with established terminology in the technology industry. Trump's branding blurs the distinction between AI and super intelligence , a hypothetical version of AI more advanced than human intelligence. What they're saying: "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday. Zoom out: Trump's executive order from September doubled down on using "SI" over "AI," though it did not offer a penalty for using the term. The order specifically defines "Super Intelligence" using the existing federal legal definition of AI. The order calls on federal agencies to change how they describe AI in official communications. The State Department already ordered diplomats to use the term after Trump's United Nations speech on Sept. 22. Yes, but: The White House still uses "AI" as a term, including on its AI-focused website, AI.gov . The White House's Office of Science and Technology Policy also makes reference to "artificial intelligence." But when an Axios reporter asked the America.gov chatbot about AI, the bot responded: "The executive branch uses Super Intelligence (SI) for this topic, not the older term you used." What we're watching: Whether the White House could update its websites to reflect Trump's preferred terminology. The White House did not respond to Axios' request for comment Thursday.

events.title: Ben Affleck is an AI nerd, and the internet is impressed
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. They cast the wrong lead in “Good Will Hunting,” apparently, because it’s Ben Affleck who is the secret genius, as it turns out. The actor who earlier this year sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix for a reported $587 million has gone viral this week for demonstrating his understanding of AI technology, neural networks, machine learning, and the like, across multiple video clips of his recent interviews. He can even write a little Python, he says. The movie star delved into his interest in technology most recently on an episode of GQ’s “One More Question” series this week, where he humbly started with “I’ve always been kind of into computers since I was young,” before nerding out on the development of AI as it relates to filmmaking, while using AI terminology like machine learning, neural networks, transformers, tensors, GPUs, inference, and more. In a clip that’s making the rounds, Affleck explains to the impressed interviewer, Zach Baron, that he got into the space when analog film moved to digital. As he spoke, he kept defining terms so the interviewer could understand what he was talking about. “I became more interested in that aspect of it, and the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning,” Affleck began. “So I can write, like, pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that. Because with convolutional neural networks — which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do — which is just much more computation simultaneously — you would do things like, look at what’s called a tensor — which is just the numerical translation of a visual image, in numbers like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame, and how many? It’s just that simple, right?” No, Ben Affleck, it is not just that simple, which is why this video is going viral. The actor then went into how neural networks were used to identify patterns and do edge detection or feature extraction, which he described as “identifying patterns enough to know — like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something.” He also admitted he used his status as a Hollywood star to get a peek at emerging AI technology, at times. OpenAI was among those he visited, Affleck said in a separate clip, which ultimately led him to understand how he could get more directly involved in the AI space. As the interviewer continued, Affleck explained how AI can help with filmmaking while not replacing it, leading to the development and sale of his own startup in this space. (He claims the $587 million figure is “not right,” noting that he didn’t own the whole company.) “I gambled on this notion that in order to do this in an ethical way and in a way that could take this technology and actually make it work hand in glove with artists in this community where there are very fixed, long-standing relationships around likeness and so forth, we had to create our own dataset,” he said. “So I raised the money. I shot for about eight months with a lot of cameras and a lot of equipment, and created a dataset that would serve as late-stage training for open models to do discrete tasks, sort of where the training code, the inference code, were related to one another and geared toward actual specific tasks that would generate value,” Affleck said. In a separate clip, also going viral, Affleck spoke to Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw at the Screentime 2026 conference in LA, where he talked about how he fine-tuned AI models by taking open source models, unfreezing the weights, then teaching them to meet certain cinematic standards. In the process, the filmmaker retains their proprietary work, while benefiting from the learning they create by training their own unique model for the movie they’re making. Ben Affleck (Hollywood star & Artists Equity CEO) talks about how he fine-tunes open video models by unfreezing weights and trained only the last cinematic layer so a film crew can hit real production standards. for context, Ben Affleck founded InterPositive in 2022, a 16-person… pic.twitter.com/xIOvD0xMyt — Rohan Paul (@rohanpaul_ai) October 1, 2026 The actor used the technique himself in his movie “Animals,” where AI aided in the post-production process. At one point, he also weighed in on the concerns around AI and its world-ending potential . His worries, however, were much more rational. “When I worry about AI, I worry about my kids in school. I worry about the 30% rise in the number of A’s given out at colleges over the last three years. I worry about learned helplessness. I worry about responsible use. I don’t worry about Skynet, and I don’t think that it’s going to take over [the movie] business in any meaningful way.

events.title: Popular AI leaderboard Arena nearly doubles valuation to $3.1B valuation in 10 months
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Arena , which originated in 2023 as a research project at UC Berkeley that crowdsourced rankings of AI models, has raised a $200 million Series B round at a $3.1 billion valuation, it said on Thursday. This comes after the company said it reached $100 million in annualized run-rate revenue in June. The round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Khosla Ventures, with Salesforce Ventures, 01 Advisors, Dell Technologies Capital, Endeavor Catalyst, a16z, Felicis, and others joining in. Arena previously announced a $150 million Series A in January at a $1.7 billion post-money valuation. At the time, its annualized revenue was $30 million , it said. So that means its valuation has nearly doubled in about 10 months. Arena provides a crowdsourced platform that is free for consumers to use. People enter prompts or request vibe-coded projects and then rate which model does it better. Arena claims it has tens of millions of monthly visitors. In September of last year, it introduced its commercial product, AI Evaluations , a service that provides model labs and enterprises with detailed performance analytics based on its community feedback. The timing proved impeccable. This year, AI labs realized that their models were gaming benchmarking tests, finding ways to rack up good scores without truly earning them. At the same time, enterprises wanted help determining which model works best for their own internal needs rather than relying only on standardized benchmarks. “AI is advancing faster than our ability to evaluate it, and static benchmarks break down once models recognize they’re being tested,” the company said in its funding announcement. “The world needs a neutral third party to measure how safe and aligned AI actually is once it’s in the hands of real people. Arena is stepping into that role today,” it added. To that end, Arena has also added a new category to its leaderboard: alignment . This is where it ranks models based on issues like unauthorized action (taking actions it wasn’t asked to take); false attribution (wrongly crediting statements or facts to the wrong source); and what it calls “deceptive completion” (lying about completing tasks that it didn’t do). Currently, a slate of OpenAI’s models are at the top of its preliminary alignment leaderboard, with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable in sixth and ninth place, respectively. A little over a week ago, it was reported that OpenAI’s annualized revenue was approaching $70 billion, a figure that would have made it competitive with Anthropic’s reported run rate . Now, however, the AI lab is said to have told investors that the real revenue is some $20 billion lower than that. The Financial Times reports that the company has told investors that its annualized revenue is “approaching $50 billion.” The $70 billion figure was previously reported by news outlets and based on information that had been shared with OpenAI investors, the outlet writes. The issue of OpenAI’s revenue has troubled the company, as it attempts to justify the gargantuan investments being made on its behalf; the AI giant raised $122 billion during a March funding round alone. The company’s leaked 2025 financials earlier this year showed it had made about $13 billion but spent significantly more. events.title: Google brings agentic AI to Gemini, starting with businesses
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface. The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots. The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts — as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work. Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers. According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these. Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals. By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future. The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’ data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others. It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network. Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress. Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another co-worker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on which team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person. The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack. The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers. Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control. events.title: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
events.summary: Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo. The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused. The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile. The Australian law firms representing Adidas and White Fox both declined to comment on the case, the first hearing due to begin on Friday. In Federal Court documents, Adidas states that its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957. The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark. White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims. It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items. This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim. The company says White Fox is "taking advantage" of Adidas's reputation, "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind". Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs. Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops. In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes. A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image. In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes. White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024. In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters The GPU giant released a fix for the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-47483 Nvidia found $1B under the couch to help secure American scientific computing dominance 3 hours ago Microsoft N1Xes Intel in favor of Nvidia's shiny new SoCs in Surface Laptop Ultra 1 day ago The question you would ask HPE and NVIDIA if nobody was recording 3 days ago Californian accused of shipping $300M worth of Nvidia chips to China without Uncle Sam’s approval 6 days ago Nvidia debuts $4,999 DGX Spark with half the RAM and storage, amid memory crunch 6 days ago Researchers found thousands of GPU servers exposing Nvidia's DCGM Exporter to the internet, with hundreds potentially vulnerable to a high-severity flaw that could let unauthenticated attackers crash the GPU monitoring service and disrupt AI workloads. DCGM Exporters read telemetry from the GPUs on a host, including its hardware, utilization, memory usage, power consumption, and error events. Each GPU has its own unique ID, or UUID, and all of these metrics are exposed in plaintext over HTTP. This exposure provides would-be attackers with detailed information useful for reconnaissance, including mapping GPU infrastructure, identifying potentially vulnerable systems, and monitoring workload activity. Michael Katchinskiy, a researcher at datacenter security startup Lava, found and reported the bug in the GPU health and performance monitoring service. In September, the GPU giant Nvidia released a fix for the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-4748 3, and gave it an 8.2 CVSS high-severity rating. “Once we realized how much these endpoints revealed, the next question was: How many of them are exposed to the internet?” Katchinskiy said in a Thursday blog. So the researchers started scanning the internet for exposed DCGM Exporters. And the scale of exposure proved “especially significant,” he wrote. Over the course of four scans between March and May, the threat hunters found about 2,100 GPU servers exposing DCGM Exporter metrics to the open internet. These included 12,000 GPU UUIDs. None of these required authentication. The hosts belonged to about 300 organizations, according to Katchinskiy, and nearly half - 5,274 of the exposed GPUs, or 44 percent of the total - were located in the US. These GPUs represented about $100 million in hardware, and included Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs, H200s, and H100s - used to run large-scale AI workloads - plus consumer RTX 5090 and 4090 systems. While investigating the exposed systems, the Lava team found that about 25 percent of the exposed DCGM hosts also revealed data from Go’s /debug/pprof/ built-in profiling tool. The profiler collects and exposes runtime performance data such as CPU and memory usage for running Go applications. This includes CPU usage, memory allocations, goroutine states, and blocking events. “With enough concurrent unauthenticated requests, the exporter could run out of memory and crash, cutting off visibility into GPU health and activity,” Katchinskiy wrote. The CPU and memory pressure could also affect AI training or inference workloads. Nvidia fixed the issue in version 4.8.2, and operators should upgrade to that version or later. In addition to GPU telemetry, Lava looked into Prometheus Node Exporter, which monitors server hardware and operating systems, and also exposes metrics over HTTP. The team found 12,096 public Node Exporter hosts exposing data on server models, operating systems, firmware versions, hostnames, storage paths and networking hardware commonly used in GPU clusters. This information reveals how environments are built and configured, which could also be used by attackers for reconnaissance, matching the system to known vulnerabilities. The publicly exposed monitoring services affected customer infrastructure across neocloud and GPU cloud providers including Nebius, Voltage Park, Lambda, Northern Data, and DigitalOcean. Lava reported all of this to the affected providers, and Katchinskiy says that these providers worked with customers to address the exposures.

Anthropic updated its usage policy on Thursday , codifying new prohibitions on election interference, weapons software, and surveillance. But perhaps the most attention-getting change is a new prohibition against prolonged verbal abuse of the model, which is now expressly forbidden. Since an update in August , Claude has been trained to end conversations with “persistently harmful or abusive user interactions” — but the new policy explicitly bars users from pursuing those conversations. “The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose,” the post explains. “It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.” The change comes after Anthropic has sought out collaborations with prominent religious scholars — in some cases, seeking to convince them that Claude could be conscious or have a soul. events.title: U.S. Lawmakers Launch Sexual Abuse Probe of Youth Sports Giant AAU
events.summary: Left image: A scene from an Amateur Athletic Union-affiliated volleyball game in 2026. Right image: Rep. Brett Guthrie, R-Ky., left, chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and ranking member Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., D-N.J. Collage by ProPublica. Photos by Sarah Blesener for ProPublica and Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images. What Happened: Bipartisan leaders from the powerful House Energy and Commerce Committee launched an inquiry on Wednesday into the Amateur Athletic Union, criticizing the sprawling youth sports organization for its handling of child sexual abuse allegations and demanding answers, citing reporting by ProPublica and The Washington Post . What They Said: “It is unacceptable that AAU is failing to implement standard reforms to protect child athletes, and is misleading the public, parents, and athletes about preventative measures in place within AAU sports,” the letter reads . The committee chair, Kentucky Republican Brett Guthrie, called ProPublica and The Post’s reporting “deeply disturbing” in a statement on Thursday, saying it “raises serious questions about the organization’s actions over the past decade.”  “Our Committee is seeking information on how the AAU’s policies have potentially fallen short, and what needs to be done in order to protect young athletes,” Guthrie said.” The members of the committee, which in 2018 investigated systemic failures surrounding sexual abuse by former USA Gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar and others, said in the letter that they were “seeing parallels” between its past investigation and “what is being uncovered within the AAU today.” The letter is addressed to Jo Mirza, the AAU’s president, and asks detailed questions about the organization’s operations, taking the extra step of demanding a briefing from Mirza to the committee by Oct. 21. Among questions about its safety policies and coach training, the committee asks Mirza to lay out how many sexual abuse allegations the nonprofit receives each year and how many coaches it disciplines, information that has long been shrouded in secrecy. The AAU declined to provide the data to ProPublica and The Post. The AAU does not publish a list of banned coaches like many other youth sports groups do, and ProPublica and The Post found that it has used confidential arbitration clauses to keep lawsuits from child sexual abuse victims from being heard in open court. The letter is signed by Guthrie, ranking Democrat Frank Pallone Jr. from New Jersey and representatives in charge of oversight and investigations. Read More A Youth Sports Giant Promised Reforms to Protect Kids From Sexual Abuse. Most Never Happened. Background: ProPublica and The Post found that the AAU, which has some 760,000 athletes and coaches nationwide, is failing on nearly every level to adequately protect young athletes from sexual abuse — breaking pledges it made in the wake of a 2011 sexual abuse scandal involving its CEO and young basketball players. The investigation found that the AAU has become a haven for coaches suspected of abuse, according to a review of public disciplinary lists and interviews with current and former executives from six national sports governing bodies and other key stakeholders. The AAU, the investigation found, does not offer child abuse prevention training, though it claims to the public that it does. And ProPublica and The Post found that it has suppressed allegations of sexual misconduct, including against another top executive in 2018. Why It Matters: The committee is one of the key congressional groups charged with overseeing the federal youth sports safety system. It has the power to push for changes in child safety law — and to force transparency from organizations like the AAU, which has repeatedly failed to deliver on past promises of reform. In 2018, in the wake of the allegations against Nassar, scrutiny from Congress led to the passage of a law known as the Safe Sport Act. It created the U.S. Center for SafeSport, an oversight group, to investigate allegations of sexual misconduct and gave it the power to suspend or ban coaches for life. But SafeSport has jurisdiction only over national sports governing bodies, like USA Gymnastics and USA Volleyball, that are overseen by the Olympic and Paralympic Committee — meaning much of the law does not apply to the AAU. The law does require “all amateur sports organizations” — not just governing bodies — to “offer and provide consistent training to all adult members … regarding prevention and reporting of child abuse.” The Energy and Commerce Committee’s letter cites that provision of the law and demands that the AAU explain how it complies. Response: In a statement, the AAU said, “As always, we will cooperate fully and respond appropriately to any questions or requests from congressional committees or U.S. government agencies.” Previously, the AAU told ProPublica and The Post that it is “committed to protecting its athletes through comprehensive protection policies overseen by our Compliance Department,” and said it has an “ongoing commitment to providing a safe, secure, supportive, and trusted environment where athletes can thrive.” The post U.S. Lawmakers Launch Sexual Abuse Probe of Youth Sports Giant AAU appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: OpenAI’s math solutions aren’t meeting the field’s standards yet
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When OpenAI released hundreds of claimed solutions to some of the world’s hardest math problems this week, the frontier lab said that it had consulted an advisory group of elite mathematicians to avoid the controversy that came with the last time one of its models solved a long-standing problem in the field. But OpenAI fell short of those standards, particularly where the mathematicians emphasized the need for human understanding of a mathematical result. That’s especially concerning after a new paper highlighted gaps between the natural language and formally expressed solution to a million-dollar problem ostensibly solved by OpenAI’s models. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), hosted by Princeton University’s Institute for Advanced Studies, is made up of nine prominent researchers at institutions around the world. The organization released guidelines for frontier labs solving math problems at the end of September. In a statement on the latest set of proofs, the AGMAI said that “it is ultimately up to the mathematical community to assess the extent to which our recommendations were followed successfully.” However, the organization’s first request was “to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models.” OpenAI’s release explicitly says that it is evaluating its proprietary models using open research problems in mathematics. The advisory group did not respond when asked by TechCrunch for a more thorough evaluation of OpenAI’s latest proof release. The lab clearly followed some of its principles, including releasing results as soon as possible and including information about how the models reached their conclusions. But not for all of them: Just 10 of the 719 manuscripts included releases of the model’s chain of thought. For papers that people don’t understand, the mathematicians suggested the proofs should be formalized — but just 42% of the proofs released by OpenAI had not undergone this process. Ultimately, it’s still not clear that OpenAI is taking “responsibility for ensuring that human understanding will follow” when releasing its proofs, in accordance to the AGMAI principles. AGMAI suggested that OpenAI should help fund the work of human mathematicians who will be required to make the lab’s solutions meaningful in any real way. “Problems are being solved autonomously by AI prompters who have no interest in the broader field itself once their initial target is ‘solved’, and do not understand the AI output well enough to answer questions on the result, give talks, or otherwise interact with the rest of the field,” Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician who has criticized OpenAI’s approach, wrote on social media after the release. That problem is exemplified by a paper released this week by mathematicians at the University of Cambridge and King’s College in London that questions the way frontier labs are approaching these challenges. When AI models solve mathematical problems, they first create a “natural language” explanation, then try to express that result in Lean, a programming language that in theory confirms the accuracy of the proof by compiling it as code. However, there may be problems with the way the models translate their natural language proofs into code; this paper documents at least two discrepancies between the natural language proof and the Lean code behind the solution OpenAI has offered to a problem derived from the Navier-Stokes equations that describe the complex behavior of fluids. These discrepancies don’t necessarily disprove either solution, but they do raise questions on whether we can simply rely on models to formalize their own solutions without human involvement. That’s one reason that AGMAI asked OpenAI to “include machine-readable metadata correlating the natural language and formal artifacts,” something that the frontier lab did not do with these releases. “Because of the phenomenon of mistranslations — as highlighted in this paper — the NL proof by OpenAI and other autoformalised Lean proofs should not prima facie be trusted without the same peer review process and scrutiny that other proofs are subjected to,” the authors of the “lost in translation” paper conclude. Mathematicians stress that when new results are discovered by humans, they take responsibility for them and engage with the broader community through papers, talks, and seminars. That process increases understanding of the solutions, finds strategies that can be used to solve other problems, and allows the new knowledge to be applied in practical fields.

events.title: Top bosses at Goldman Sachs to share bonus pot worth up to $500m
events.summary: Eye-watering sum, to be split between 20 bankers, is one of the biggest payouts in the bank’s history Top bosses at Goldman Sachs are in line to share a bonus pot worth up to $500m (£378m) this year, marking one of the biggest payouts in the Wall Street bank’s history. The eye-watering sum will be shared between 20 bankers, with its chief executive, David Solomon, due to take about $100m (£75.6m) of the reward, which is made up of Goldman Sachs stock. That is more than double the value of the record $47m (£35.5m) annual pay packet he was granted last year. The $500m bonus pot is the culmination of a long-term investment plan first crafted by the bank in 2021. The final sum, which is due to be confirmed later this month, is tied to how high Goldman’s share price has climbed over the past five years, as well as how its stock price has performed compared with peers such as JP Morgan and Bank of America over that period. Goldman Sachs said the bonuses were meant to persuade bosses to stay at the bank “in an increasingly competitive market”. The bank’s president, John Waldron, who is widely expected to succeed Solomon as chief executive, is also in line for a payout, alongside other top bosses such as the co-heads of global banking and markets, Ashok Varadhan and Dan Dees. News of the bumper bonus, which was first reported by Bloomberg, comes days before Goldman is due to report third-quarter earnings on 13 October. The bonuses reflect the value of Goldman Sachs stock, which has surged roughly 146% over the past five years, and climbed about 300% since Solomon took the helm as chief executive. A spokesperson for the bank said: “The board created these awards to achieve three principal objectives: align compensation with rigorous performance thresholds, ensure leadership continuity and enhance retention of our top talent in an increasingly competitive market. It’s no secret our firm has performed exceptionally well in the years since.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The payouts are the latest in a string of large payouts for executives in the US, particularly on Wall Street. The US lender Citigroup announced earlier this year that its chief executive, Jane Fraser, had been paid a record $42m (£31.8m) for 2025. Meanwhile, JP Morgan’s chief executive, Jamie Dimon, took home a total pay package worth $43m (£32.5m) last year , up 10% from a year earlier. Dimon’s own long-term incentive award is worth about $270m (£204.1m), according to Bloomberg.

events.title: Trump's foreign worker crackdown comes for Microsoft, Adobe, IT firms
events.summary: Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that the Trump administration is suspending Microsoft , Adobe and several other IT firms' ability to hire foreign-born workers for permanent residency in the U.S. Why it matters: The move will affect hundreds of companies owned by the tech giant, escalating the Trump administration's crackdown on immigrant labor. What they're saying: " We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector," Vance said during a Thursday news conference. "We're the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers." "And so our message to Microsoft is, you're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants." Zoom in: The permanent labor certification program , which is administered through the Department of Labor, allows a company to hire foreign workers to live permanently in America. It's typically the first step in receiving an employer-sponsored green card. It's also separate from H-1B visas, which allow workers to live and work temporarily in the U.S. H-1B visas primarily go to highly skilled workers in specialized occupations. Technology companies are among the program's biggest users. The Trump administration has made reducing the number of foreign workers in the country a rallying cry, and accused foreign-born workers of taking jobs that could — and, in its view, should — go to Americans. Driving the news: Vance specifically singled out Microsoft, slamming them for laying off 6,000 workers last year. Vance said Thursday that "[a]t the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants. Now that is a scandalous system that we've allowed in this country for far too long." Microsoft owns hundreds of companies, including LinkedIn, Skype and gaming studio Activision Blizzard . Adobe and IT outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini are also suspended from the program. The other side: "We believe in the strength and talent of the American workforce," Microsoft said in a statement . "That is why the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans. We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information." "For example, of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. These were not to hire new people. The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country." Microsoft also said it only files H-1B petitions for people who "meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," and that they pay H-1B workers comparable compensation to other employees." Worth noting: Trump will award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at the White House today. Microsoft did not respond to Axios' request for comment.
