events.title: New generation of Gulf philanthropists want a seat at the table
events.summary: The Scene As Western governments slash foreign aid, many organizations are seeking Gulf philanthropy to fill the gaps. While wealthy individuals and governments in the region are ready to take on a larger role, a younger generation of donors isn’t content with plowing money into existing programs, and is instead seeking new approaches with more effective and measurable outcomes. Sonia Ben Jaafar, CEO of the Abdulla Al Ghurair Foundation, told Semafor that private donors from the Gulf want to be more involved in designing development programs rather than simply financing them. She said the region’s charities have developed their own expertise that can help inform changes to improve existing charitable programs. The foundation she runs — established in 2015 by Emirati billionaire Abdulla Al Ghurair and chaired by his son Abdul Aziz — has become one of the Arab world’s largest privately funded education initiatives, reaching about 500,000 young people over the past decade. The foundation runs like a business, using performance metrics to evaluate its grants and tying funding decisions to outcomes such as job placement rates, Ben Jaafar said. The approach fits within a broader push by Badr Jafar, the UAE’s special envoy for business and philanthropy, to bring private donors, businesses, and governments together to address humanitarian needs. In an interview in New York during the UN General Assembly, Ben Jaafar discussed the changing role of private wealth in the region, and why her foundation is quick to drop programs that don’t deliver results. Why is private philanthropy hesitant to step in to cover underfunded programs that have been abandoned by many governments? The narrative that philanthropic capital will just fill that up is not going to happen. What we’re hearing in the discussions, at least that I’m in, in the closed rooms, is: What does the new framework look like? Because it cannot be more of the same, and philanthropic capital shouldn’t be coming in as a gap filler. We need a new model of how public, private, and philanthropy — this is the new three Ps — are going to partner together. How does the Abdulla Al Ghurair Foundation measure the success of its programs? We have a strategy that would look like any business, except instead of generating revenue, we need to generate impact for the communities we serve. We have, on average, a [jobs] placement rate of 78%, which is a very high placement rate in my field. We don’t count just who we train. We want to know that that training landed them into a revenue-generating life. You were early to get into Syria after the war ended. What are you focusing on there? We’re training young Syrians to learn construction skills, and paying them to attend an apprenticeship program. Those graduates will then work on the schools we started to refurbish there. During the war, we started a fund in 2018 that was focused on educating refugees in Lebanon and Jordan. Some of those Syrians are now returnees and are being picked up by government administration and companies to support the reconstruction. Have you funded programs that didn’t work? We have funded programs that we were sure would work, and we were sure we had the right partner to implement it. Because it’s outcomes-based funding, if you cannot meet the milestone and you don’t have a good reason, or we can’t find a solution with you, then we will defund that. We’ll stop. We’ll sunset that, and we’ll find a new way of doing it. Notable Abdul Aziz Al Ghurair runs his philanthropy like a business. The foundation’s chairman urged donors to set measurable goals and work with governments and businesses to maximize impact. The Gulf’s wealth transfer could reshape charitable giving. Badr Jafar, the UAE’s special envoy for business and philanthropy, told Semafor that more than $1 trillion will change hands in the region by 2030 , accelerating a shift toward impact-driven philanthropy.

events.title: New rules to make long-term investment funds clearer
events.summary: The FCA has set out clearer expectations for asset managers about long-term investments, such as property. This will help give the market more confidence to invest in funds that support private markets.The new rules mean that investors will have to give 90 days' notice to access their funds but will be more certain that they will receive their money.For investors, this means the fund should be clearer from the start about how quickly they can get their money back and whether the fund is right for their needs.Currently some of these funds allow people to take money out daily with no notice period. During periods of stress or volatility there is a risk that some funds may suspend all payments due to lack of available cash. Some are also holding extra cash, leaving less invested in their intended assets.Rushed sales can lower prices, harm investors who stay invested and put pressure on markets.The new notice period would give managers time to sell assets in an orderly way and make liquidity-driven suspensions less likely.Existing funds would have 2 years to comply and give investors at least 1 year’s notice.The proposals bring the UK into line with new international liquidity standards for open ended funds.Michelle Beck, director, markets, at the FCA, said: 'Funds should be clear about whether they offer quick access or are built for longer-term investments like property. Our rules will help firms make that clearer and give the market more confidence to invest.'Notes to editorsRead CP26/35: Fair redemption terms for authorised funds investing in illiquid assets.The FCA is asking for feedback on the proposals by 11 December 2026.The consultation covers authorised fund managers of non-UCITS retail schemes, known as NURS.The FCA uses the term 'inherently illiquid assets' for assets that cannot normally be sold quickly without a significant loss in value. These can include property and infrastructure investments.Fund managers could set a notice period longer than the minimum where the fund’s assets or investment strategy require it.

events.title: How a multibillion-dollar oilfield has ignited the UK-Argentina feud over the Falklands
events.summary: How an oil project reignited UK-Argentina Falklands dispute Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Now, the multibillion-dollar Sea Lion oil project has reignited old tensions, with Buenos Aires seeking to put a stop to the plans. Home to fewer than 4,000 people and located in an isolated corner of the South Atlantic Ocean, the Falkland Islands don't often feature in global business headlines. However, a UK-Israeli oil exploration project in the North Falkland Basin is stoking long-running tensions between Argentina and the people of the archipelago. Argentina has laid claim to the islands, which it calls Las Malvinas, for two centuries . In 1982, the dispute over the islands' sovereignty led to a war between the UK and Argentina , though British control was quickly restored after Argentine forces invaded the islands. A 2013 sovereignty referendum on the islands returned a 99.8% vote in favor of remaining tied to the UK as a self-governing British Overseas Territory. The Sea Lion oilfield project has brought the issue back to the surface. Last month, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to launch an international legal challenge against the UK unless the project was stopped within two weeks. The oil project is being run by Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and the UK's Rockhopper Exploration and has the full support of the Falkand Islands Legislative Assembly, which has pursued the project since 2010. The companies plan to begin extracting oil from the Sea Lion oilfield by early 2028. Milei says the project is "the illegal plundering of our resources" and that he will take the matter to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, an independent judicial body responsible for the application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea. Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falklands Islands' 12-member assembly, told DW that the dispute was "nothing new" and that Argentina is using the oil project as "a vehicle to pursue their sovereignty claim." He thinks Milei may be stepping up rhetoric ahead of the 2027 elections in Argentina. "When there's elections coming up, the Falklands is a very convenient tool to use in order to rally people together and distract them from domestic problems," he said. Henry Ziemer, an analyst with the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, says the Falklands is "a perennial sore spot in Argentine politics" and that since the 1980s, various governments have raised the issue in an attempt to rally support and to "stoke the fires of nationalism." Howerver, he thinks Milei's intervention is noteworthy given that he had previously been open to better relations with the UK on the issue. He agrees that it may be a strategy to "boost approval ratings at a time when the government is under a lot of strong domestic pressure." Potentially transformative for the Falklands Even if Milei sees political gain in the issue, the possibility of the Sea Lion project being successful would significantly raise the economic stakes for all concerned. The project has a budget of $1.8 billion (€1.6 billion) and could generate revenues of more than double that for the Falkland Islands. The companies hope that at its peak, the field will produce up to 50,000 barrels per day and could last for up to 35 years. That would substantially increase the Falklands' current annual GDP , which is almost entirely dependent on the volatile fishing sector and tourism. The administration is even looking into the possibility of creating a sovereign wealth fund if the oil project is successful. "It's a very significant project for us with a lot of potential for our future," said Bragger. "It's been a big effort to get to this point and assuming all goes to plan, we want to retain as much value as possible." However, beyond playing to domestic politics, Milei may also spy an opportunity for Argentina to position itself as an energy player amid the war in Iran and the troubles in the Strait of Hormuz . Argentina's own domestic oil sector is growing, with production surging at Patagonia's Vaca Muerta, one of the world's largest shale developments. Were Milei's legal efforts to prove successful, there may be further gains. "When natural resources overlay existing territorial disputes and bad blood, that tends to galvanize a lot of conflict," said Ziemer. However, Bragger counters that Milei and Argentina have no legitimate claim to either the Falklands or whatever oil wealth may be extracted over the coming years. "They don't respect our right to self-determination," he added. "They don't respect our right to develop our own resources. They just want to colonize us." More economic pressure from Argentina Milei plans to put pressure on the Falklands by stepping up existing economic sanctions. Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falklands since 2025, recently described this campaign as "economic warfare.

events.title: Windows Search learns to take orders
events.summary: Microsoft's latest Windows Search preview promises faster results and less clutter, while adding a new sideline: carrying out commands such as muting audio or minimizing windows. Following July's improvements, Microsoft began rolling out the new preview yesterday. The Actions feature lets users change settings directly from Windows Search. Typing "mute" into the search box and selecting the resulting action silences the speakers, with a "Done!" message confirming the change. The same applies to other actions. We tried "minimise all my windows" (note the non-US spelling) and Windows performed the Show Desktop action. Search is now more results-focused, rather than showing a large preview pane, and there is better handling for typos and synonyms (although there is clearly more work to do: "turn on" and "switch on" confused the preview in our testing). Inline previews and richer file details will follow later this year, helping users distinguish similar results without restoring the separate preview pane. The Windows Search experience is built on WinUI 3 and Microsoft claims "substantial improvements in performance and memory usage." However, this is still an English-only preview, gradually rolling out to Windows Insiders in the Experimental channel. Eligible users can enable it sooner through the Windows Insider Program's Feature flags settings. Faster, less cluttered search results are welcome in a tool that has long been a Windows punchline. Whether a box marked Search should also double as a command launcher is another question. ®

events.title: UAE and Thailand conclude Cepa talks to boost trade and investment
events.summary: The UAE and Thailand have concluded negotiations for their Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement , which is expected to remove trade barriers and boost bilateral relations. The countries began talks on the deal in 2023 and launched a joint business council the same year. As part of the negotiations, they discussed avenues to enhance trade, investment and opportunities to expand co-operation, the ministry of Foreign Trade said in a statement on Thursday. In the coming phase, the UAE and Thailand will finalise the legal and technical procedures required for the agreement to be signed and implemented, it said. The Cepa is expected to accelerate trade flows, unlock new investment opportunities and strengthen private sector co-operation in priority sectors, including advanced manufacturing, logistics, food security, digital trade, renewable energy and precious metals. “The conclusion of negotiations … embodies our shared commitment to building stronger economic bridges between South-East Asia and the Middle East,” said Minister of Foreign Trade Dr Thani Al Zeyoudi “Thailand is one of the most dynamic and diversified economies in the region, and this agreement will open new avenues for companies, investors and entrepreneurs in both countries to expand and access high-growth markets.” The Cepa builds on strong ties between the UAE and Thailand. Bilateral non-oil trade in the first half of 2026 jumped by more than 75 per cent year-on-year to $10.2 billion. Trade last year also grew more than 65 per cent to $12.3 billion. The UAE's key non-oil exports to Thailand include gold, aluminium and other industrial goods. “These figures reflect the growing integration of the two economies and the scale of opportunity the agreement can unlock,” the ministry said. “By reducing trade barriers, enhancing market access and stimulating investment flows, the Cepa will support our long-term economic objectives and generate new opportunities across a wide range of strategic sectors,” Dr Al Zeyoudi added. The UAE has signed 38 Cepas with trading partners as it seeks to boost investment ties, expand its non-oil economic base and broaden exports. The Cepa programme is a key pillar of the UAE's foreign trade agenda, which aims to increase non-oil foreign trade to Dh4 trillion ($1.1 trillion) by 2031.

events.title: Oil prices jump 5% on Middle East tensions and US hurricane threat
events.summary: Global bond market sell-off continues and stocks fall amid reports White House has asked to see options for more strikes against Iran Oil prices have risen sharply amid fears about escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast. Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 5% to $105.3 a barrel on Thursday, triggering a wave of selling in the global bond and stock markets. In the UK, the yield – or interest rate – on the 10-year government bond hit its highest level since July 2007, rising by six basis points to 5.515%. Investors appear concerned that rising oil prices could stoke higher inflation. The yield on the 30-year bond – the UK’s benchmark cost for its long-term borrowing – rose by three basis points to 6.0117%, after touching 6.036% on Wednesday, the highest since January 1998. The climbing cost of government borrowing places further pressure on John Healey, as he prepares to deliver his first budget, on 28 October . The market swings came after the Atlantic reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to draw up options for strikes against Iran before the US midterm elections. The report cited unnamed officials in Donald Trump’s administration who said the size and targets of potential strikes, and whether they would go ahead, were still being debated. The report has weakened hopes that Trump will refrain from escalating the conflict with Iran before the midterm polls next month. A “limited operation” could be followed up with more substantial action after the midterms, it states. Another wave of strikes against Iran represents further risk to oil supply from the Middle East, with the US-Israeli war against Tehran now entering its eighth month. Attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz have reached their highest levels of ⁠the war, ⁠cutting ​traffic through the waterway and deepening fears about supply. The latest attack came ⁠on Wednesday, when a tanker was hit by projectiles off the north coast of Qatar , causing casualties, according to ​United Kingdom Maritime ‌Trade Operations. Oil prices also rose in response to a squeeze on production in the Gulf of Mexico, after Tropical Storm Isaias strengthened to become the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. Shell and Chevron said they were shutting down production as the storm approached the region, forecast to make landfall on Friday or Saturday. The Danish shipping group Maersk added to worries around rising energy prices on Thursday after it said it was increasing its emergency fuel surcharge on all its export collections and import deliveries. The rise in energy prices has fed fears about inflation, reinforcing expectations that central banks will have to raise their interest rates in order to control rising prices. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning A sell-off in global bond markets continued on Thursday. In France, which has been hit particularly hard over worries about its rising debt and growing spending , the 10-year yield rose by six basis points to 4.931%, just behind the 24-year high of 4.994% it hit last week. Yields rise when prices fall. The German 10-year yield, the benchmark for European debt, rose by two basis points to 3.504%. The yield on the US 10-year treasury, which is widely considered the best quality government debt on the market, rose by five basis points to 5.331%. Global stocks also fell, with Japan’s Nikkei share index falling 1.4% and the South Korean Kospi down 2.6%. In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, dropped 0.9%. The UK’s FTSE 100 slipped by 0.4% in early trading on Thursday.

events.title: AI bubble risks worst S&P 500 crash since 2008, strategist says
events.summary: Panmure Liberum’s Joachim Klement advises investors to develop contingency plans and timing tools that would help identify the start of a crash. Panmure Liberum’s Joachim Klement warns the AI trade may burst in 2027 or 2028, which could trigger the worst S&P 500 crash since 2008. He says rising debt costs, stubborn inflation and weaker cash flows could hit hyperscalers and cut the S&P 500 to 5,000, down 36% from current levels. Klement urges investors to prepare now, use crash timing tools, and turn “full defensive” if the S&P 500 falls below its 200-day moving average. LONDON – The head of market strategy at a London investment bank has a stark warning for investors: The artificial intelligence trade may soon be over in what could trigger the most severe market crash since the global financial crisis. Equities have powered to record levels across the globe in 2026, fuelled in part by optimism over surging spending on AI infrastructure. But Panmure Liberum’s Joachim Klement said his base case is for that trade to disintegrate as soon as 2027, sending stocks sharply lower. “My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement said in an interview. Hyperscalers’ free cash flows are largely depleted, while the cost of debt is rising quickly and becoming prohibitive for these firms, he said. Klement’s 2027 year-end target of 5,000 points for the S&P 500 implies 36% downside from current levels. That’s by far the most bearish of seven other strategists tracked by Bloomberg, who on average look for potential upside of 14%. Klement sees Europe’s Stoxx 600 falling to 430 points, more than 30% below current levels. Having been vindicated in taking a bullish stance on European equities in 2025, the strategist is among the first to call an end to the stock market’s current rally. As recently as mid-September, his key assumption was that the S&P 500 would hit 8,300 points by the end of 2027. The change of mind reflects Klement’s concern that stubborn inflation and an associated surge in the cost of borrowing needed to fund investment could derail the bonanza in AI-related infrastructure. That echoes a warning earlier in October from Temasek International’s chief investment officer Rohit Sipahimalani that a reversal of the AI trade is a key risk facing global markets. Data centre capital spending by hyperscalers in 2026 could more than double from 2025’s level to hit US$713 billion (S$914 billion), according to Bloomberg Intelligence estimates. That number is set to increase further in 2027, albeit at a slower pace, and has underpinned many of the projections for US tech companies’ projected earnings. “It is a situation where people are just focusing on one thing and one thing only, and that is earnings and in particular tech earnings,” said Klement, who started his career at UBS Group AG more than two decades ago. “And they excuse every macro, credit or whatever headwind that you can come up with with that story.” Citigroup strategists said that solid 2027 earnings can support further gains for global equities, despite higher interest rates and geopolitical risk. Klement acknowledges that his bearish call may be premature. The Stoxx 600 ended within striking distance of his above-average target in 2025, and he remains the most bullish among Bloomberg-tracked strategists for the Stoxx 600 until the end of 2026, predicting gains of about 10% in the regional benchmark. His outlook on US stocks for 2026 is also optimistic. “I’m starting to worry people today for something that I think might happen in six to nine months,” he said. Rather than advising clients to sell now, the strategist advises they develop contingency plans and timing tools that would help identify the start of a crash. His No. 1 recommendation is “to go full defensive” once the S&P 500 drops below the benchmark’s 200-day moving average, a technical indicator that averages the index’s closing price to help identify long-term market trends. In such a case, he advocates ultra-defensive sectors, including food, tobacco and pharmaceutical stocks. “What I tell people is now is the time to prepare,” Klement said. “Now is the time to make contingency plans for when the market goes into a bear market.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: How Massive Is Elon Musk’s Trillion-Dollar Fortune? Spend It Yourself
events.summary: On any given day, Elon Musk is worth about a trillion dollars . This does not mean that he has a trillion dollar bills sitting in an old-timey vault in a dusty basement somewhere; his wealth is mostly tied up in shares of SpaceX and Tesla . But if he were to cash those out, sell Neuralink and the Boring Company, and scrounge together some extra change, his checking account would hit 13 digits. “Trillionaire” is an easy enough word to say. It’s fun, even! Rolls off the tongue. But research has shown that the human brain has a very hard time comprehending the actual size and scope of large numbers. “Trillion” sounds like a short hop from “billion,” after all, even though it is in fact 1,000 times bigger. And even if you are somehow able to wrap your mind around that immense scale, it still feels abstract, no matter how many times you compare it to the area of Central Park or the weight of a fleet of trucks. Maybe a better way to visualize a trillion dollars, then, is through what you can actually buy with it. WIRED has partnered with Neal Agarwal, the proprietor of the consistently delightful website Neal.fun , to do just that. Spend Elon Musk’s Money is a new visualization that lets you, well, spend Elon Musk’s money, on anything from Big Macs to aircraft carriers to the Las Vegas Sphere . It keeps a tally as you go, so you can actually see how far a trillion dollars gets you these days, and it shows the items you’ve bought in a physical space. WIRED spoke with Agarwal about this new project, why it feels so relevant now, and the state of building things on the web. You can read that interview below, and waste a few hours on Spend Elon Musk’s money right here. This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length. WIRED: I’ve known about Neal.fun for a long time, I’m a big fan. But describe it for someone who’s never been there. Neal Agarwal: I never wanted to constrain the site to one thing, so it ended up being almost like a journal at this point. I’ve been running it since I was 19, and it’s kind of a catalog of everything I’m interested in: visualizations, science, weird game mechanics. For me, it’s mostly an exploration of what you can do with a website. Why is that important to you, the idea of exploring what a website is and means? If there’s one thing I know about you it’s that you love the web. Very much so. I grew up on the web; I was 8 years old on forums. I probably spent more time in Club Penguin than any real-world walls. I’m definitely a child of the web, and it’s interesting that I’m around the same age as it. It’s a privilege. Painters are working in a medium that’s a thousand years older, a million years older, so a lot of things have already been found out, been fleshed out. But on the web there’s so much that we haven’t figured out yet. I think there’s still a lot of new stuff to discover, and that’s really interesting to me. I think every medium has distinct things you can do with it. You can turn a book into a movie but it’s not quite the same. There are some things a book is always going to be better at, and vice versa. I think that’s true of the web too. This visualization we’re working on, you can’t print it in a newspaper. I suspect people might be familiar with some of your individual projects, if not your site itself. To list some off that are huge in my household: The Password Game , Space Elevator , The Deep Sea , Infinite Craft . When something goes viral, as so many of these have, what’s it like on your end? Is it almost boring now to see things blow up? I think each project has been very different. The ones that excite me the most now are where a lot of people play it and start doing things with it that I did not expect or intend. Within a few days of Infinite Craft launching, people started crafting Japanese words within the game. And they crafted enough Japanese words that they could play the whole game in Japanese. I’ve never released a game before where they unlocked a language. I had another one called Internet Road Trip; it’s like a simulated road trip but through Google Street View. A Discord formed around that, and people started backseat driving and arguing over which city to go to next, should they make a pit stop here so they can see this monument. People started birdwatching within that game. All these emergent things started happening, and I think the web is really good at that, too. It’s really good at forming communities out of the silliest things, which I find really exciting. There’s also this contrast with a more closed-off app environment; you don’t really work in apps as a medium. When I was a teenager I did make some apps, but I always really disliked that Apple and Google had to approve what I could put in them, and you have to wait a week for approval, and if they don’t like your app you have no recourse. So just the idea of having a homepage where it’s like, this is my homepage. Nobody can tell me what to do with it. I can put whatever I want.

events.title: UK’s ASOS says cyberhack accessed customers’ personal data
events.summary: ASOS said the hacker also had access to “certain non-personal account-related information”, but no payment card information or account passwords. - ASOS said a cyber breach exposed some customers’ names and contact details, but not payment card data or account passwords. - The hacker used social engineering to steal an employee login and access third-party platforms linked to ASOS. - ASOS locked the affected systems, said its website and app were safe, and is working with police and regulators. LONDON – British online fashion retailer ASOS said on Oct 8 that a cybersecurity breach earlier this week had exposed some customers’ personal information, including names and contact details, according to its initial investigation. It said the hacker also had access to “certain non-personal account-related information”, but no payment card information or account passwords, ASOS said in an e-mail to customers. “We discovered that an unauthorised party gained access to an ASOS employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log-in credentials,” ASOS said. “Those credentials were then used to access information on certain third-party platforms used by ASOS.” It said the affected platforms were immediately locked down, ensuring that no further information could be accessed, adding that the ASOS website and app were safe to use throughout, and remain safe to use. ASOS said it is working with the relevant law enforcement and regulatory authorities. So-called “social engineering” operations, where hackers impersonate workers to gain access to companies’ computer networks, are prevalent. British companies and institutions have been increasingly hit by aggressive and regular cyber and ransomware attacks in recent years. The British Library, a blood testing service, the London Underground, Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Jaguar Land Rover are some that have suffered months of disruption due to such breaches. REUTERS

events.title: Deeptech unicorn PhysicsX opens regional hub in S’pore to scale AI-powered industrial engineering
events.summary: PhysicsX CEO Jacomo Corbo said that having its Asia-Pacific hub in Singapore brings its technology closer to the organisations shaping the region’s industrial future. SINGAPORE – British deeptech AI software company PhysicsX opened its Asia-Pacific hub in Robinson Road, Singapore, on Oct 8. Founded by two former Formula 1 engineers in 2019, the firm develops AI models for manufacturing parts of jet engines and machines that make semiconductors. It alre ady has 20 employees in Singapore and aims to grow its local team to more than 100 over the next three years, including forward-deployed engineers, physics AI researchers and simulation engineers. A Temasek-led US$300 million (S$384 million) Series C funding round in June pushed PhysicsX’s valuation to US$2.4 billion. The company, which has seen rapid business growth in Europe and the US, aims to partner local public and private entities as it scales its presence across the region. PhysicsX said that the Singapore hub will bring its technology and engineering capabilities closer to customers and partners in the region. In Singapore, the scale-up and A*STAR have announced a $ 40 million five-year partnership to develop AI-powered engineering simulation capabilities that could help researchers and engineers explore and optimise complex designs and manufacturing processes more efficiently across a range of industrial domains. PhysicsX’s simulation platform has helped offshore energy engineering company Seatrium reduce the time required to optimise pipe-layout designs by about 40%. Speaking at the PhysicsX launch event at Temasek Shophouse, its chief executive officer and co-founder Jacomo Corbo said: “Some of the most consequential applications of AI over the coming decade will be in the physical world, helping us design better aircraft, chips, energy systems, vehicles and industrial infrastructure.” He added: “Singapore is an extraordinary place from which to build that future.” The Republic combines world-class advanced industry with a deep pool of technical talent, research excellence, long-term capital and a government with a clear ambition for AI. “Establishing our Asia-Pacific hub here brings our technology and people closer to the organisations shaping the region’s industrial future.” Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said Singapore aims to help leading companies move beyond isolated pilots to embed AI at the core of their operations, while redesigning jobs and upskilling their workforce. The National AI Missions initiative will drive transformation in four sectors – advanced manufacturing, connectivity, finance and healthcare – which together account for more than 40% of the Republic’s gross domestic product. That makes PhysicsX a natural partner for Singapore. “Our industrial strengths can help the company develop its technology further and scale up faster. In turn, its solutions can help our manufacturers build new capabilities, become more competitive and expand. “Their growth can create further opportunities for PhysicsX, while strengthening Singapore’s position as an advanced manufacturing hub,” said Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade). Temasek CEO Dilhan Pillay said that in engineering-intensive industries, designing and optimising design and production systems remain highly complex, requiring engineers to balance safety, cost and performance. Companies, even in Temasek’s own portfolio, face real operating challenges, from cost pressures and manpower constraints to energy efficiency, supply chain resilience and the need to innovate faster. “We believe AI applications can help address many of these challenges,” he said. Pillay said PhysicsX operates at the intersection of advanced AI and deep engineering expertise, applying frontier AI to help organisations simulate, optimise and improve complex physical systems. That makes the scale-up a compelling investment for Temasek. Temasek first invested in PhysicsX in its US$135 million Series B funding round in June 2025. Le e Wey Lii, Seatrium’s digital senior vice-president, said as industries navigate increasing complexity and demand greater efficiencies, AI-driven innovation has emerged as a strategic lever for the company’s growth. “We see opportunities to harness and scale physics-based AI across our business footprint – from engineering, procurement and construction delivery and next-generation product development to lifecycle services – augmenting human expertise, accelerating innovation and improving project outcomes for our global customers,” he sa id. events.title: 5 traders jailed for rigging key interest rates have their convictions quashed
events.summary: A British court has quashed the convictions of five traders accused of manipulating benchmark interest rates, in a scandal stemming from the 2008 financial crisis LONDON -- A British court on Wednesday quashed the convictions of five traders accused of manipulating benchmark interest rates in one of the biggest banking scandals to come out of the 2008 global financial crisis . The Court of Appeal threw out the fraud convictions of former Barclays employees Jonathan Mathew, Jay Merchant, Alex Pabon, Philippe Moryoussef and Colin Bermingham. The five were sentenced between 2016 and 2019 for offenses connected to influencing the London Inter-Bank Offered Rate, or Libor, and its euro currency equivalent Euribor. The rates were used to set the interest rates on trillions of dollars of financial products around the world. In July 2025, the U.K. Supreme Court quashed the convictions of two other traders: Tom Hayes, a former Citigroup and UBS trader, and Carlo Palombo, who worked for Barclays. It ruled that the convictions were unfair because the judges in their separate cases gave inaccurate instructions to jurors. Lawyers for the five others argued that juries in their cases received almost identical instructions and therefore “their trials were unfair and their convictions are unsafe.” The U.K.’s Serious Fraud Office said it would not seek retrials for Hayes and Palombo and did not oppose the five other defendants' appeals. Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Army to execute Fort Hood mass shooter by firing squad Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Libor and Euribor were critical benchmarks that were once used to set the interest rates on everything from business loans to home mortgages and credit card debt. They were based on figures submitted daily by major international banks, reporting the rate at which they could borrow money from other banks. During the financial crisis, regulators became aware that some banks were making artificially low Libor submissions to make their institutions seem more creditworthy, or submitting fake numbers to achieve a rate that better suited them. The Serious Fraud Office began investigating alleged efforts to manipulate Libor in 2012. That ultimately led to the conviction of nine bankers and the acquittal of 11 others. The rates were phased out in recent years, in part because they were seen as worsening the financial crisis. events.title: Supermarket shake-up: why Asda or Morrisons could vanish within a decade
events.summary: Talks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons have set industry tongues wagging, with analysts saying the market is ripe for change Tesco lifts profit forecast and says shoppers are resilient T hey may be two of the most recognisable brands in Britain, with a combined 188 years serving shoppers, but industry watchers agree that either Asda or Morrisons – or both – could disappear within a decade. This week, it emerged that Sainsbury’s and Morrisons – the UK’s second- and sixth-largest supermarket chains – had held merger talks between last November and February, before the larger player decided to walk away. News of the potential deal has relaunched speculation that the UK grocery market is now ripe for consolidation and revealed that the Sainsbury’s boss, Simon Roberts – who has been in post for six years – is at least willing to consider the possibility of buying one of his troubled rivals. Sainsbury’s, which has 600 supermarkets and almost 900 convenience stores, has until recently been seen as wary of trying to revive merger talks with its rivals after its bid to buy Asda for £7bn in 2019 was blocked . However, industry experts say Asda and Morrisons’ owners have held informal talks with each other – and both with Sainsbury’s team – and predict that talks could restart. “The three of them, one way or another, are talking to each other,” one said. He suggested that a combination of Asda and Morrisons could happen but was likely to be a weaker deal than a Sainsbury’s takeover of either, as both businesses struggle with costs and interest on debt piles. The industry has undergone significant change since the collapse of the Sainsbury’s-Asda deal. While riding the wider retail trends towards online shopping and convenience stores, the supermarket groups have been jockeying for market share. Aldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third-largest supermarket, with less than 1 percentage point separating them. Aldi is rapidly opening stores while Asda has struggled to find growth since a £6.8bn, debt-fuelled takeover in 2020 and heavy price competition from the discounters and from its bigger rivals Tesco and Sainsbury’s. Another big change could emerge this month when the UK’s competition watchdog is due to publish its final ruling on whether Aldi and Lidl should now officially be classified as “large grocery retailers” like Tesco , Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons. In August, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it had found provisionally that Aldi and Lidl no longer qualified as “limited assortment discounters” as they now carry a “full range” of groceries and operate stores larger than 1,000 sq m (10,700 sq ft) across the UK. The change means the German-owned discounters are now taken into account when assessing competition in different locations. This is the strongest hint yet that the CMA has changed its stance blocking the Sainsbury’s buyout of Asda on the basis that shoppers would be worse off. It also indicates that the CMA’s “balance of competition” – its estimation of the impact of a deal based on drive times for customers around stores – has shifted, meaning Sainsbury’s might have to dispose of dozens fewer stores to gain regulatory clearance for a merger. A figure of 150 was suggested when it tried to buy Asda. Clive Black, an analyst at Shore Capital and Sainsbury’s broker, says the CMA preliminary ruling indicates “the shape of the pitch has adjusted a little” and “the change encourages another chapter of consolidation”. It is a step-change from 2019 when analysts accused the singing former Sainsbury’s boss Mike Coupe and his board of directors of “arrogance” and “folly” for pursuing Asda. Now they say that consolidation is almost inevitable. That comes amid what is seen as a more welcoming regulatory environment backed by the UK government’s growth agenda combined with the appointment of Doug Gurr, a grocery industry veteran who has spent time at Asda and Amazon, to lead the CMA. One analyst described Sainsbury’s as the “kingmaker” in any industry consolidation as it uniquely has the resources to snap up a rival without the market dominance to immediately prevent any deal. Analysts agree it is unlikely to face significant competition if it opts to buy Morrisons or Asda – Tesco is too big to buy a rival , while Marks & Spencer and Waitrose appear unlikely to have the financial firepower or desire to pursue such a deal. Amazon should not be ruled out as a player in consolidation, according to one analyst, who said the online specialist might be prompted into action by any of the supermarkets announcing plans to merge. “The last cards are coming on to the table,” he said, suggesting that Amazon might consider buying Asda, Morrisons or even Sainsbury’s, now that it had effectively disposed of Argos which may have caused competition concerns for Amazon. However, Amazon has not fared well with its dip into high street retail.

events.title: StarHub to acquire MyRepublic’s mobile business amid ongoing telco consolidation
events.summary: The acquisition will have no impact on MyRepublic’s mobile service customers, who are being progressively migrated to StarHub’s network. StarHub will acquire MyRepublic’s mobile business and move its 4G customers from M1’s network to StarHub’s network. MyRepublic mobile customers will keep the brand, while StarHub gains both broadband and mobile businesses after buying broadband in August 2026. The deal supports telco consolidation in Singapore, as smaller players face falling revenue and stronger price competition, with StarHub calling for more scale to invest in networks. SINGAPORE – StarHub said on Oct 8 that it will acquire MyRepublic’s mobile business. The value of the transaction is not fixed, but is dependent on the total 4G and 5G MyRepublic mobile subscribers, average revenue per user (ARPU) of active 4G and 5G subscribers, as well as subscriber lifetime. The transaction is expected to be completed by April 30, 2027. In addition to the transaction value, a bonus cash amount of $1 million will be paid by StarHub when 25,000 subscribers migrate from MyRepublic’s network to StarHub’s network. An additional $1 million will be paid when 50,000 subscribers migrate to StarHub’s network by March 14, 2027. MyRepublic’s mobile business attained a net profit of $2.4 million for the 12 months ended June 30, with about 85,000 active subscribers. MyRepublic’s blended ARPU stood at $13 per month. This follows an earlier agreement between the two parties to migrate all of the mobile virtual network operator’s (MVNO) 4G mobile customers from M1’s network – which MyRepublic mobile ran on – to StarHub’s mobile network. “The acquisition brings together complementary strengths while preserving the distinct MyRepublic mobile brand and proposition for customers,” said StarHub in a bourse filing. StarHub will then own both MyRepublic’s broadband and mobile businesses, having acquired the broadband business in August 2026. As Singapore’s digital needs continue to grow, the acquisition will allow greater scale to be directed towards sustained network investment, service innovation and customer experience, StarHub noted. In a statement to The Straits Times on Oct 8, StarHub said: “MyRepublic Mobile will retain its brand and offerings, with customers continuing on their existing plans and services without disruption. “There will be no workforce reductions arising from the acquisition.” At an earnings briefing in August for the first half of 2026, StarHub chief executive Nikhil Eapen said he expects smaller MVNOs to be bought by larger players as the industry consolidates. “There’s a natural progression in which MVNOs will gravitate (around) and then be absorbed and adopted by the large, well-capitalised players,” he noted. Analysts have long pushed for a consolidation of Singapore’s telco industry amid falling mobile revenue and ARPU. Mobile service revenue for StarHub fell 10.5% year on year to $245.3 million in the first half of the year ended June 30, from $274.1 million. StarHub’s underlying net profit, excluding Ensign, fell 76.1% to $12.4 million, from $51.9 million the year before, said CGS International analyst Prem Jearajasingam. Singtel Singapore’s first-quarter operating revenue fell 3.1% year on year to $901 million, from $929 million. Singtel attributed the dip to “continued intense price competition”. StarHub, in particular, has been “driving consolidation”, said Eapen in August. In addition to the consolidation of MyRepublic’s mobile customers, StarHub recently migrated customers from MVNO redOne to its budget brand, eight. More recently in September, both StarHub and Keppel confirmed that they are in talks over a potential deal involving M1 . “With ongoing consolidation, we are bringing greater scale to invest more effectively in the networks, resilience and innovation that Singapore will increasingly depend on,” said Eapen. events.title: The fight to uncover the Nigerian president’s FBI files
events.summary: The News Nigeria’s president is locked in a fierce reelection battle — one that is not just playing out among voters ahead of January polls, but pitting teams of lawyers and lobbyists against a lone litigant half a world away in California. Remarkably, this latter-day David just won a significant victory over Goliath. For three years, Bola Tinubu has fought to keep old FBI records tied to a 1990s Chicago drug probe about him sealed, hiring US lawyers to support the Justice Department in the fight. His main adversary is not a political rival or a diaspora activist, however. It’s a Freedom of Information Act litigant in California with no apparent connection to Nigeria who says he just wants to get to the truth. Tinubu’s efforts to prevent disclosure have partly failed. In August, the FBI acknowledged for the first time that it holds an investigative file on him and alongside the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) has released hundreds of pages of partially redacted records. The fight now underway is over whether that is enough. On one side is Tinubu’s team of US attorneys, led by Chicago firm Henderson Parks. On the other is Aaron Greenspan, founder of legal document website PlainSite, who argues more documents should be released, with fewer redactions. The FBI declined to comment on this story. The DEA did not respond to requests for comment. Know More The case centers around an alleged heroin trafficking network run from Nigeria: A 1993 affidavit drafted by an Internal Revenue Service agent describes the scheme, and cites an associate of the narcotics-selling group as saying the network’s ringleader — allegedly Mueez Adegboyega Akande, a businessman who had returned to Nigeria in 1990 — directed its finances by phone and periodic US trips — and that Tinubu helped move money for him. In the 1990s, Nigerian rings often trafficked drugs from Southeast Asia to Chicago via couriers, according to the Justice Department . The Nigerian president has repeatedly denied wrongdoing. And his links to the case have been known and partially reported within Nigeria, often in the run-up to elections where opponents have used it to raise questions about his past. But the latest release — though unlikely to materially affect the results of the upcoming election — once again concentrates attention on Tinubu’s time in the US. A young Tinubu first arrived in Chicago in the 1970s to study accounting, graduating in 1979. By the time of the alleged scheme at the center of this case, he split time between Lagos and the US, having risen to treasurer at Mobil Oil Nigeria, and eventually winning a seat in Nigeria’s Senate — all while still opening bank accounts, and moving “large” amounts of money in the Chicago metro area, according to the IRS affidavit. Bank records cited show Tinubu went on to deposit nearly $1.9 million in Chicago-area accounts in 1990 and 1991. Tinubu’s then-employers at Mobil Oil told investigators his treasurer role did not involve moving large sums and that the company never authorized him to hold its funds personally. US authorities said that several of the transactions were linked to the alleged drug-trafficking ringleader Akande and seized roughly $460,000 from accounts tied to Tinubu in a 1993 civil forfeiture, alleging that the money was likely the laundered proceeds of drug dealing. Tinubu was not criminally charged, and the case was dismissed with prejudice after the money was forfeited. Tinubu’s US lawyers have argued that the latest files that Greenspan wants released are shielded by FOIA exemptions that protect against “an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy.” In a filing, the lawyers said that curiosity about a foreign leader’s background was not a FOIA-protected interest, and described Greenspan’s requests as driven by Nigerian politics rather than by an effort to expose US agency misconduct. They also said the records concern Tinubu’s life as a private “student” who “should retain his full privacy interests because he was not a public official in 1993.” However, Tinubu was not a student in 1993 — he had graduated over a decade earlier — and he was, in fact, a public official for most of that year, serving in Nigeria’s Senate until November. Greenspan protested the inaccuracies in subsequent filings, and Tinubu’s team later recanted the claims. In a statement to Semafor, Henderson Parks attorney Christopher Carmichael argued that commentary on the case had outpaced the facts: “Interested persons and parties are attempting to infer what they believe may be in undisclosed records, but that is speculation.” He said Tinubu’s team would not speculate on non-public records while the FOIA case was pending. Tinubu’s aides have long presented the 1993 case as a closed civil matter. In a July statement, presidential spokesman Bayo Onanuga called it “a civil forfeiture case from 1993 — a matter long settled, with no criminal conviction or finding of guilt ,” and added that the issue had been “thoroughly litigated, explained, and rendered moot” by Tinubu’s electoral victories. Representing himself, Greenspan said in an interview with Semafor that he had no personal or national stake in Nigerian politics and had kept his distance from partisans on both sides. He is not new to protracted fights with well-resourced opponents: A Los Angeles-area tech entrepreneur, Greenspan has spent years trading lawsuits with Elon Musk and Tesla, often alone and against larger legal teams. When a lobbyist for former Nigerian Vice President Atiku Abubakar — an electoral opponent of Tinubu — filed an amicus brief, Greenspan sought to make clear that the two were not working together. The case has been a political flashpoint in Nigeria for years, flaring up ahead of the 2023 election that brought Tinubu to office and again now with the 2027 vote fast approaching. An organization retained by the Nigerian government has targeted Greenspan online . Another of Tinubu’s main opponents called it “profoundly embarrassing” that Tinubu was asking a foreign court to withhold his records. Nonetheless, there are doubts about whether the matter is viewed as important by voters. Much like Tinubu’s presidential tenure, the campaign has been dominated by conversations around economic tumult and insecurity. “It is unlikely to impact [voters’] decision,” said Ebenezer Obadare, an analyst with the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington, “though the situation might change if a highly damaging piece of information unavailable previously were to suddenly turn up.” Notable One of Europe’s most wanted criminals is using close ties to Sierra Leone’s first family to transform the West African country into a hub for his drug dealing empire . Questions over Tinubu’s background persist, with critics citing educational records that have shifted from his initial campaigns to present day.

events.title: Republicans squirm as Latino support slips in South Texas
events.summary: Republicans are in a dogfight to defend the Latino gains that had them dreaming of a lasting political realignment just two years ago. Why it matters: Nowhere is that reversal of fortune more visible than in South Texas, where President Trump ran up historic numbers in 2024 — and Republicans redrew the map in 2025, assuming those Latino gains would last. Trump won 55% of Texas Latino voters in 2024 exit polls, carried 14 of the 18 counties within 20 miles of the border and won all four Rio Grande Valley counties. Polling shows Trump's disapproval ratings have skyrocketed among Latinos in Texas since 2024. Democrats and allied groups are now pouring money into races across the Rio Grande Valley. Zoom in: The reversal is starkest in TX-15, where Rep. Monica De La Cruz was one of the GOP's most visible symbols of its South Texas breakthrough. Trump would have carried the newly-drawn district by 18 percentage points in 2024. De La Cruz won her 2024 race under the previous map by 14 points. Cook Political Report moved the race from Lean Republican to Toss Up on Sept. 25, saying public and private polling shows the race tied or even favoring Tejano singer and Democrat Bobby Pulido . By the numbers: Democratic campaigns and allied groups are outspending Republican campaigns and groups on Spanish-language ads in two of the three competitive House districts covering the Rio Grande Valley, according to AdImpact data reported by the Texas Tribune . In TX-34, held by Vicente Gonzalez (D), Democratic campaigns and groups have spent $2.7 million on Spanish-language ads, compared with $1.6 million on the Republican side. In TX-15, Democratic groups have spent more than twice as much as Republican groups on Spanish-language ads. TX-28 bucks the trend: Republicans have narrowly outspent Democrats on Spanish-language ads to unseat Henry Cuellar (D). Zoom out: TX-34 is also a Toss Up, while TX-28 is Lean Democratic. The newly redrawn TX-35 has moved from Likely Republican to Lean Republican. House Majority PAC launched another round of ads Tuesday in TX-15, TX-28 and TX-34, defending two Democratic incumbents while continuing to target De La Cruz. The bottom line: A new NBC News/Telemundo poll shows Latinos nationally favor Democratic control of Congress 59%-35%, a 24-point advantage — roughly double the margin the same poll found for Democrats in 2024. A recent TelevisaUnivision poll found Latino voters in the three competitive Texas House districts shifting from a 44%-44% split in their 2024 presidential vote to 56%-36% Democratic on the 2026 congressional ballot.

events.title: Why we’re watching these climate tech companies
events.summary: This week, we released our 2026 version of our Climate Tech Companies to Watch list. It’s an annual project that the MIT Technology Review team puts together. Our goal is to highlight some of the promising, interesting advances and firms we think are worth paying attention to in the world of climate and energy technology. The list is always a little ray of hope for me—there are some fascinating ideas out there for changing how we power our world or moving away from fossil fuels to reduce the greenhouse-gas emissions that cause climate change.  Our chosen companies tend to reflect several aspects of the current moment. Here are some of the companies we picked and the key themes worth highlighting.  China is the center of the climate and energy tech world Forgive me—I know I’ve made this point before. Feel free to call me Captain Obvious. But I think China’s dominance in energy technology is a global trend that bears repeated mentioning.   China is home to the world’s largest grid, and renewables are coming online more quickly than I can wrap my head around. Contributing to that boom is Envision Energy , a renewables giant appearing on our list for the second time. The company has installed over 100 gigawatts of wind power worldwide, as well as over 50 gigawatt-hours of battery storage. Like many other Chinese companies right now, Envision is looking beyond the crowded Chinese market and setting its sights abroad, with projects in Germany, Brazil, and Australia and upcoming work in Vietnam. China is also leading innovation in key technologies. I’ve been fascinated by the potential for next-generation batteries coming out of its companies: All the big ones, along with a host of smaller ones, are racing to develop solid-state batteries. They could be both safer than existing EV batteries and longer in range. WeLion New Energy is particularly interesting. The battery company announced a big lab result last year, achieving 824 watt-hours per kilogram—more than three times the energy density of a standard lithium-ion battery today. Lab results in battery research are notoriously difficult to scale, but WeLion is also working to deploy semi-solid-state batteries, which could come to fruition faster than purely solid-state cells while still improving on lithium-ion’s performance. Everybody wants a piece of the data center pie We included just three companies from the US on the list, and two of them have received a major boost from Big Tech as companies look to power data centers. (The third, Brimstone , is leaning into another political hot topic, critical minerals.) Technologies that can provide consistent power are in high demand. Fervo Energy is bringing next-generation geothermal power to the grid by using horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to make it practical in more places. The company went public in May, raising $2.2 billion in its IPO, and plans to have a gigawatt’s worth of plants operational by the end of 2030. X-energy is building helium-cooled small modular nuclear reactors. The reactors’ small size lends flexibility, and the company is currently working on a 320-megawatt cluster of them in collaboration with Amazon in Richland, Washington. (For what it’s worth, I’m interested in what this technology could do for industrial facilities—the company has a deal with Dow that could see it deployed at one of the company’s chemical plants in the early 2030s.) The grid needs support, and energy storage will be a key piece moving forward I know, I know—I haven’t stopped talking about batteries since I started writing this newsletter four years ago. But the energy storage market has surpassed even my expectations over that time. And as solar and wind quickly come online, they need storage to help them meet more of the grid’s demand.  Form Energy is on the list for a third time for its iron-air batteries, which could enable cheaper long-duration energy storage. The company has a massive project in the works, to the tune of 30 gigawatt-hours, which will be used to help power a Google data center. It could be the world’s largest battery project in terms of capacity by the time it comes online, which is expected to happen in phases between 2028 and 2031. Taking another tack, Energy Dome is using compressed carbon dioxide to store energy on the grid. This technology is already cheaper than lithium-ion batteries for longer durations (think 10 hours or more), and the company is working to scale quickly. I covered the company in 2022 , before it had its first commercial plant running. Now it has plans for over 30 gigawatt-hours’ worth of plants around the world, including one with Google in Ireland that’s slated to come online in 2028. And Moment Energy is working to use the million EV batteries that are expected to reach the end of their life by 2030. The company has a facility in Vancouver, British Columbia, that repurposes used batteries for backup power. This year hasn’t been all sunshine and rainbows for climate tech. But I’m hopeful that some of the companies on this list, and the technologies they build, will keep nudging us in the right direction.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. events.title: Club Med, a Disney Cruise and an Exploding Starship: SpaceX Used Bystander Videos to Track Falling Debris
events.summary: Illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica. Source images: FAA report obtained by ProPublica, Eric Gay/AP. When SpaceX’s giant Starship rocket exploded over the Caribbean last year, the internet lit up with videos from airline passengers, island tourists and locals showing flaming debris shooting across the sky. Even some airline pilots recorded the fiery aftermath as planes scrambled to move out of its path . Some of those videos of Starship’s seventh test flight — including ones taken from Disney and Royal Caribbean cruise ships and a Club Med resort — went on to play a role in the company’s efforts to count and track pieces of debris after the explosion, a report obtained by ProPublica says. The report — obtained by ProPublica from the Federal Aviation Administration through a freedom of information request — shows video captured a fireball, then a shower of sparkling debris in the sky moments after the explosion. It includes maps pinpointing where the images were shot, which helped the company understand how debris tumbled to earth after the blast. “At 1 minute 42 seconds, the debris cloud is observed transiting behind the cruise ship,” says the report, which SpaceX provided the FAA two weeks after the so-called mishap. Such reports are required by federal rules in the days after a rocket failure and are supposed to describe what happened and where hazardous debris landed. The information is key for the FAA’s efforts to keep busy air traffic corridors safe at a time of rapid growth in the commercial space industry as companies like SpaceX develop and test rockets that they hope will eventually reach the moon and Mars. During launches, the FAA preventively closes airspace. It has also been forced to clear areas quickly after test flights of massive spacecraft went wrong. Starship flights 7 and 8 broke apart last year and scattered debris above airline traffic over the Caribbean. Before Flight 9, the FAA moved to greatly increase the size of the airspace it walled off pre-launch. The agency defined its no-fly zones, which are closed to airplane traffic during a launch, and its so-called debris response areas, which are closed after a mishap, using information from SpaceX and modeling from Space Force, the branch of the military that deals with the nation’s space interests, to predict where debris might fall. Nearly doubling those pre-launch no-fly zones “only makes sense if the prior margin was judged inadequate rather than just unlucky,” said Moriba Jah, a professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Texas at Austin. Read More “We’re Too Close to the Debris” Earlier this year, the FAA issued a warning that rocket launches could “significantly reduce safety” for airplanes, after ProPublica reported that 21 planes appeared to make sudden turns to exit or avoid an FAA-designated emergency no-fly zone in the minutes after the Flight 7 explosion. Such disruptions are likely to become more frequent. SpaceX is seeking to launch Starship up to 76 times a year from Cape Canaveral, Florida. The FAA provided ProPublica the reports on Starship flights 7, 8 and 9 — all of which involved mishaps — after we requested them under the Freedom of Information Act. The FAA redacted the vast majority of all three reports, citing, among other things, exemptions in the law that protect confidential business information from disclosure. The blackouts were, in part, a reflection of SpaceX’s objections; FAA allowed the company to challenge the release of information it deemed proprietary. The FAA refused to release information that would show SpaceX’s estimates of where debris fell during the three rocket failures. It’s unclear what the agency or the company knows about how close any airplanes came to falling debris. “Withholding the underlying debris estimates makes it impossible for anyone outside SpaceX and FAA to check whether that pattern is improving or repeating,” Jah said. “Given a regulator already revised its own safety margins once, the public has a real interest in seeing the data behind both the old margin and the new one.” The unredacted part of the report did not show whether the debris from the Flight 7 explosion fell where SpaceX and the FAA expected it to. But the references to Disney and Club Med guests’ video suggest SpaceX did not have a full picture of where the debris landed without them. “I would read it as evidence their own tracking did not carry cleanly through the debris cloud phase, so they used the public to fill the gap,” Jah said. A page from SpaceX’s report shows the company used public video, including from near a Disney cruise ship, to track debris from Starship Flight 7. Obtained by ProPublica. Redactions in original document. SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. The company has said that it learns from its mistakes and that each test improves Starship’s reliability. Last December, it said on X that “SpaceX is committed to responsibly using airspace during launches and reentries, prioritizing public safety to protect people on the ground, at sea, and in the air.” The FAA did not respond to a request for comment, nor did Disney, Royal Caribbean or Club Med. Ron Madler, a professor of aerospace engineering at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, said the videos could help SpaceX “either confirm their breakup models or possibly to improve them.” The mishap report for Flight 8, which rained debris near the Bahamas, said before that flight’s explosive failure, SpaceX did not have the proper “test stand” that was capable of testing the rocket’s engines “for a full Starship mission.” The remainder of the page was blacked out, so it was unclear from the report whether the company had found another way to fully test the engines before launch.  Flights 7 and 8 both involved the same model. Both ended in engine-related failures. Text in the report around the statement about the test stand was redacted. But Jah said it “means some part of the engine’s actual flight behavior was being verified for the first time in flight rather than on the ground.” John Crassidis, an aerospace engineering professor at the University at Buffalo, said launching before having a fully capable test stand was likely “a cost-saving decision.” In building rockets, he said, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has used both the old approach of launching and then fixing any issues that arise, and the newer approach of running simulations and ground tests first to head off problems. “Doing too much of the old school can lead to too many mishaps and cost overruns,” he said. “Doing too much of the new school leads to long times to get things done and a reduction in flexibility.” The post Club Med, a Disney Cruise and an Exploding Starship: SpaceX Used Bystander Videos to Track Falling Debris appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: NT government departments hit by massive network outage
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NT government departments hit by massive network outage affecting hospitals, police Topic: State and Territory Government Hospitals across the NT, including Royal Darwin Hospital, were affected by the outage. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) A wide-reaching network outage has affected the whole of the Northern Territory government today. Systems experienced intermittent interruptions, forcing services such as hospitals to initiate continuity plans, and the NT Police Force says three Triple Zero calls were missed. The NT government says it has identified the problem and that systems should be back to normal by this evening. A massive network outage interrupted all government departments in the Northern Territory today, affecting services from hospitals to police. The widespread, intermittent outage began about 3am and affected all government agencies, from education to housing, in both urban and remote areas. Earlier today, NT Police said the outage was not affecting Triple Zero (000) calls. However, this afternoon, Assistant Commissioner Terry Zhang said three Triple Zero calls had been missed. Terry Zhang says police were informed by Telstra of the three missed Triple Zero calls "very soon after". ( ABC News: Michael Franchi ) "Since the start of the outage … there have only been three phone calls that we couldn't answer in time that were referred to us very soon after that by Telstra," he said. "We have conducted follow-ups with all three of those missed telephone calls, and there have been no issues identified. "None of them were high risk or had any consequences; it was just routine police follow-ups." NT Police advised there had been interruptions to the police non-emergency line throughout the day. The NT government said the issue occurred inside a "core" IT gateway for NT government services. The outage impacted police services across the NT. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said the Territory-wide IT outage had caused "significant disruption to all of our IT networks". "We have mechanisms in place to continue with business as usual until we find the source, which will be subject to a serious inquiry," she said. Department of Corporate and Digital Development deputy chief executive Greg Connors said a team of up to 40 people had been working all day to isolate the cause of the outage. Mr Connors said workarounds had been implemented this afternoon and the systems were effectively back to normal. He also said the team believed it had identified the root cause and expected to resolve it this evening. Greg Connors says workarounds are now in place and the issue is expected to be resolved later today. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi ) "I can guarantee you this is not a cyber hack; this is something that is internal," he said. "It's a bit like getting in your car one day, and it goes, even though there have been no signs it was going to break down prior. "It is just one of those things that happens. We have found [the issue], which is great kudos to all my team that spent all day looking for it. "We are confident once we have fixed it, it will be back to normal." Mr Connors said the outage had a "widespread impact", including in hospitals, where staff had to initiate continuity plans. "Clinicians in hospitals would have experienced delays, [they] would have experienced not being able to get to services, not being able to get to impacted systems," he said. He said he could not rule out future outages, but said any that did occur would not be because of the same problem.

events.title: A partial building collapse in Istanbul kills 2 and traps at least 2 more
events.summary: A seven-story building in Istanbul has partially collapsed, killing two and trapping at least two other people ISTANBUL -- A seven-story building in Istanbul partially collapsed on Thursday, killing two people, officials said. Emergency crews were trying to reach at least two people that remained trapped inside. The reason for the collapse was not immediately known and an investigation was underway. Rescue teams were working to reach those trapped even as there were warnings of a further collapse of the building. The building’s three lower floors, including a ground-floor shop, caved in before dawn in the district of Maltepe, on the Asian side of Istanbul, a city that is bisected by the Bosporus Strait. Residents from the upper floors were safely evacuated while search teams rescued eight more people from the rubble. The rescuers recovered two bodies and were trying to reach two people still believed to be inside, according to the Istanbul governor's office. It was not immediately clear if the child was among those rescued. He warned that the building was at risk of further collapse, hampering the rescue efforts. Nearby buildings were also evacuated for safety, the governor said. Istanbul and other parts of Turkey are undergoing an urban transformation program that aims to replace old and earthquake-risky buildings with safer housing. events.title: New direct train services from London to Wrexham and Rochdale rejected
events.summary: Regulator also vetoes extra Blackpool service, citing lack of space on west coast mainline for new trains to capital Plans to run direct train services to Wrexham and Rochdale from London have been rejected by the rail regulator because of “significant pressure” on the line. The Office of Rail and Road said that there was insufficient space on the crowded west coast mainline to introduce the two new separate train services. It also vetoed plans for additional London-Blackpool train services wanted by Avanti. The ORR had last year knocked back plans for a new independent open access service linking Wrexham and the capital put forward by the Wrexham, Shropshire & Midlands Railway Company (WSMR). WSMR had submitted plans for a slightly less frequent service but the ORR said the new routes would still put the reliability of the wider railway at risk. The new service could have allowed Wrexham to capitalise further on the town’s Hollywood-meets-football mini-boom, fuelled by the Wrexham AFC co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney. Proposals for a new Lumo service between London and Rochdale, again slimmed down after being rejected in 2025, were once more rebuffed. The ORR also said Avanti could not add more Blackpool services from London. However, it did approve one extra London-Chester evening service from Avanti, which would otherwise have run as a “ghost train”, with crew and the rolling stock returning north to the depot overnight. The decision follows the outcry over the ORR’s initial ruling on a Manchester-London service which was barred from taking passengers last year. The regulator said its assessment, backed by external reviews, was that the “capacity and performance of the southern section of the west coast mainline has not materially changed since similar applications were rejected in 2025”. It said gaps in the current timetable were needed to provide important space for trains to recover when things went wrong, rather than escalating chaos. Stephanie Tobyn, ORR’s director of strategy, policy and reform, said: “New services, destinations and greater choice can bring real benefits for passengers and communities. But the west coast mainline is already under significant pressure, with performance reflecting limited resilience on a heavily used part of the rail network. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Our detailed analysis has shown that adding more trains to the current timetable would reduce the ability to recover when disruption occurs, increasing the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers.” Private operators such as First Group, owners of Lumo, have been looking to increase open-access routes as Labour has renationalised major rail contracts in the transition to Great British Railways. London-Wrexham direct trains briefly ran from London Marylebone from 2008 to 2011 as an open-access service but stopped owing to financial losses.

events.title: Bahrain F1 race in Malaysia delivers $108.1 million windfall to local micro SMEs
events.summary: Based on the success and economic spillover effect, Malaysia could benefit from international sporting events such as the G1 as a platform for SMEs to have wider opportunities and market access. Malaysia’s Bahrain F1 Grand Prix at Sepang brought over RM345 million in spillover effects for local micro, small and medium enterprises, said Minister Steven Sim. Almost half of the 261,000 spectators were foreign tourists, who spent more on hotels, food, transport, shopping and leisure. The government says big sports events can help SMEs grow by boosting tourism, local demand and links with larger firms and event organisers. KUALA LUMPUR – Local micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSME) reaped over RM345 million (S$108.1 million) in economic spillover effects of the Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix at Sepang International Circuit. Malaysia’s Entrepreneur Development and Cooperatives Minister Steven Sim added that almost half of the 261,000 spectators were foreign tourists. “The impact reflects the important role of large-scale international sporting events in stimulating economic activities, especially through the rise in tourism expenditure and demand for local goods and services. “The Bahrain F1 GP in Malaysia has had a very drastic impact on the SMEs, especially those in the hospitality, food and beverage, retail, transport, entertainment, tourism-related services and support industries,” he said in a statement on Oct 8. Those who attended the F1 race were projected to have spent 2.17 times more than ordinary events, he said, adding that foreign tourists usually spend more due to longer stays and expenditure spent for accommodation, food and beverages, transport, shopping and recreational activities. “This effort includes strengthening ties between SMEs and bigger industry players, event organisers, tourism operators and local suppliers so that the economic benefits generated by such large-scale events can be enjoyed by more small businesses,” he said.
